en: May Bhava—the moon made his crest-jewel, Vāsuki made his bracelet, and he who is skilled in the playful tāṇḍava dance—be for the welfare of the virtuous. 1.

Out of curiosity, and indeed constrained by my devotion to Rājīva, I shall clarify my own composition of kārikās—which is extremely concise due to its reliance on the expressions of ancient masters. (2)

Possessing real substances, strung with qualities, indicative of the virtuous deeds of the meritorious, eternally united with existence, generality, and particularity, and radiant with the excellence of non-existence—may this *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*, composed by Viśvanātha and resting upon the breast of Viṣṇu, long spread joy to the minds of those who employ sound reasoning. (3)

"Salutation to that Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, who is the thief of the silken garments of the cowherd maidens, and who is the seed of the great tree of worldly existence. With the words "nūtana...

and so forth, he composes this auspicious invocation at the beginning of the book for the purpose of instructing his disciples. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that auspiciousness is neither the cause of the destruction of obstacles nor the cause of successful completion? For we observe that even among atheists and others, there is the completion of works without obstacle despite the absence of such auspicious rites. To this, we reply: No.

Since the efficacy of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) is established by their being the object of the uncontradicted practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), and since, when there is a desire to know their fruit, it is improper to postulate an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) when an observed result (*dṛṣṭa*) is possible—and because completion (*samāpti*) is the most proximate candidate—it is concluded that completion itself is their fruit. Thus, even where no auspicious rite is observed, it is postulated as having occurred in a previous birth.

Furthermore, where completion is not observed despite the presence of auspicious rites (*maṅgala*), one should understand that there is either an exceedingly powerful obstacle (*vighna*) or an abundance of obstacles. It should be understood that it is precisely this [abundance] which serves as the cause for the removal of the more powerful obstacles. The ancients have said that the destruction of obstacles is the "door" (*dvāra*) through which the auspicious rite functions.

The moderns, however, hold that the fruit of *maṅgala* (auspicious rite) is solely the destruction of obstacles, whereas completion [of the work] results from a collection of causes such as intelligence, creative genius (*pratibhā*), and so forth. Nor should it be argued that this leads to the consequence of *maṅgala* being fruitless when performed by one who is naturally free from obstacles; for this is an accepted position, since the rite is performed out of apprehension of obstacles, and because such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭas*). Nor should it be argued that if it were fruitless, there would follow the invalidity of the Veda which teaches it; for the Veda teaches only the destruction of obstacles when they exist.

For this very reason, even though an expiation performed under the delusion that it was a sin may be fruitless, there is no lack of authority in the Veda that teaches it. Furthermore, auspiciousness (maṅgala) is the cause for the destruction of specific obstacles, and the recitation of the Vināyaka hymn and so forth is the cause for the destruction of specific obstacles.

In some cases, the absolute absence of obstacles (*vighnātyantābhāva*) alone is the means for completion, because it is precisely the absence of the connection with an obstructing factor (*pratibandhakasaṃsargābhāva*) that produces the effect. Thus, they say that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the works of atheists and others, since in those instances there exists either the destruction of demerit (*durita*) produced by auspicious rites (*maṅgala*) in a previous birth, or an absolute absence of obstacles established by its own nature.
Thus ends the discourse on auspiciousness.
Salutation to that Kṛṣṇa, the seed of the great tree of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
"Saṃsāre" means for the sake of the seed—that is, as the instrumental cause—for the tree that is transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) itself.

By this, the proof for the existence of God (*īśvara*) is also demonstrated. For instance, just as an effect such as a jar is produced by an agent, so too are [effects] such as the earth and the sprout. Since agency over these cannot possibly belong to beings such as ourselves, the existence of God is established by virtue of His being their creator.

Nor should it be argued that there is a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on the fact that [the world] is not produced from a body, which would prove that it is not produced by an agent; for that reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). For me, however, the favorable logical reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) is precisely the causal relationship between "being an agent" and "being an effect. Furthermore, scriptural authorities (*āgama*) such as, "The one God, generating heaven and earth, is the maker of all and the protector of the world," should also be taken into account. || 1 ||
Thus concludes the inference for the existence of God (Īśvarānumāna).
Substance, quality, action, generality along with particularity, inherence, and non-existence—these are proclaimed as the seven categories. || 2 ||

Regarding the term "substance" (*dravya*): here, by the very statement that the seventh category is non-existence (*abhāvatva*), it follows that the other six possess existence (*bhāvatva*). Therefore, they were not mentioned separately as "existence. These categories are well-known in the Vaiśeṣika system and are not contradictory to the Naiyāyikas. This has been established in the Bhāṣya as well. For this very reason, in the *Upamānacintāmaṇi*, the status of power (*śakti*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and so forth as distinct categories was raised, on the grounds that they are different from the seven categories.

But how can these alone be the categories? For power (*śakti*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and so forth are also distinct categories. To illustrate: when fire is conjoined with a jewel (*maṇi*) or the like, burning is not produced; however, when it is devoid of such things, burning is produced. In that case, it is postulated that the power conducive to burning in the fire is destroyed by the jewel and the like, and is produced again by a catalyst (*uttejaka*) or by the removal of the jewel and the like.

If it is argued that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is likewise a distinct category (*padārtha*), because it is not included among the six positive categories (*bhāva*)—since it exists even in universals (*sāmānya*), as the cognition of similarity arises from such instances as "just as cowness is eternal, so too is horseness"—and because it is not included among absences (*abhāva*), since it is perceived as being existent (*sat*), [we reply: no.

It is postulated that either fire and so forth as qualified by the absence of a jewel and other such factors are the cause of burning and so forth, or rather, the absence of the jewel itself is the cause independently. Since this alone suffices, it is improper to postulate an infinite number of potencies (*śakti*), their prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and their destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). Nor should it be asked: "If an excitant (*uttejaka*) is present, how can there be burning even when the inhibitor (*pratibandhaka*) exists?
For the cause is the absence of the jewel as qualified by the absence of the excitant.
Furthermore, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is not a distinct category of entity; rather, it is the possession of many common attributes while being different from that [object].
For example, the similarity of the face to the moon consists in its possessing qualities such as the power to delight, which reside in the moon, while being distinct from the moon itself. ||1||
Thus ends the treatise on the enumeration of categories.
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, the embodied self, and mind—these are the substances.

He classifies the substances with the words "earth, etc. Here, *kṣiti* means earth; *āpaḥ* means waters; *tejaḥ* means fire; *vāyuḥ* means air or *marut*; *vyoma* means ether or *ākāśa*; *kālaḥ* means time or *samaya*; *dik* means space or *āśā*; *dehī* means the embodied self or *ātman*; and *manaḥ* is the mind. The meaning is that these nine are the substances (*dravyāṇi*).

If it is asked: "What is the proof for the universal *dravyatva* (substance-ness)? For there is no perception as a means of knowledge regarding it, since substance-ness is not apprehended in things such as clarified butter or lac"—we reply: No. The universal *dravyatva* is established by virtue of being the delimiting property (*avacchedaka*) of the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of an effect, or by virtue of being the delimiting property of the inherent causality of conjunction or disjunction.

[Objection: Why has darkness (*tamas*) not been stated as the tenth substance? For it is perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, because it possesses color and possesses action, it must be a substance. Since it is devoid of odor, it is not earth; and since it possesses a blue color, it is not water or the other [elements]. Furthermore, in the perception of that [darkness], the eye is the cause independently of light. [Reply: No. Since its existence is established by the necessary absence of light (*tejo'bhāva*), it is improper to postulate another substance. The cognition of its possessing color is merely an error (*bhrānti*). Likewise, the cognition of its possessing action is also simply an illusion conditioned by the removal of light.

If darkness were a substance distinct [from light], there would be the cumbersome necessity of postulating infinite constituent parts and so forth; how gold is included within fire will be explained later. (2)
Thus ends the section on the classification of substances.
Now, the qualities (guṇas) are color, taste, and smell; after that [comes touch]. || 3 ||

He divides the qualities: "Now, the qualities. These qualities number twenty-four; they have been explicitly shown by Kaṇāda and indicated by the word "and" (ca). Among them, the establishment of the universal "quality-ness" (guṇatva) will be explained later. Thus ends the section on the division of qualities.
Tangibility, number, dimension, and separateness; after that, conjunction and disjunction, as well as priority and posteriority. (4)
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impressions, unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), and sound alone [are the qualities of the self]. ||5||
Throwing upward, then throwing downward, as well as contraction,
extension, and locomotion— these are the five types of action.
He classifies actions as follows: "Throwing upward," and so forth: Action-ness [is common to] throwing upward, whirling, contracting, flowing, ascending, and blazing;
even oblique motion is included here under the very category of "going. (7)
The genus (jāti), however, is established by perception; the same applies to [the universals] such as "throwing upwards-ness" (utkṣepaṇatva) and so forth. //6//

Now, one might ask: why are actions such as *bhramaṇa* (whirling) not mentioned separately as additional [actions]? To this he says: "Whirling" (*bhramaṇam*), etc. || 7 || Thus ends the section on the classification of the category of action (*karmapadārtha*).
Generality is said to be of two kinds: the higher (para) and the lower (apara). Existence (sattā), which subsists in the triad beginning with substance (dravya), is called the higher generality. (8)

He defines the universal (*sāmānya*)—namely, "the universal. Its definition, however, is: being inherent in many (*anekasamavetatva*) while being eternal (*nityatva*). Since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other categories also possess the quality of being inherent in many, he says "while being eternal. Since the mere state of being inherent while being eternal also applies to the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of space (*gagana*) and so forth, he specifies "in many. Since the state of existing in many while being eternal also applies to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), he avoids the general term "existence" (*vṛttitva*) and instead uses "inherent" (*samaveta*). A universal, moreover, does not subsist in only a single individual. Thus it has been said:
"Non-difference of individuals, equality, confusion, infinite regress, loss of form, and lack of relation— this is the summary of the factors that invalidate a universal (jāti).
Furthermore, a universal that is distinct from another [higher] universal is itself called "lower" (apara).
The genus such as substantiality (dravyatva) and so forth is described as being both higher and lower. || 9 ||

Remoteness (*paratva*) is the state of existing in a greater number of locations; nearness (*aparatva*) is the state of existing in a smaller number of locations. Existence (*sattā*) is remote because it exists in a greater number of locations than all other universals (*jāti*); consequently, all other universals are near in relation to it. Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is remote because it is more pervasive than earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like, as it exists in a greater number of locations; however, it is near in relation to existence, as it exists in a smaller number of locations and is thus less pervasive. || 7-8-6 ||
Thus concludes the general definition.

Because it is pervasive, it is also "para" (distant); because it is delimited, it is also "apara" (near). The ultimate particular (antyaviśeṣa), which resides in eternal substances, is thus proclaimed. (10)

He defines *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity) with the words "the last" (*antya*). That which exists at the end, at the limit, is "the last"; the meaning is that there is no [particularity] beyond it. For objects such as jars down to binary atoms, their mutual distinction arises from the difference between their respective constituent parts;

however, for atoms, the *viśeṣa* alone is the means of establishing their mutual distinction, and that [particularity] is itself inherently distinct. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no requirement for another *viśeṣa* in that case. || 10 ||
Thus ends the determination of the particular.

The relation of jars and the like to their shards, of substances to qualities and actions, and of universals to those [substances, qualities, and actions], is proclaimed to be inherence (samavāya). ||11||

He demonstrates inherence (samavāya) with the words "of jars and so forth. That relation which exists between part and whole, genus and individual, quality and possessor of quality, action and actor, and eternal substance and its particularity, is inherence.

Inherence (*samavāyatva*) is the state of being an eternal relation. The proof for this is as follows: the cognition of a qualified object, such as "a quality-possessor" or "an action-possessor," has as its object the relation between the qualifier and the qualified, because it is a qualified cognition, just like the qualified cognition "the man with a staff. Since this inference excludes other relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence is established. Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of a relation of essential nature (*svarūpasambandha*), nor the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*). For it would be more cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate an infinite number of essential natures as relations; therefore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), a single inherence is established.

Nor does it follow that if inherence (*samavāya*) were one, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving color in air; for although the inherence of color exists there, color itself is absent.

Nor should it be argued that, by this same logic, a further relation called "specific relation" (*vaiśiṣṭya*) must be established even for absence (*abhāva*); for if that were eternal, the cognition of the absence of a jar would necessarily arise on the ground even after a jar has been brought there, since the absence of the jar would still exist there.

And because that [relation] is eternal, otherwise there would be no cognition of the absence of a jar even in another location; for the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) exists there as well. For me, however, in the state when a jar has been baked red, there is no cognition of its possessing the dark color, because that dark color has perished. If the relation of qualification were non-eternal, then the assumption of an infinite number of such relations would result in a greater complexity for you alone. Thus, the respective locations, such as the ground, at their respective times, are themselves the relations of those respective absences. ||11||
Thus concludes the exposition on inherence.

Non-existence (abhāva), however, is twofold, due to the distinction between relational non-existence (saṃsargābhāva) and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva). [The author] analyzes non-existence with the words "Non-existence, however... Non-existence-ness (abhāvatva) consists in possessing the mutual non-existence that is distinct from the six categories beginning with substance (dravya). Regarding the phrase "relational...": the meaning is "due to the distinction between relational non-existence and mutual non-existence. Since mutual non-existence is of only one kind and thus lacks internal subdivisions, [the author] analyzes relational non-existence with the words "Prior non-existence (prāgabhāva)... Relational non-existence-ness consists in being a non-existence distinct from mutual non-existence. Mutual non-existence-ness consists in being a non-existence whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the relation of identity (tādātmya).

The state of being an antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*) is the state of being an absence that has not yet come into existence. The state of being a destructive absence (*dhvaṃsa*) is the state of being an absence produced by an event. The state of being an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) is the state of being an eternal relational absence. However, in cases where a jar or the like has been removed from a surface such as the ground and then brought back again, the cognition of an absolute absence arises because [the absence] does not constitute a relation with the time of the jar; thus, even though it is eternal, there is no absolute absence of the jar at the time the jar is present. Regarding this, some maintain that this is a fourth type of absence, characterized by arising and destruction.

Regarding this, the view of the ancients (*prācām matam*) is that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) does not reside in the locus of either destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, the cognitions "redness does not exist in the black pot" and "blackness does not exist in the red pot" apprehend prior non-existence and destruction respectively, but not their absolute non-existence, because of the mutual contradiction between those two. However, the moderns (*navyās tu*) say that since there is no evidence for such a contradiction, absolute non-existence exists even at the time delimited by destruction and so forth.
Prior non-existence, as well as destruction, is indeed nothing other than absolute non-existence. (12)
Thus, non-existence through relation (saṃsargābhāva) is held to be of three kinds;
furthermore, the common properties (sādharmya) of all seven categories, such as being knowable and so forth, are now stated. (13)

If it is argued that non-existences may indeed consist of their locus because of parsimony (*lāghava*), we say no; for the postulation of a distinct entity is simpler than the postulation of an infinite number of loci. Furthermore, in this way, the relationship between the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) is also established.

In this way, the perceptibility of various absences—such as the absence of sound, taste, smell, and so forth—is also established. Otherwise, since their respective substrates would not be graspable by those respective sense organs, they would lack perceptibility. By this, the view that absolute non-existence consists of specific cognitions, specific times, and so on, is refuted, because it would result in its being imperceptible. Thus ends the section on the classification of the category of non-existence (abhāva).

Now he begins to state the similarities (*sādharmya*) and differences (*vaidharmya*) of the categories—starting with the words "of the seven. Those which possess a common property (*samāna-dharma*) are *sadharmāṇaḥ*; their state is *sādharmya*. The resulting meaning is: "a common property. Similarly, those which possess a contrary property (*viruddha-dharma*) are *vidharmāṇaḥ*; their state is *vaidharmya*. The resulting meaning is: "a contrary property. Knowability (*jñeyatva*) is the status of being an object of cognition; and that exists everywhere, because the status of being an object of God’s cognition is a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayin*).
The five categories beginning with substance (dravya) are multiple and inhering;
in the same way, being denotable, being knowable, and so forth, should be understood. ||13||
Thus ends the exposition of the similarities among the seven categories.

Regarding the phrase "substance and so forth": the common property (*sādharmya*) of substance, quality, action, generality, and particularity is plurality (*anekatva*) and inherence (*samavāyitva*). Although plurality exists even in non-existence (*abhāva*), nevertheless, being existent (*bhāvatva*) while possessing plurality is the common property of these five;

thus, the resulting meaning is "the state of possessing a category-delimiting attribute (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) that resides in multiple existents. By this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in individual instances such as a jar or space.

And "being an inherent cause" (samavāyitva) means being related by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya-sambandha), but not possessing inherence itself, because [the latter] is absent in universals (sāmānya) and so forth. Thus ends the statement on the common properties (sādharmya) of the five categories.
The first three possess existence (sattā), while the [category] beginning with quality (guṇa) is devoid of qualities and action.
"Endowed with existence" means that substances, qualities, and actions possess existence (*sattā*).
Thus ends the explanation of the similarity among the first three categories.

Regarding the phrase "guṇādi" (beginning with quality): although the mere absence of quality and action is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) in the case of a jar and the like at the first moment of its existence, and the absence of action is over-extensive in the case of space and the like, nevertheless, the intended meaning is "the state of possessing a property that does not subsist in that which possesses quality," and "the state of possessing a category-delimiting attribute (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) that does not subsist in that which possesses action. For neither jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) nor substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth fail to subsist in that which possesses quality or that which possesses action; rather, it is quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and the like that do so. Furthermore, space-ness (*ākāśatva*) and the like are not category-delimiting attributes. ||14||
Thus ends the exposition on the similarities among the six categories, beginning with qualities.
All [categories] beginning with "birth" (jāti) are considered to be devoid of universals (sāmānya).
It has been stated that for all things except spherical dimension (pārimāṇḍalya), causality is established. (15)
Regarding the term "sāmānya": the meaning is that universals and so forth do not have a common substratum (sāmānyānadhikaraṇatva).
Thus concludes the exposition of the similarities among the four categories, beginning with generality (sāmānya).

Regarding the term "pārimāṇḍalya": *pārimāṇḍalya* means atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). The meaning is that causality belongs to things other than that [atomic dimension]. Atomic dimension, however, is not the cause of anything. For it would have to be the originator of the dimension of a substance commenced by its own substratum; and that is not possible. This is because of the rule that a dimension necessarily produces a dimension of its own kind that is equal to or greater than itself; for if it were produced from an atom, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of it being even more minute, just as a large object commenced by large parts is larger still. In this same way, the ultimate large dimension (*paramamahatparimāṇa*), the supersensible universal (*atīndriyasāmānya*), and the particulars (*viśeṣas*) are to be understood.

This [statement] was also said with the intention that the object is not a cause even in the case of yogic perception; that a universal (sāmānya) being known is not a means of proximity (pratyāsatti); and that a logical mark (liṅga) being known is not the instrument of inference. Others hold that the teacher’s intention is that even the supreme magnitude (paramamahat-parimāṇa) of ether and so forth—which is a cause in the case of mental perception of the self—is not a cause [in the case of yogic perception]. That is not correct, because the teachers have stated that the lack of causality applies only to things other than cognition itself. ||15||
Thus concludes the exposition on the common characteristics of categories distinct from atomicity (*pārimāṇḍalya*).
Now, what is this causality? To this he says: "anyathāsiddhi" [and so forth]. Of that [causality]... ||16-17||
Thus concludes the investigation into the nature of incidental causality.
The state of being a cause belongs to that which possesses an invariable antecedence devoid of any other way of being established (anyathāsiddhi); its threefold nature has been proclaimed. (16)
The nature of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva) should be known, as well as the nature of being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyihetutva);
likewise, the third, the nature of being an efficient cause (nimittahetutva), has been stated by those who know the system of Nyāya. || 17 ||

That in which the effect inheres should be known as the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa). That which is proximate to it and productive is the second [non-inherent cause]; beyond these two would be the third [the efficient cause]. || 18 ||

Regarding this: the meaning is that a cause proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the second [type of] cause, namely the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Although, in this context, the conjunction of the shuttle and the threads would be the non-inherent cause of the cloth, and velocity (*vega*) and so forth would be the non-inherent causes of impact (*abhighāta*) and so forth, and likewise cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth would be the non-inherent causes of desire (*icchā*) and so forth—nevertheless, in the definition of the non-inherent cause of a cloth, the qualification "distinct from the conjunction of the shuttle and the threads" must be included.

The conjunction of the shuttle threads is indeed the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to the conjunction of the shuttle-cloth; likewise, velocity and so forth are also indeed the non-inherent causes of velocity, motion, and so on. Therefore, in the definition of the non-inherent cause of each respective effect, the qualification "being distinct from those [specific effects]" must be included. However, the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self never function as non-inherent causes anywhere. Consequently, the qualification "being distinct from those" must certainly be included in the general definition.

In this context, that which is proximate to the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is of two kinds: by way of proximity through a single object with the effect, and by way of proximity through a single object with the cause. The first is, for example, the conjunction of the potsherds and so forth, which is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a jar and the like; in that case, there is a proximity of the cause, namely the conjunction, with the effect, the jar, in a single potsherd. The second is, for example, the color of the potsherds, which is the non-inherent cause with respect to the color of the jar.

The pot is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to its own color and so forth; there is a proximity between the color of the potsherd and that [color] within a single potsherd. Thus, the resulting meaning is that [proximity] occurs sometimes by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and sometimes by way of the relation of "inhering in that which inheres in itself" (*svasamavāyisamavetatva*). And in this way, the general definition is established: an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) is a cause distinct from knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth, which is proximate to the inherent cause through either the relation of "residing in the same object as the effect" (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*) or the relation of "residing in the same object as the cause" (*kāraṇaikārthasamavāya*). Thus ends the determination of the nature of the non-inherent cause.

"From these two"—meaning from the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*)—"another," that is, a distinct cause, "the third," meaning the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Thus ends the determination of the nature of the efficient cause. [That which has a prior existence] either together with [the effect], or of which there is a prior existence by taking the cause as its reference.

Now, [the author] states how many [factors] possess "establishment otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhatva*): "By which... The meaning is that the form by which the antecedence of a cause with respect to an effect is apprehended—that form is "established otherwise" with respect to that effect. For example, the "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) with respect to a jar. This concludes the definition of the first type of establishment otherwise.

He states the second type of "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) with the words "the cause" (*kāraṇam*). That for which there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) independently, but rather whose concomitance is apprehended only by taking the cause into account, is "established otherwise. For example, the color of a staff (*daṇḍarūpa*).
Thus ends the definition of the second type of "established otherwise."
When priority with respect to another has been known, that which is the cognition of its prior existence [is the cause]. (19)

He states the third [type of superfluous cause]: "with respect to another. That which has its priority (pūrvavṛttitva) with respect to a certain effect grasped only after its priority with respect to another [effect] has been grasped, is superfluous (anyathāsiddha) with respect to that effect. For example, consider the ether (ākāśa) with respect to a jar and the like. Its causality with respect to the jar and the like would exist only by virtue of being ether; for that [ether-ness] is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of sound. Thus, its status as a producer with respect to the jar and the like can only be grasped after its causality with respect to sound has been grasped; therefore, it is superfluous.

If it is asked, "In that case, what constitutes the 'otherwise-established' (*anyathāsiddhi*) nature of space as a cause by virtue of being the substratum of sound?", take it to be the ablative case (*pañcamī*). If it is further asked, "What is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for ether's status as a generator of sound?", it is its possession of the quality of sound (*śabdatva*) and so forth, or else the category of particularity (*viśeṣa*). Thus ends the determination of the third type of otherwise-established cause.
[That which] is not apprehended as having a prior existence relative to the generator [of an effect]...
Furthermore, whatever may be in excess of that which is necessarily and invariably antecedent [to the effect], [is redundant]. || 20 ||

He states the fourth type of *anyathāsiddha* (redundant causality) as follows: "With respect to the producer" (*janakaṃ prati*). When the antecedence of one thing with respect to a certain effect is apprehended only after its antecedence with respect to the producer of that effect has been apprehended, then that thing is *anyathāsiddha* with respect to that effect. For example, the father of a potter with respect to a jar. For his being a producer of the jar by virtue of being the potter’s father is a case of *anyathāsiddhi*; however, if he were a producer by virtue of being a potter, there would be no objection, since any potter whatsoever is a producer of a jar.
Thus ends the definition of the fourth *anyathāsiddha*.

He states the fifth type of "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*) with the words "the redundant" (*atiriktam*). The meaning is that when an effect can be accounted for by something already necessarily established as an invariable antecedent, anything other than that is "otherwise established. For this very reason, in the case of perception, "largeness" (*mahattva*) is the cause, while "possessing multiple substances" (*anekadravyavattva*) is otherwise established; for in that case, largeness is necessarily established, and thus possessing multiple substances is otherwise established. Nor should it be asked what the deciding factor is against the reverse being the case, because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in taking the universal "largeness-ness" (*mahattvatva-jāti*) as the delimiting condition of causality. (20–21)
These five are [examples of] otherwise-established (anyathāsiddha); the first is the nature of a staff (daṇḍatva) and so forth;
the second is also shown as the color and other qualities of the staff in relation to a jar.
The third would be space (ākāśa), another is the potter's father, and the fifth would be the donkey and so forth; among these, however, that [the donkey] is indispensable.

Regarding the term "donkey" (*rāsabha*): although a donkey has the property of being an invariably antecedent (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) to some particular individual jar, nevertheless, since that individual jar can also be produced by means of the staff and other factors whose causal status as producers of jars of that class is already established, the donkey is "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*). This is the sense. Among these five types of otherwise-established factors, the fifth type of otherwise-established factor is necessary, because by it alone the others are rendered superfluous.

For instance: when an effect can be accounted for by means such as a staff, which are necessarily established as its invariable antecedents, the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth is "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddha*). Nor should it be asked what the decisive factor (*vinigamaka*) is against the reverse case; for if the property of being a staff were the cause, one would have to postulate a complex relation consisting of a chain involving the staff, which results in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
In this same way, the status of other [supposed causes] is also resolved by this very principle. ||22||
Thus concludes the exposition of the five kinds of non-establishment (*asiddha*).
It should be understood that the state of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva) belongs to substance alone;
furthermore, the state of being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyihetutva) is to be known as residing only in qualities and actions. (23)
"Inherent" (samavāyī) is clear.

Regarding "quality" (guṇa): the intended meaning is that being an non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇatva) is a specific property (vaidharmya) of things distinct from qualities and actions, rather than a common property (sādharmya) shared by qualities and actions themselves.

Alternatively, its meaning is the possession of a genus (jāti) distinct from existence (sattā) that resides in non-inherent causes. By this, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) even for cognitions and the like, despite their absence of being non-inherent causes. ||23||
"Except for eternal substances, being dependent is what is stated here.
This concludes the statement of the two points of similarity consisting in the nature of being inherent and non-inherent causes.

Regarding the phrase "elsewhere": the meaning is that, setting aside eternal substances—such as atoms, space, and so forth—the property of being dependent (*āśritatva*) constitutes their common characteristic (*sādharmya*). Dependence, moreover, consists in having existence (*vṛttimatva*) through relations such as inherence (*samavāya*); however, even eternal things exist in time and the like by way of qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*). Thus ends the statement of the common characteristics of those things other than eternal substances.
For the nine [categories] beginning with earth, however, there is substantiality (dravyatva) and the possession of qualities (guṇa). (14)

Now he begins to state specifically the similarity (*sādharmya*) of substance alone—starting with "of earth and so forth. This is clear. (24) Thus ends the statement on the similarity of substances in general.

Earth, water, fire, air, and mind as well. Regarding "earth": the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth, water, fire, air, and mind are the possession of priority and posteriority (*paratvāparatva*), corporeality (*mūrtatva*), possession of velocity (*vega*), and possession of action (*karma*). It should not be argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases such as a jar where priority or posteriority has not been produced; for what is intended [by the definition] is the possession of a genus (*jāti*) subordinate to substancehood (*dravyatva*) which resides in the same locus as priority and so forth. Corporeality (*mūrtatva*) is the possession of a limited dimension (*parimāṇa*); and this belongs only to these [five], because the dimension of space (*ākāśa*) and the rest cannot be limited by anything.

As before, "possessing action" (*karmavattva*) should be understood as the state of possessing a genus (*jāti*) that is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and is co-located with action; and "possessing velocity" (*vegavattva*) should be understood as the state of possessing a genus that is pervaded by substanceness and resides in that which possesses velocity. (25) Thus ends the statement of the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth, water, fire, air, and mind.
These—priority and posteriority, corporeality, action, and velocity—are the substrata [of these qualities]. (25)
Time, space, self, and direction possess omnipresence and supreme magnitude.

Regarding "time": time, space, self, and direction possess omnipresence. Omnipresence is the state of being conjoined with all corporeal objects, as is supreme magnitude. Supreme magnitude is a specific genus, or alternatively, it is the possession of a dimension that does not admit of further diminution.
Thus concludes the statement on the common properties of time, space, self, and direction.
The five elements, beginning with earth, indeed consist of four that possess tangibility.

Regarding the phrase "earth and so forth": the nature of being an element (*bhūtatva*) belongs to earth, water, fire, air, and ether. This consists in possessing a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that is perceptible by an external sense organ. Here, "perceptibility" should be understood as the capacity for ordinary (*laukika*) perception. By this definition, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the self (*ātman*), which possesses knowledge, because in the perception "the jar is known," knowledge is merely an object of presentation (*upanītabhāna*). Nor is there non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in atoms and the like, which possess color and other qualities that are not objects of ordinary perception, since they too possess the capacity for perception in their own nature.

Furthermore, it is not perceptible because of the absence of other causes characterized by magnitude (*mahattva*). Alternatively, its nature consists in possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that do not reside in the self (*ātman*).
Thus ends the statement on the common properties of earth, water, fire, air, and space. Regarding the phrase "four [are tangible]": earth, water, fire, and air possess tangibility.

Regarding "the origination of substance": the quality of being the originator of a substance belongs to the four—earth, water, fire, and air. Nor is there an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in the case of jars and the like, which do not originate other substances; for what is intended is the possession of a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a substance.
Thus ends the statement of the common properties of earth, water, fire, and air.

Now, regarding "ākāśa" (space): the meaning is that the common characteristic (*sādharmya*) of those whose self is space is the possession of momentary particular qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that do not pervade their locus (*avyāpyavṛtti*). Sound is the particular quality of space. And it is non-pervasive because when a sound arises with respect to a certain delimitation (*avaccheda*), at that same time its absence also exists with respect to another delimitation. Furthermore, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of a destruction occurring in the third moment.

Because the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a fit and all-pervading substance (*yogyavibhu*) are destroyed by the subsequent specific quality that arises immediately after them, the first sound is destroyed by the second sound. The same applies to cognition (*jñāna*) and other such qualities. When cognition and so forth arise in the all-pervading self (*ātman*) as delimited by the body, at that very time their absence exists as delimited by [other locations] such as a jar. Thus, cognition and the rest also endure for only two moments. Consequently, the meaning [of the definition] is "possessing specific qualities that do not pervade [their locus]" and "possessing momentary specific qualities."

It has been stated that [the definition] is not too narrow because color and other such qualities exist as specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) in earth and the other substances. It has been stated that it is a "specific quality" because conjunction and other such qualities exist in earth and the others only as non-pervasive occurrences (*avyāpyavṛtti*). Nor should it be argued that the possession of momentary specific qualities is over-extensive (*ativyāpta*) in the case of earth and so forth, since even color and other qualities can sometimes undergo destruction at the third moment.

The meaning of that [definition] is the possession of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) which possesses a genus (*jāti*) that does not reside in what is produced by a process lasting four moments (*catuḥkṣaṇavṛttijanya*). An *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition) lasts for three moments, whereas the genus "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), etc., resides in color and so forth even when they persist for four moments; thus, those [genuses] are excluded. Since God’s knowledge lasts for four moments, the term "produced" (*janya*) is included to exclude the genus "knowledge-ness" (*jñānatva*), which resides therein. If this is to be a common characteristic (*sādharmya*) between space (*ākāśa*) and the individual self (*jīvātman*), then the word "produced" need not be added, because the definition is applicable to the self by taking the genus "hatred-ness" (*dveṣatva*), etc., as the basis.

Because the supreme magnitude (*paramamahattva*) possesses such a quality [of being produced by conjunction], and because it is accepted that duality (*dvitva*) and so forth are destroyed in the fourth moment—and since duality and the like are likewise [produced by conjunction]—the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) is used to exclude them; or else, "subsisting for three moments" (*trikṣaṇavṛttitva*) should be stated [in the definition]. This is because the definition applies to the self (*ātman*), taking desire-ness (*icchātva*) and other such qualities into account. Thus ends the statement of the common properties (*sādharmya*) of ether (*ākāśa*) and the self.
The production of substance occurs in four [elements]; however, for ether and embodied beings (souls), a specific quality is held to be non-pervasive and momentary. (27)
The first three [substances] possess color, fluidity, and perceptibility;
two are heavy and possess taste; in two of them, fluidity is occasional (caused by heat). (28)

"Having color and fluidity" means that earth, water, and fire possess color, possess fluidity, and are objects of perception. Nor should it be asked what proof there is for the possession of color in the eyes and other sense organs, in the fire within a frying pan, or in heat;

for even in those cases, color is inferred by virtue of their being fire (*tejas*). Likewise, it should be understood that color is inferred in the portions of earth, water, and fire brought along by the wind, by virtue of their being earth and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that the definition of possessing fluidity (*dravatvavattva*) is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to jars and the like, or to fire which is distinct from molten gold and such; for what is intended is the possession of a genus (*jāti*) subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that subsists in that which possesses fluidity. Since fluidity exists in earths such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), lac (*jatū*), and so forth, in water, and in fire such as molten gold, and since the genus "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) and others exist therein, the definition is fully applicable to all of them by taking those instances into account.

Nor should it be said that being an object of perception (*pratyakṣa-viṣayatva*) is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like, or over-extended (*ativyāpta*) to color-form (*rūpa*) and the like; for what is intended is the possession of a genus subordinate to substanceness (*dravyatva*) that resides in the objects of ordinary visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-laukika-pratyakṣa*). The term "visual" (*cākṣuṣa*) is included to exclude over-extension to the self (*ātman*).
Thus ends the statement of the common properties of earth, water, and fire.

Regarding the term *gurūṇī*: the meaning is that both earth and water possess heaviness (*gurutva*) and taste (*rasa*). Nor should it be asked what proof there is for the possession of taste and so forth by the olfactory organ and other sense organs, as well as by the portions of earth and other elements brought along by the wind; for even in those cases, such qualities are inferred through their being earth and so forth.
Thus ends the statement of the common properties (*sādharmya*) of earth and water.

"Of the two" means of earth and fire. Nor should it be argued that "occasional liquidity" (naimittika-dravatva) is under-extended (avyāpta) to jars and the like, or to fire and the like; for what is intended is the possession of a genus (jāti) subordinate to substanceness (dravyatva) which co-exists (samānādhikaraṇa) with occasional liquidity. Thus ends the statement of the common properties (sādharmya) of earth and fire. Regarding "the selves" (ātmānaḥ): the meaning is that earth, water, fire, air, ether, and the self possess specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa). Thus ends the statement of the common properties of the elements and the self.

Regarding what was stated: it should be understood that this excludes "being knowable" (jñeyatva) and so forth. However, that [property] is not the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) of anything, because it is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property. ||26||
Thus concludes the examination of dissimilarity.
The selves and the classes of elements possess specific qualities;
that which has been stated as the similarity of one thing is the dissimilarity of the other. 29.
The eight qualities beginning with touch, along with the momentum known as *vega*, are the qualities of air (*marut*).
The eight qualities beginning with touch, together with color, momentum, and fluidity (*dravatva*), are the qualities of fire (*tejas*). (30)
Touch and the other eight qualities, the velocities, heaviness, fluidity, color, taste, and viscidity—these fourteen reside in water. (31)
These fourteen, beginning with smell and excluding viscidity, reside in earth:
the six starting with intellect, the five beginning with number, and likewise mental cultivation (bhāvanā). || 32 ||
Dharma and adharma—these are the fourteen qualities of the self (ātman).
The pentad beginning with number (saṅkhyā), as well as time and space, and sound—these reside in the ether (kha).
In the case of God (Īśvara), there is the pentad beginning with number—namely, intellect (buddhi), desire (icchā), and effort (yatna)—as well as priority and posteriority.
In the internal organ (mānasa), there are the five beginning with number, along with velocity (vega).
"Touch and the rest"—these are the five, beginning with number (saṅkhyā) and so forth; "in the void"—that is, in space. Thus ends the general description of substances and qualities.
In this context, earth is considered the cause of odor and possesses various forms.

Having examined similarity and dissimilarity, he now defines each element beginning with earth—starting with the phrase "In this context. "Cause of odor" means the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) of odor. Although it would have been more appropriate to define earth simply as that which possesses odor, [the author provides a more detailed definition].

Nevertheless, causality has been presented here in order to provide a proof for the genus "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva). For earth-ness is established as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of the inherent causality (samavāyikāraṇatā) of odor; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of odor being produced without a cause (ākasmikatva).

Nor should it be argued that the definition of "possessing odor" (*gandhavattva*) is under-extended (*avyāpta*) because odor is absent in stones and the like; for odor exists there as well, its non-perception being accounted for by its lack of intensity (*anutkaṭatva*). Otherwise, how could odor be perceived in the ash of such a stone? For since ash is produced from the destruction of a stone, it is established that it is derived from the same material cause (*upādāna*) as the stone, according to the pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever substance is produced from the destruction of a certain substance is derived from that substance's material cause.

This is observed in the case of a fragmentary cloth produced from the destruction of a large cloth. Likewise, since a stone-atom possesses earthness, the stone produced from it also possesses earthness; thus, there is no sublation to its possessing odor as well.
In that regard, earth is considered the cause of odor and is held to possess various colors;
its taste is of six kinds, and its odor is held to be of two kinds. (35)
Its touch, however, should be understood as neither hot nor cold and produced by maturation (*pākaja*).

Regarding the term "various" (*nānā*): color (*rūpa*) of various types—distinguished by white, blue, and so forth—exists only in earth and not in water and the like, because in those [elements] only white exists; whereas in earth, even in a single substrate (*dharmin*), multiple colors are possible due to the process of maturation (*pāka*). Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in cases where multiple colors have not arisen.

This is because what is intended is the possession of a genus subordinate to substancehood (*dravyatva*) that subsists in that which possesses two colors, or alternatively, the possession of a genus subordinate to substancehood that subsists in that which possesses the destruction of color; for in the Vaiśeṣika system, both the destruction of color and the presence of another color exist in the earth-atom (*pṛthivī-paramāṇu*), and in the Nyāya system, they exist even in jars and the like—thus the definition is consistent.

Regarding the phrase "of six kinds": that taste which is of six kinds through the division of sweet and so forth exists only in earth. In water, there is only the sweet taste. Here too, as before, the meaning of the definition should be understood as the possession of a genus pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in two types of taste. The statement "of two kinds" is merely a description of the actual state of things; it is not the definition [of air] as possessing two kinds of smell, because the quality of being "two-fold" is redundant. Furthermore, this twofold nature should be understood through the distinction between fragrance and foul odor.

Regarding the term "touch": this refers to that [earth]. It has been stated that the possession of a touch that is neither hot nor cold exists in air as well, which is why it was specified as being "produced by heating" (*pākaja*). Thus, it was stated in that way for the purpose of making known that the touch of earth is neither hot nor cold; however, the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) consists merely in the possession of a touch produced by heating, since anything more would be redundant. Although a touch produced by heating does not exist in things such as cloth, the intended meaning should nevertheless be understood as: "the state of possessing a genus subordinate to substantiality (*dravyatva*) that resides in that which possesses a touch produced by heating."
Thus ends the description of the definition of earth within the investigation of earth.
It is twofold, being both eternal and non-eternal; that which is eternal is characterized by atomicity.

But that other [earth] would be non-eternal; that very [earth] which possesses parts is eternal—meaning that earth is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal. Earth characterized by atoms, in the form of ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), is eternal. (36)
The meaning is that all earth other than that [monad], distinct from atoms—beginning with dyads—is impermanent. That very same impermanent earth is possessed of parts; this is the meaning.

Now, what is the proof for the existence of a whole (*avayavin*)? It is established by the mere collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Nor should it be argued that because atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), there would be no perception of jars and the like; for even though a single atom is imperceptible, its aggregate can be perceptible. It is just as a single hair is imperceptible from a distance, yet its collection is perceptible. Nor should it be argued that the cognition "one large jar" would be inexplicable; for this is justifiable, as in the case of the cognition "one large heap of grain."

Not so; for since an atom is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), its aggregate (*samūha*) cannot possibly be perceived either. As for hair situated at a distance, it is not itself beyond the reach of the senses, because that very same hair becomes perceptible when in close proximity. Nor should it be argued that there is no contradiction in its being perceptible because, at that time, a collection of visible atoms has been produced; for that which is invisible cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of that which is visible. Otherwise, it would follow as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the series of the eye, heat, and so forth, might occasionally become visible.

Nor should it be asked: "How can a visible flame arise from a sequence of invisible flames, as in the case of excessively heated oil and the like? For in that instance, it is accepted that a gross fire arises from the visible parts of the fire contained within it. Nor should it be asked: "How can a visible triad (*trasareṇu*) arise from an invisible dyad (*dvyaṇuka*)."

For we do not assert that visibility or invisibility belongs to anything by virtue of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); rather, visibility belongs to that which possesses a collection of causes such as magnitude (*mahattva*) and manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*), while invisibility occurs in the absence of those. Thus, a thread (*trasareṇu*) is perceptible because it possesses magnitude, whereas a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth are not, due to the absence of that [magnitude]. Indeed, even in your own view, this is not possible, since magnitude is absent in the atom (*paramāṇu*).

And thus, once the composite whole (*avayavin*) is established, its impermanence follows from the fact that its production and destruction are established through perception. This concludes the inference for the composite whole.

Furthermore, if the series of parts and wholes were infinite, it would follow that Mount Meru and a mustard seed would be equal in size. Therefore, one must assert that the series rests somewhere. Since that point of rest, if it were impermanent, would entail the production of an effect that is not inhered in (asamaveta), it must be eternal. Just as the gradation of large dimensions finds its limit in space and so forth, there must likewise be a limit somewhere for the gradation of minute dimensions; thus, the existence of the atom (*paramāṇu*) is established.

Nor should it be argued that the process of division should simply rest at the *trasareṇu* (the mote of dust). For the parts of the *trasareṇu* are established by the inference: "The *trasareṇu* has parts, because it is a visible substance, like a jar. Furthermore, the parts of those parts are established by the inference: "The parts of the *trasareṇu* have parts, because they are the originators of something large, like potsherds. Nor is this [inference] inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), because the state of being composed of multiple substances is the necessary condition (*prayojaka*) for having a degree of largeness (*mahattva*). Nor should it be argued that, by such a sequence, an infinite series of parts would be established.
"Because that [infinite regress] is not established due to the fear of infinite regress. Thus ends the proof of the atom.
And that [matter] is threefold: the body, the sense organs, and likewise the objects.

"The body may be born from a womb and so forth; the sense organ is characterized by the sense of smell. And "that" [refers to the following]: that earth, which is of the nature of an effect, is threefold, meaning it is divided into body, sense organ, and object. Among these, he illustrates the body with the words "born from a womb and so forth," meaning it is both womb-born and not womb-born. Womb-born is also twofold: viviparous and oviparous. Viviparous refers to humans and the like; oviparous refers to snakes and the like. Not womb-born includes those born from sweat, sprouts, and so forth.
The sweat-born are worms, gadflies, and the like; the sprout-born are trees, shrubs, and so forth. The bodies of hell-beings are likewise not born from a womb.

Nor should it be asked what proof there is for the fact that human and other bodies are composed of earth (pārthiva); for their possession of smell and other qualities is itself the proof. Nor should it be argued that because moisture, heat, and so on are perceived, they must also possess the nature of water (āpyatva) and the rest; for if that were the case, it would lead to the fallacy of confusion (saṅkara) between the categories of "water-ness," "earth-ness," and so on. Nor should it be argued that they should therefore be considered as consisting only of water and the like, rather than being earthly; for even when moisture and such perish, they are recognized as "bodies" (śarīra).

Furthermore, because of the perception of odors and so forth, the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) is established. Therefore, in bodies composed of earth and other elements, water and the rest should be understood as having only a causal role (*nimittatvamātra*).

Corporeality (*śarīratva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), because it would involve a cross-division (*sāṅkarya*) with the nature of earth and so on. Rather, it is the state of being a substratum of volitional activity (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*). Since trees and the like are also substrata of volitional activity, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Nor should it be asked what proof there is for the corporeality of trees and such.

This is because its connection with internal air (*ādhyātmika-vāyu*) serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is asked what the proof for this is, it is inferred from such phenomena as the healing of broken or wounded parts. If the designation "body" does not apply to the hands and so forth, then it should be qualified by the property of being a final composite whole (*antyāvayavin*). Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a body where no movement has occurred, for there is no evidence for such a thing.

Alternatively, that [the definition of a body] consists in possessing a genus (jāti) that is pervaded by substanceness (dravyatva) and resides in a final whole (antyāvayavin) that possesses motion; or it consists in possessing a genus that resides in a final whole exclusively and resides in that which possesses motion. The application of the definition is achieved by taking such genera as "humanity" (mānuṣatva), "Caitra-ness" (caitratva), and so forth. And how is there an application of the definition in the case of the body of Nṛsiṃha? For in that case, "Nṛsiṃha-ness" lacks the status of a genus because it resides in only a single individual.

It should not be argued that [the definition] fails because water and fire bodies do not exist as modes of a body, and thus divinity (devatva) also lacks the status of a universal (jāti); for since the Nṛsiṃha body is manifold due to differences in its constituent parts, the definition is applicable through the universal of "Nṛsiṃhahood" (nṛsiṃhatva).
Thus concludes the description of the earthy body.

Regarding the term "sense organ" (*indriya*): the meaning is that the olfactory sense organ (*ghrāṇendriya*) is composed of earth (*pārthiva*). If one asks how it is known to be composed of earth, it is as follows: the olfactory sense organ is composed of earth because, among color-form (*rūpa*) and the other qualities, it manifests only odor (*gandha*), just like cow's ghee which manifests the fragrance of saffron.

Nor should it be argued that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because one's own color and so forth are manifestors [of the jar] in the example; for the meaning of the term is "not being a manifester of another's color and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding water which manifests the fragrance contained within a new earthen bowl; for that water manifests the taste of the barley-flour (*saktu*). Alternatively, the word "another's" (*parakīya*) need not be included, since the fragrant particles brought by the wind can serve as the example. Nor should it be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case because the contact of the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya-saṃnikarṣa*) manifests fragrance alone; for the qualification "provided it is a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) is added.
Thus concludes the examination of the earthy sense-faculties.

He states the definition of the object (*viṣaya*): "The object," he says. An object is a means for experience (*upabhoga*). Every entire collection of effects is dependent upon unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). Whatever effect is dependent upon a particular unseen force, that effect necessarily produces experience for that [agent], either directly or through a series; for nothing whatsoever comes into existence without a seed (cause) and a purpose (motive). Therefore, everything from the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) up to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) constitutes an object. Although the body and the senses are also objects, they are mentioned separately for the sake of clarifying the student's understanding.
Thus ends the examination of the objects belonging to the earth; thus concludes the section on the earth.
The objective domain is said to extend from the binary atomic compound (dvyaṇuka) up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 38 ||

The color of water is white, and its taste and touch are sweet and cold. [The author] defines water: "the color is white. The universal *jalatva* (water-ness) is established as the delimitor of the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of viscidity (*sneha*). Although the property of viscidity (*snehatva*)—because it subsists in both eternal and non-eternal things—is not a delimitor of effecthood (*kāryatāvacchedaka*), nevertheless, the property of produced viscidity (*janyasnehatva*) should be understood as such.

If it is argued that "water-ness" (*jalatva*) cannot exist in an atom because of the absence of produced moisture (*janya-sneha*) therein, and because there is a rule that for a permanent entity, if it possesses intrinsic capacity (*svarūpa-yogyatā*), the effect must necessarily follow—[we reply]: No. Once the universal of "produced water-ness" (*janya-jalatva-jāti*) is established as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the generative capacity for produced moisture, the universal of "water-ness" (*jalatva-jāti*) is established by virtue of being the delimitor of the generative capacity delimited by that [universal].

To show that water possesses only a white color, it was stated that "its color is white"; however, possessing a white color is not the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, its meaning is: either possessing a genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) which resides in that which possesses a color not residing in that which possesses adventitious fluidity (*naimittikadravatva*); or, possessing a genus directly pervaded by substanceness which resides in that which possesses a color not co-located with a non-luminous white color other than [the color of water]. By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to crystal and the like.

Regarding "taste and touch": the taste of water is exclusively sweet, and its touch is exclusively cold. The definition [of water] is: "the state of possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), which resides in a substance possessing a sweet taste, but does not reside in a substance possessing a bitter taste. By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sugar and the like. (The definition is: "the state of possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substanceness, which resides in a substance possessing a touch, but does not reside in a substance possessing a touch other than cold.")

But why must it be only white in color? If it is argued that this is because blueness is perceived in the waters of the Yamunā (*Kālindī*) and so forth, we say no. Since the genus "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvajāti*), which is the delimiting factor for the production of blue, is absent in water, a blue color is impossible there; the perception of blueness in the Yamunā's water is merely due to the limiting condition of its substrate. For this very reason, when the spray is dispersed into the air, whiteness is perceived. Now, what is the proof for sweetness in water? Certainly no taste is experienced there through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Nor should it be said that sweetness is indeed perceived in coconut water and the like, for that too is due to the limiting condition of its substrate.

If it is argued that otherwise, because an acid taste and so forth are perceived in the juice of the *jambīra* fruit and the like, those substances would also possess acidity and other such tastes, we say no. This is because the consumption of *harītakī* and similar fruits serves merely to manifest the taste already present in the water. Nor should it be said that a different taste is produced in the *harītakī* itself through contact with the heat of the water; for this would involve an unnecessary complexity of assumptions (*kalpanā-gaurava*), and because the property of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is the delimiting factor for the production of acidity and the like, there is no acidity in water. As for the perception of such qualities in the juice of the *jambīra* and so forth, that is merely due to the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its substrate.
In that case, viscidity (*sneha*) is present, while fluidity (*dravatva*) is cited as being natural (*sāṃsiddhika*). || 39 ||

In this way, it should be understood that "produced-water-ness" (*janyajalatva*) is the delimitor of the generality of producing a produced cold touch, while "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is the delimitor of the generality of producing that which is delimited by [produced-water-ness]. As for the perception of coldness in rubbed sandalwood and the like, it belongs solely to the much colder water existing within the sandalwood. The perception of heat in water due to contact with fire is clearly adventitious (*aupādhika*), since cooking (*pāka*) is impossible therein. Regarding the statement "moisture (*sneha*) resides there": even in ghee and the like, the moisture belongs only to the water existing within them, because water is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of moisture. Therefore, it should be maintained that moisture exists only in water.

Regarding "fluidity": the specific universal (jāti) of "intrinsic fluidity" (sāṃsiddhikadravatvatva) is established by perception; the meaning is that this very [universal] is also the delimitor of the generative capacity (janakatāvacchedaka) for that which is delimited by it. He will state later that even in oil and the like, it is indeed the fluidity of water itself, and its suitability for fire is due to the excellence of its viscidity (sneha). ||36||
Thus ends the description of the definition of water within the investigation of water.
Its eternity and other qualities are as [stated] for the first [element], but its body is not born from a womb;
the sense organ is the tongue, and its object is considered to be water, snow, and so forth. (40)

"As in the case of the first" means "like the earth. To explain: water is of two kinds—eternal and non-eternal. That which is in the form of atoms is eternal; everything from the binary atomic compound (*dvyaṇuka*) onwards is non-eternal and is inherent in its constituent parts. Even the non-eternal is threefold, distinguished as body, sense organ, and object. He states the distinction [of water] from earth with the words "but... The body is not born from a womb (*ayonija*)—the meaning being that it is exclusively not born from a womb. A watery body not born from a womb is well known in the world of Varuṇa. Thus ends the description of the watery body.

"Indriya" means that which is watery (jalīya). To explain: the sense of taste (rasana) is watery, because, while not manifesting smell and other qualities, it manifests taste, just like water which manifests the taste of flour (saktu). The term "substance-ness" (dravyatva) must be added [to the definition] to exclude the contact of the gustatory organ with its object.
Thus ends the description of the watery sense organ.

He shows the scope [of the example] with the word "sindhu" (river/ocean). "Sindhu" means the ocean; "hima" means snow. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), everything such as rivers, lakes, hailstones, and so forth, is to be included. Nor should it be argued that snow and hailstones are earthy (*pārthiva*) because of their hardness; for when they are melted by heat, their watery nature is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, based on the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever substance is produced by the destruction of another substance, it is derived from the material cause of that substance," it is established that they are derived from water as their material cause.

Because the perception of solidity in a hailstone is an error, due to the obstruction of fluidity by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). Thus ends the examination of the aqueous object; thus ends the section on water.

Heat is the touch of fire, while its color is white and luminous. He defines fire as "heat. Heat-ness (*uṣṇatva*) is a specific universal residing in touch, established through perception. Thus, fire-ness (*tejastva*)—a specific universal—is the delimitor of the inherent causality of produced hot touch; its subsistence in atoms should be understood in the same manner as that of water-ness (*jalatva*). Nor should it be argued that the possession of hot touch is non-pervasive (*avyāpta*) in the case of moonbeams and the like, for hot touch exists there too, though it is not perceived because it is overwhelmed by the touch of the water contained within them.

Similarly, in the case of the rays of a gem and the like, there is non-perception because they are overwhelmed by the touch of the earth-element, and in the case of the eyes and the like, because [the color] is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*). Regarding "color" and so forth: in the case of fire and the rays of an emerald and the like, there is no perception of the white color because it is overwhelmed by the color of the earth-element. If it is argued that if that color is not perceived, the substratum (*dharmin*) itself would also not be visible to the eye, we say no; for it is possible to perceive the substratum through the color belonging to something else, just as a conch shell is perceived through the yellow tint of bile. Others, however, maintain that the white color of fire is not overwhelmed; rather, its quality of whiteness (*śuklatva*) is overwhelmed.

The occasional fluidity and its permanence and so forth are as previously described. Regarding the term "occasional" (*naimittika*): it is because that [fluidity] exists in fire in the form of gold and the like. Nor should it be argued that the property of possessing occasional fluidity is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to burning fire and over-extended (*ativyāpta*) to ghee and the like; for what is intended is the possession of a genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) which resides in that which possesses occasional fluidity, but does not reside in earth. Thus ends the statement of the definition of fire within the investigation of fire.

"As before" means "just like water. To explain: it is of two kinds, eternal and non-eternal; the eternal is in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*), while that which is other than this is non-eternal and composed of parts (*avayavin*). Furthermore, it is threefold, distinguished as body (*śarīra*), sense organ (*indriya*), and object (*viṣaya*). The body is exclusively non-womb-born (*ayonija*); it is well known in places such as the world of the Sun (*sūryaloka*). || 42 ||
Thus concludes the description of the fiery body.
Fluidity is occasional, while its eternity and other properties are as previously described.
The sense organ is the eye; fire is considered its object, such as gold and so forth.

Regarding this, he states the specific distinction: "the sense organ" and so on. Now, if it is asked what the proof is for the ocular organ being composed of light (*taijasa*), [the answer is]: the eye is composed of light because, while not manifesting the touch and other qualities of another, it manifests the color-form of another, like a lamp.

To exclude the lamp from the example—since a lamp does manifest its own touch—the first qualification "of another" (*parakīya*) is added. To avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to objects like a jar, which manifest their own color-form, the second qualification "of another" (*parakīya*) is added.

Alternatively, since light can serve as an illustrative example, the term "belonging to another" (parakīya) need not be supplied. To exclude the deviation [of the definition] in the case of visual contact (cakṣuḥ-saṃnikarṣa), the property of being a substance (dravyatva) must be included. Thus ends the description of the luminous sense organ (taijasa-indriya).

He shows the subject matter—namely, "fire. Now, one might ask: what is the proof that gold is luminous (taijasa)? It is not so; for gold is luminous because, in the absence of an obstructing factor, it possesses fluidity that is not destroyed even by continuous contact with fire. Whatever is not thus is not so, like earth. Nor is this argument unproven (*aprayojaka*), because the fluidity of earth and the fluidity of water produced [by heat] are both destructible by continuous contact with fire.

If it is objected that there is a deviation [from the rule] because even the substratum of yellow weight is then in a state of flow, we say no; for like a powder of ink placed in the midst of water, it does not flow.

Others, however, postulate a distinct liquid substance as the obstructer [of the color change], because even when the substratum of the yellow color is subjected to extreme contact with fire, no transformation of its prior color is observed. To explain: the substratum of the yellow color and gravity, when subjected to extreme contact with fire, is conjoined with a liquid substance that obstructs a dissimilar color, because—even while under extreme contact with fire—it is not the locus of a color dissimilar to its prior color, being of an earthly nature, like a yellow cloth situated in water; and because it is necessarily of the nature of fire, being distinct from earth and water.
Thus ends the determination of the objects of light; thus ends the section on light.
The touch of air, however, is considered to be non-produced [by combination] and neither hot nor cold. || 42 ||

This [wind] is to be known as possessing horizontal motion and having touch and so forth as its indicative marks. He defines wind: "not produced by heat" (*apākaja*). Since a touch that is neither hot nor cold exists in earth as well, he says "not produced by heat. Since a touch not produced by heat exists in water and other substances as well, he says "neither hot nor cold. By this, a specific (heterogeneous) touch belonging to wind is shown; the meaning is that the property of being wind (*vāyutva*) is the delimiting factor for the causal capacity to produce that [touch]. (42) Thus ends the statement of the proof for the genus "wind-ness" (*vāyutva-jāti*) in the definition of wind.

This—wind—is characterized by touch and other marks; for wind is inferred from touch, sound, support, and trembling, as before: by an atypical touch, by a distinct sound, by the support of grass and such, and by the trembling of branches and the like. Wind is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal. That which is atomic in form is eternal; that which is other than this is non-eternal, being inherent in parts. That too is threefold, through the division of body, sense organ, and object.
As stated previously regarding eternality and so forth, the sense organ of the skin pervades the entire body. (43)
And [the existence of] air is established through inference. How air is not perceptible will be explained later.
