Thus ends the statement regarding the means of knowledge for air in the investigation of air.

In that regard, the body of Piśācas and others is not born from a womb; however, bodies composed of water, fire, or air possess the capacity for experience due to being supported by an earthly portion. They are classified as watery and so forth because of the predominance of water and the other elements. Thus concludes the description of aerial bodies.

Regarding this, he states the specific distinction: "pervading the body" (*dehavyāpi*). The sense organ that pervades the body and perceives touch is the skin (*tvak*); and it is composed of air (*vāyavīya*), because among color and the other qualities, it manifests touch alone, just like the breeze from a fan which manifests the coldness of water touching the limbs. (43) Thus ends the description of the sense organ composed of air.

He shows the object [of the sense of touch]—namely, "the vital air (prāṇa) and so forth. Although it is stated in the authoritative treatises (*ākara*) that air, though impermanent, is of four kinds, and its fourth variety is the vital air (*prāṇa*) and so on, nevertheless, for the sake of brevity, only three kinds have been mentioned here. However, the vital air (*prāṇa*) is in fact one alone; it receives various designations due to its presence in various locations such as the heart and so forth, and due to the differences in its various functions such as exiting through the mouth and so on. Thus ends the determination of the objects pertaining to air. Thus ends the section on air (*vāyugrantha*).
The objects of touch are considered to range from the vital breath (prāṇa) up to the great wind (mahāvāyu);
however, sound is to be known as the specific quality (vaiśeṣika-guṇa) of space (ākāśa). || 44 ||

He defines space with the words "of space. Since ether, time, and direction each exist as single individuals, "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like are not universals (*jāti*); rather, space-ness is the state of being the substratum of sound. The mention of the term "Vaiśeṣika," however, is for the purpose of excluding other specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

By this, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has also been shown. For instance: "Sound is a quality (*guṇa*), because it possesses a genus that is perceptible by an external sense organ but not by the eye, like touch. Once it is established by inference that sound is inherent in a substance (*dravyasamaveta*)—namely, "Sound is inherent in a substance, because it is a quality, like conjunction"—it follows: "Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of a substance possessing touch, because, while lacking the state of having the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of fire-conjunction, it is perceptible without being preceded by qualities of its own causes, like pleasure."

The term "produced by maturation" (*pākaja*) is included in the definition to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of color and other qualities produced by heat. The phrase "preceded by qualities of its own causes" (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvaka*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of the color of a cloth and so forth. The term "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of the color of water-atoms (*jalaparamāṇu*) and so forth. Sound is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ (*manas*), because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), just like color.

Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self, because it is perceptible by an external sense organ, like color. And thus, a ninth substance is established as the substratum of sound. Nor should it be argued that sound is produced in the air—preceded by the qualities of its causes—in the form of a sequence of subtle sounds within the parts of the air; for, since it does not persist as long as the substance itself, it lacks the status of being a specific quality of the air. (44) Thus concludes the statement of the proof regarding space.

And therein, because of the absence of both a body and an object, he indicates the sense organ by the word "indriyam" (the sense organ). Now, if it is argued that space is established as one due to parsimony (*lāghava*), whereas the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is distinct according to the difference between individuals, so how could it be space? To this he says: "ekaḥ" (one). Although space is one, it becomes the auditory organ—which is essentially space—divided by the difference of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). Thus ends the determination of the auditory organ; thus ends the section on space.

He defines time with the words "of produced things. Thus ends the statement of the definition of time in the exposition of time. To demonstrate the proof for its existence, he says: "the substratum of the worlds. (For instance: when the cognition "the jar is now" and so forth takes the solar motion and the like as its object, then something must be postulated as the connector of the relation between the solar motion and the jar etc. And in this way, its status as a substratum is perfectly established. (45)

He shows another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with the words "priority and posteriority" (*parāparatva*). The unique cause for the cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth, is time alone; the sense is that, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), one postulates a distinct entity called time as the substratum of the non-inherent cause of conjunction (*asamavāyikāraṇa-saṃyoga*) for priority and posteriority. This concludes the statement of the proof regarding time.

But surely, if time were established as a single entity, there would be no distinction between temporal divisions such as moments (*kṣaṇa*), days, months, and years; therefore, he says: "The moment and so forth arise from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Although time is one, it becomes the object of conventional usage as a "moment" and so on due to the difference in its limiting adjuncts. As for the adjunct: it is either (1) an action delimited by the prior non-existence of the disjunction produced by itself, or (2) a disjunction delimited by the destruction of a prior conjunction. It should not be argued that the conventional usage of a "moment" would not occur immediately after the posterior conjunction delimited by the destruction of the prior conjunction.

This is because other actions also exist. If there is a conventional usage of "moments" (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth even during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), then it must be accounted for by means of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) alone. However, the conventional usage of "days" (*dina*) and so forth is established by aggregates (*kūṭa*) of those respective moments. Thus concludes the establishment of the unity of time.
Thus ends the section on time.

He defines direction (*diś*) with the words "distant and near" (*dūrāntika*). Distance and proximity are to be understood as spatial priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*). Space itself is the unique cause for the cognition of these. The sense is that, because it serves as the substratum for the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the conjunction [responsible] for spatial priority and posteriority, a single space (*dik*) is established by parsimony (*lāghava*). ||46||
Thus ends the statement regarding the measurement of the directions.
The sense of hearing may belong to Indra; though he is one, he appears as such due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
Time is considered the progenitor of all things produced and the substratum of the worlds. 45.

Space is said to be one and eternal, serving as the cause for the cognition of priority and posteriority, while time—consisting of moments and so forth—is the cause for the cognition of such [relative] states through limiting adjuncts (upādhi). It is also the cause for the cognitions of "far" and "near," and so on. 46.

Now, one might object: if there is only one direction, then how can the conventional usage of terms such as "east" (*prācī*) and "west" (*pratīcī*) be justified? To this, he says: "due to the difference of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhimedāt*). That direction which is adjacent to a person's mountain of sunrise (*udayagiri*) is the east for that person; likewise, that direction which is separated from the mountain of sunrise is the west. Similarly, that direction which is adjacent to Mount Meru for a person is the north (*udīcī*), while that separated from it is the south (*avācī*). "Mount Meru stands to the north of all regions"—this establishes the unity of direction. Thus ends the section on direction (*diggrantha*).

He defines the self: "The self is the presiding agent over the body, the senses, and their objects. The universal property of selfhood (*ātmatva-jāti*) is established as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the inherent causality (*samavāyikāraṇatā*) of pleasure, pain, and so forth. This universal indeed exists even in God; however, because of the absence of causes such as the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), there is no production of pleasure, pain, and so forth. This is because the rule that "for that which is eternal and essentially capable [of producing an effect], the effect must necessarily occur" is not invariably applicable.

Others, however, say that this genus does not exist at all in God, because there is a lack of evidence; nor does it follow that [God] would become a tenth substance, because He is classified as being of the nature of consciousness (*jñānatva*). This concludes the statement of the proof for the genus "selfhood" (*ātmatva*).
The presiding deity of the senses and so forth is that which brings about consciousness in the senses and the body through a continuous series.

Although the Self is one, it receives designations such as "eastern" and so on due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi). The Self is the presiding deity of the senses and so forth, for an instrument must have an agent. (47)
The body does not possess consciousness, because that would lead to an inconsistency in the case of dead bodies.

Although the fact that "I am happy" or "I am miserable" is not actually an object of the senses even with respect to the self, nevertheless, it is impossible to demonstrate to one who holds a contrary view right from the outset that the object of such cognition is distinct from the body and so forth; therefore, he shows another means of knowledge—namely, "the instrument."

It is observed that instruments such as axes and the like do not bring about their results in the absence of an agent; likewise, the production of results by instruments of cognition such as the eyes is not possible without an agent. Therefore, an additional agent is postulated. ||47||
Thus ends the exposition of the means of valid cognition regarding the self.

[Objection: Let agency belong to the body; to this he says: "of the body. [Objection: Consciousness is simply cognition and so forth; what harm is there if that exists even in dead bodies, as it does in the case of liberated souls (*muktātman*) according to your own view? [Reply: No, because the absence of cognition is established by the absence of vital breath (*prāṇa*). If you say this, we reply: no, because if the body were conscious, the recollection in old age of what was seen in childhood would be impossible, since bodies are subject to production and destruction through the accumulation and diminution of their constituent parts.

Nor should it be said that a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is produced in a second body by means of an impression produced in a previous body; for this would involve the fault of over-complication (*gaurava*) in postulating an infinite series of impressions. Furthermore, if the body were conscious, an infant’s inclination toward suckling milk would not occur, because the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end is the cause of such activity, and at that time there would be no means to recall that it is a means to a desired end. In my view, however, activity arises precisely from the recollection at that time of its being a means to a desired end as experienced in another birth. Nor should it be argued that other things experienced in another birth might also be recollected; for there is an absence of any factor to awaken those specific memories (*udbodhaka*).

In this case, however, since there is no other means of subsistence in the future, the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) itself is postulated as the awakener [of the latent impression]. And thus, since the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is beginningless, the beginninglessness of the self is established; and since a positive entity that is beginningless cannot be destroyed, its eternity is proven—this is how it should be understood.
Thus concludes the refutation of the Cārvāka doctrine which asserts that the body is the self.

Now, one might object: let the eyes and other senses themselves possess both the status of instrument (*karaṇatva*) and agent (*kartṛtva*) with respect to cognition and so forth, since there is no proof for a contradiction; to this, he says: "tathātva" (that state). "Tathātva" means consciousness (*caitanya*). When there is destruction due to injury...

[This refers] to the eyes and so forth alone. How [could there be] memory? There would be no recollection of things previously experienced by the eye in the absence of that eye, because the experiencer is absent; for what is experienced by one cannot be remembered by another, since the relationship of cause and effect between experience and memory requires a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is the intended meaning. (4) Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of those who maintain that the sense organs are the self.

[Objection: Let it be that the eyes and other [senses] lack consciousness; however, let the eternal mind (*manas*) possess consciousness. To this, he says: "The mind also... It is not so—it is not conscious. At that time, [consciousness] would be imperceptible, because the mind is atomic (*aṇu*), and magnitude (*mahattva*) is a necessary condition for perception. The meaning is that if knowledge, pleasure, and so forth were to exist in the mind, their perception would be impossible. How the mind is atomic will be explained later. Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine that the mind is the self.

Let it be granted that consciousness alone is the self (*ātman*), since its nature is self-luminous and thus it possesses sentience. Knowledge, pleasure, and so forth are merely particular modes (*ākāra*) of that very consciousness. Because these too are existent entities (*bhāva*), they are momentary; for each preceding cognition serves as the cause for each succeeding cognition. Even during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the stream of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) remains entirely unimpeded. There is no logical inconsistency, because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by preceding cognitions serve as the causes for subsequent cognitions, just as a garment perfumed with musk retains its fragrance.

If it is argued that [the self is known] through recollection and so forth, we say no. For if that [recollection] had the entire world as its object, it would follow that [the self] is omniscient; if it had only some particular thing as its object, there would be no reason for determining which one; and furthermore, because knowledge must have an object, it would follow that objects would appear even during deep sleep. If it is argued that at that time a formless stream of consciousness continues, we say no. This is because there is no evidence for the luminosity of such a stream; otherwise, it would follow that jars and other objects are also forms of knowledge. And this is not an acceptable consequence.

It must be stated that there is no entity distinct from consciousness, because it is impossible to deny the jar and other objects that are being experienced. If it is argued that this is merely a specific form (*ākāra*) of consciousness, we ask: is this form something separate from consciousness?

In that case, [the object] would have arrived as something distinct from consciousness. If it is not distinct, then in a cognition apprehending a collection [of objects], the form of blue would also be the form of yellow, because there is no difference in the nature of consciousness itself. If it is argued that "blueness" and so forth, being of the nature of *apoha* (exclusion), are properties of consciousness, we say no; for contradictory properties such as blueness cannot coexist in a single [entity], otherwise it would be impossible to even establish their mutual contradiction. Nor is the transfer of mental impressions (*vāsanā*) possible, as that would lead to the absurd consequence of the transfer of impressions between mother and son.

Nor should it be argued that the relationship of material cause (*upādāna*) and effect (*upādeya*) is the regulator [of memory], because the transference (*saṅkrama*) of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is impossible. If it is argued that "transference" is simply the arising [of the impression] in a subsequent moment, we say no; for there is no producer of such an impression. If it were the cognitions themselves (*cit*) that produced them, it would follow that there is an infinite regress of mental dispositions (*saṃskāra*).

If it is argued that a specific excellence (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*) is postulated within the momentary cognitions, we say no; for there is a lack of evidence (*mānābhāva*) and because it involves the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
Thus ends the refutation of the Buddhist doctrine of the self as momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñānātmavāda*).

By this, consciousness in momentary bodies alone is refuted, due to the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*) and the absence of evidence for any such excellence (*atiśaya*). Even in the case of seeds and the like, [the production of sprouts] is accounted for simply by the presence or absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), without postulating a "productive nature" (*kurvadrūpatva*).
Thus ends the refutation of the doctrine of those who maintain that the self consists of a momentary body.

[Objection: "Let it be then that, due to the complexity of momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*), the eternal consciousness itself is the Self, on account of such scriptural passages as: 'Verily, this Self is imperishable,' and 'Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. [Response: This is not so, because it has already been shown that such [eternal consciousness] cannot have an object; furthermore, there is no evidence for something being knowledge if it is devoid of an object. Therefore, it is established that the eternal Self is distinct from consciousness and the like."

The phrase "truth and knowledge," however, refers to Brahman and is not applicable to the individual soul (*jīva*). Since the distinction between individual souls is established through their varying states of knowledge and ignorance, as well as happiness and suffering, the distinction from the Lord (*īśvara*) is all the more firmly established. Otherwise, the systematic arrangement of bondage and liberation would be untenable. Even that Vedic scripture which teaches non-difference from the Lord does so by extolling the soul's belonging to Him through such non-difference; it does not mean that one should strive for identity, but rather that one should strive with the contemplation of non-difference.

For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "All selves are surrendered. Nor can it be said that non-difference arises at the stage of liberation upon the cessation of ignorance; for since difference is eternal, its destruction is impossible. Even if difference were destroyed, the two individual entities would certainly remain. Nor should it be argued that even duality perishes; for just as you might say of Brahman—which is devoid of attributes—that it possesses the nature of reality despite the absence of "reality" (as a property), so too it can be easily asserted that those two exist as two individuals despite the absence of duality.

If it is argued that truth (*satyatva*) consists in the absence of falsity (*mithyātvābhāva*), which is of the nature of its locus (*adhikaraṇātmaka*), then one might as well say that duality (*dvitva*) consists in the absence of oneness (*ekatvābhāva*), which is of the nature of two individuals; for although each [of the two] is individually one, it is established by all people that "the two are not one," just as it is said that "there is no fragrance in earth and water [taken together], though there is in each. Furthermore, even the Vedic scripture that proclaims non-difference at that time establishes equality in terms of being free from suffering and so forth, just as one says, "This priest has become a king" when there is an abundance of prosperity.

For this very reason, it is heard in scripture: "The stainless one attains supreme equality. Even Īśvara is not of the nature of knowledge and bliss, but rather the substratum of knowledge and so forth; for in such passages as "Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss," the word *vijñāna* denotes precisely the substratum of knowledge, in accordance with [texts] such as "He who is all-knowing is all-perceiving. Furthermore, the term "*ānandam*" means "possessing bliss" (*ānandavat*), where the suffix *-ac* is used in the sense of possession according to the *arśa-ādi* group; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of it being masculine.

Bliss (*ānanda*) is also used figuratively for the absence of suffering, just as one says, "I have become happy," upon the removal of a burden or the like. Or, let there be bliss in that state; yet this [state] is not bliss itself, because of the scriptural text: "not happiness" (*asukham*). If it is asked why the meaning "that in which happiness does not exist" is not accepted, we say no; for that would involve the fault of forced interpretation (*kliṣṭakalpanā*), it would contradict the context, and it would conflict with the suffix *matup* (expressing possession) in the word "ānandam. This is the summary.
Thus concludes the refutation of the Vedāntin position that the self is eternal consciousness.

By this [it is shown]: Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is the agent, while the Spirit (puruṣa), though conscious like a lotus leaf and untainted, is not the cause; for since cause and effect are non-different, if the effect were to perish, the Spirit would also perish in its form as that effect, and thus it follows that he is not the cause.

The postulation of that [consciousness] follows from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the conceit of consciousness residing in the intellect (*buddhi*). The intellect is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); it alone is called the "Great Principle" (*mahattattva*) and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation (*apavarga*) of the person (*puruṣa*) depend upon the presence or absence of that [intellect]. Through the channel of the senses, a transformation of that very [intellect] in the form of cognition constitutes its connection with objects such as a jar. The conceit of agency in the person and the conceit of consciousness in the intellect arise from the non-apprehension of their difference. The aspect of "mine" in the thought "this must be done by me" is the reflection of the person upon the intellect due to its transparency; it is not real.

Like the coloring of a face upon a mirror, the coloring by an object as "this" is a real modification (pariṇāma) through the channel of the senses; like the tarnish on a mirror struck by breath, the aspect of activity is "it must be done"; thus, the intellect (buddhi) possesses these three aspects.

Through the transformation of that [intellect], there occurs an unreal connection between the Person (puruṣa) and knowledge; this is said to be the perception of the Self, just as the reflection of a face is perceived in the impurity of a mirror. Furthermore, the view that pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, merit, and demerit belong to the intellect alone—on the grounds that they are perceived as being in a common locus with volitional effort—is refuted, because the intellect is not conscious, owing to its nature of undergoing transformation.

Furthermore, because consciousness is perceived as being in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with volition, perception, and enjoyment—just as these are with respect to one another—and because there is no evidence for its being distinct from them; and if it is argued that the cognition "I, who am conscious, act" is an error regarding the aspect of consciousness, why is it not likewise accepted as an error regarding the aspect of volition? Otherwise, if the intellect (*buddhi*) were eternal, there would be no liberation; if it were non-eternal, there would follow the consequence that there was no transmigratory existence prior to it. If it is argued that the intellect is insentient because it is an effect of insentient primordial matter (*prakṛti*), since cause and effect are identical in nature, we say no, because this is unproven.

There is no evidence for the agent being produced; rather, because the birth of one free from passion is never observed, [the self] is beginningless, and because that which is beginningless cannot perish, it is eternal. So what is the use of postulating primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and so forth? Nor should it be argued that this contradicts the statement: "All actions performed in every way by the qualities of *prakṛti*, the self, deluded by egoism, thinks 'I am the doer'"—for here, "of *prakṛti*" means of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), "by the qualities" means by desire and so forth produced by the unseen force, and "I am the doer" refers to...
This is because the meaning of that [scriptural passage] is "I alone am the agent.

This intention has been made manifest by the Blessed One in the subsequent passages, such as: "In this situation, he who [regards] the isolated Self alone as the agent," and so forth. This is the summary.
Thus ends the refutation of the Sāṅkhya doctrine.

Regarding "dharma and adharma": the term "self" (ātman) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. If the body were the locus of these, then it would be impossible for actions performed in one body to result in experience in another body. Regarding "particularity" (viśeṣa): the self can be perceived through its connection with specific qualities such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth that are capable of being perceived; it cannot be perceived otherwise, because of such cognitions as "I know" and "I act. (46) Thus ends the statement of the means of knowledge regarding the self.
If that is the case, how can there be memory when the sense organs are impaired? (48)
The mind also is not so; otherwise, it would be imperceptible like cognition and other qualities.
[But] it is perceptible as the substratum of dharma and adharma, due to its connection with specific qualities. (49)

It should not be said that this contradicts the statement: "All actions performed in every way by the qualities of *prakṛti*, the self deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer. For *prakṛti* here refers to *adṛṣṭa* (the unseen merit/demerit), which is inferred from activity and so forth, just as a charioteer is inferred from the movement of a chariot.
This is the substratum of egoism and the object of the mind alone. ||50||
The pervasive [self] possesses qualities such as intellect; however, intellect is considered to be of two kinds.

"By activity" (pravṛttyā): this self is inferred through activity and so forth in another's body and the like. Here, "activity" (pravṛtti) means volitional effort (ceṣṭā), because it has already been stated that knowledge, desire, and effort do not exist in the body, and because volitional effort is achieved through exertion; thus, the sense is that the self, which possesses effort, is inferred by means of volitional effort. He provides an example for this: "as in the case of a chariot" (ratha). Although the motion of a chariot is not volitional effort, nevertheless, just as a charioteer is inferred by that motion, so too the supreme self is inferred by the action consisting of volitional effort. This is the intended meaning.
Thus concludes the exposition of the means of valid cognition regarding the self in relation to another body and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "of the ego-sense" (ahaṅkārasya): the ego-sense is the notion "I"; its substratum—its object—is the Self, and not the body or other such things.

Regarding the word "mind" (manaḥ): it means that [the Self] is not an object of perception produced by sense-organs other than the mind, but is an object of mental perception, because, due to the absence of color and other qualities, it is unsuitable for the other senses. ||50||

"Omnipresent" (vibhu): omnipresence is the state of possessing the dimension of supreme magnitude. Although this has been stated previously, it is mentioned here again for the sake of clarity. "Possessing qualities such as intellect" (buddhyādiguṇavat): the fourteen qualities—intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth—should be understood as having been mentioned previously.
This concludes the description of the nature of the self.
There would be both direct experience and memory; and direct experience is of four kinds. (51)

In this very context, as an incidental discussion, he demonstrates a brief elaboration of cognition (*buddhi*). He explains its twofold nature with the words "anubhūti" (experience). The instruments for these four types of experience are to be understood as the four means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) mentioned in the aphorism: "Perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony are the means of valid knowledge. Knowledge produced by the sense organs is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Although every cognition whatsoever is produced by the mind as a sense-organ (*manas*), nevertheless, that cognition in which the sense-organs function as instruments (*karaṇa*) specifically in their capacity as sense-organs is intended here as perception (*pratyakṣa*). Divine perception (*īśvara-pratyakṣa*), however, is not included in this definition, because it was stated exactly so in the Sūtra: "Perception is cognition produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object, which is non-verbal, non-erroneous, and determinate."

Alternatively, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is knowledge whose instrument is not another knowledge. Since inferential knowledge (*anumiti*) has the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) as its instrument, analogical knowledge (*upamiti*) the knowledge of similarity (*sādṛśya*), verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) the knowledge of words (*padajñāna*), and recollection (*smṛti*) experience (*anubhava*) as their respective instruments, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of this definition to those cases. This definition applies equally to the perception of the Lord (*īśvara*). Inferential knowledge is knowledge produced by a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*). Although perceptual knowledge of the subsumptive reflection itself is also produced by a subsumptive reflection, only that knowledge which is produced by a subsumptive reflection and does not have the logical reason (*hetu*) as its object is inferential knowledge.

Nor should it be argued that there is no definition for inference regarding an object whose cause is occasional (*kādācitka*), because what is intended is the possession of a genus (*jāti*) pervaded by "experientiality" (*anubhavatva*) residing in such a cognition.
Alternatively, inference is a cognition whose instrument is the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*);
likewise, comparison (*upamiti*) is a cognition whose instrument is the knowledge of similarity (*sādṛśya*).
Verbal cognition is a cognition produced by the instrument of word-knowledge.
Perception, inference, comparison, and that which is born of words [are the types of valid knowledge].
Perception is considered to be of six kinds, distinguished as olfactory perception and so forth. (52)

In reality, taking any particular instance of inference (*anumiti*), the nature of being an inference (*anumititva*) consists in possessing a universal (*jāti*) that resides in that particular instance but does not reside in any particular instance of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Similarly, taking any particular instance of perception and so forth, the nature of being perception (*pratyakṣatva*) and the like should be stated as possessing a universal that resides in that particular instance but does not reside in any instance of inference.
Thus concludes the statement of the definitions of the means of valid cognition, such as perception.

He classifies produced perception (*janyapratyakṣa*)—namely, that which is born of the nose and so forth. Perception is sixfold: olfactory, gustatory, visual, tactile, auditory, and mental. Nor is there a deficiency due to the non-classification of God’s perception (*īśvarapratyakṣa*), because it is only produced perception that is to be defined, in accordance with the stated sūtra. ||41||42||

"Object of perception" (*gocara*) means that which is apprehended (*grāhya*). By the phrase "odor-ness and so forth," qualities such as fragrance and the like are included. Since odor is perceptible, the genus (*jāti*) residing therein is also perceptible; however, it should be understood that the sense of smell lacks the capacity to grasp the substratum of that odor.

Similarly, "taste" means accompanied by taste-ness (*rasatva*) and so forth. Likewise, "sound" also means accompanied by sound-ness (*śabdatva*) and so forth. It should be understood that both odor and taste must be manifested (*udbhūta*). Regarding "manifested color" (*udbhūtarūpa*): in cases such as summer heat, color is unmanifested and thus not perceptible. "Possessing that" means possessing manifested color.

Regarding the term "suitable" (*yogya*): even properties such as distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and so forth should be understood as residing in suitable individuals. Such [a property] resides in a suitable individual. How is it that visual suitability itself [is established]? To this he says: "perceives. Conjunction with light (*āloka-saṃyoga*) and manifested color (*udbhūta-rūpa*) are the causes for visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*). Among these, with respect to the visual perception of a substance, these two function as causes by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); whereas with respect to the perception of qualities such as color which inhere in a substance, they function as causes by way of the relation of inherence-in-what-is-inherent-in-their-substratum (*svāśraya-samaveta-samavāya*). ||54||57||
Odor is known as the object of the sense of smell, as well as the quality of odor-ness and so forth;
likewise is taste for the sense of tasting, and sound for the sense of hearing. (53)

Visible form is the object of the eye; substances possessing it, as well as distinctness, number, disjunction, conjunction, priority and posteriority, viscidity, fluidity, and dimension, are likewise its objects. ||54||
Through its connection with light and manifested color, the eye perceives action, genus, the appropriate function, and suchlike inherence. (55)
A substance possessing manifested touch is the object of the skin; that [touch] is also the cause of the skin's perception.
Whatever else besides color-form is suitable for the eye, color-form is likewise the cause in this case as well. (56)

Regarding the term "manifested" (*udbhūta*): a substance possessing manifested touch is the object of the sense of touch (*tvac*). That [touch] as well—meaning the manifested touch, together with the universal *sparśatva* (touch-ness) and so forth—is [perceived]. Regarding the phrase "other than color" (*rūpānyat*): whatever is distinct from color and distinct from the universal *rūpatva* (color-ness), and is suitable for the eye, that is also graspable by the tactile organ. Thus, the meaning is that those qualities such as separateness (*pṛthaktva*) and number (*saṅkhyā*) which were stated to be graspable by the eye, as well as action (*kriyā*), universals (*jāti*), and so forth, when they reside in a suitable substrate, are graspable by the sense of touch.

In this regard as well—it has been held that color (*rūpa*) is the cause for the perception of a substance by the sense of touch (*tvagindriya*), and thus color is the cause for the perception of a substance by any external sense organ (*bahirindriya*). However, the moderns (*navīna*) maintain that color is not the cause for every perception of a substance by the sense of touch, as there is no evidence for such a claim; rather, color is the cause for visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*), while touch (*sparśa*) is the cause for tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*), based on positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

If it is asked what the cause is for the mere perception of a substance by means of an external sense-organ, the answer is: none whatsoever; or rather, let the presence of a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) that does not reside in the self and is distinct from sound be the determining factor. If it is argued that there is parsimony (lāghava) in taking color (rūpa) as the cause, we say no.

[Otherwise], there would be the undesirable consequence that air could not be perceived by the sense of touch. If you argue that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), then let it be that only manifest touch (*udbhūta-sparśa*) is the cause [of perception] due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Why, then, is the non-perception of light (*prabhā*) not likewise accepted as an acceptable consequence? Therefore, just as one says "I see light," since the cognition "I touch air" exists, the perceptibility of air is indeed possible. In the case of all external sensory perceptions of substances, neither color (*rūpa*) nor touch (*sparśa*) is a necessary cause.

They say that in the case of air and light, unity is indeed perceived; sometimes duality and so forth are also perceived, while at other times there is a non-perception of number, dimension, and so on, due to a defect [in the sense organ]. Thus ends the description of visual and other types of perception, as well as the objects of the eye and so forth.
In the case of substances, the contact of the skin with the mind is the cause of cognition.

Regarding "the contact of the skin": the meaning is that the conjunction of the skin and the mind is the cause for cognition in general. What is the proof for this? It is that during deep sleep, when the mind has left the skin and resides in the *purītat*, no cognition is produced.

Now, what kind of cognition will exist at the time of deep sleep—is it of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*) or of the nature of recollection (*smaraṇa*)? It cannot be the first, because of the absence of the causal conditions for experience; for instance, in visual and other types of perception, the conjunction of the mind with the eyes and other sense organs is the cause, and in its absence, visual and other perceptions do not occur. Due to the absence of [objects such as] knowledge and so forth, there is no mental perception; and since even the self is not perceived in the absence of knowledge and the like, there is no perception of the self either.
Furthermore, due to the absence of the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no inference, and due to the absence of the knowledge of similarity, there is no analogy.

"There is no verbal cognition because of the absence of the knowledge of the word-meaning; there is no experience because of the absence of the causal complex for experience; and there is no recollection because of the absence of an excitant. Do not say this, for it would follow that the self and the specific instance of desire produced at the time immediately preceding deep sleep would be perceptible by virtue of their connection [with the sense organs].

This is because there is no evidence for its being beyond the senses, and likewise, there is no proof for the claim that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) necessarily arises immediately prior to deep sleep. Furthermore, if the contact between the skin and the mind (*tvag-manas-saṃyoga*) were the cause of all cognition in general, then at the time of visual or gustatory perception, tactile perception would also occur, since both the contact between the object and the eye (or tongue) and the contact between the skin and the mind are present; or else, due to mutual obstruction, not even one of them would occur.

On this point, some maintain that once it is established—by the reasoning previously stated—that the contact between the skin and the mind is a cause of cognition, the fact that the causal complex for visual perception and the like obstructs tactile perception must be postulated in accordance with experience. Others, however, argue that the contact between the skin and the mind is postulated as the cause of cognition in order to account for deep sleep; thus, at the time of visual or other types of perception, no tactile perception occurs because of the absence of the contact between the skin and the mind.
Thus concludes the establishment of the conjunction between the skin and the mind as a cause of cognition.
Pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, cognition, and volition are apprehended by the mind. ||57||

"Cognizable by the mind" (manogrāhya) means that it is the object of perception produced by the mind. "Cognition" (mati) refers to knowledge; "volition" (kṛti) refers to effort, but since it was previously stated [in verse 56] that these are "within the range of the mind alone" (manomātrasya gocaraḥ), they are not mentioned here again. ||57||
Thus concludes the examination of objects perceivable by the mind.

That knowledge which is called *nirvikalpa* (indeterminate) is held to be beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Immediately following the contact of the eye [with an object], a cognition in the form "this is a jar" (*ghaṭa*)—which has as its object the jar as qualified by the property of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth—is not possible, because prior to that there is no cognition of the qualifier, jar-ness, etc.; for the cognition of the qualifier is a necessary cause for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*). Thus, at first, a cognition arises that does not even apprehend the relation of qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) between the jar and jar-ness; that alone is the indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition. And that is not perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance: a cognition that does not apprehend a relational qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) cannot be perceptual, because of the awareness "I know the jar. In that [awareness], knowledge appears as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in relation to the self; the jar [appears] in relation to the knowledge; and in that [jar], jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) [appears]. That which is the qualifier is called the "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). That which is the qualifier of the qualifier is called the "delimitor of the qualifierhood" (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*).

A cognition having the qualifier-determinant (viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka) as its mode is the cause of a cognition of the qualified-qualifier-relation (viśiṣṭavaiśiṣṭyajñāna). In indeterminate cognition (nirvikalpaka), however, "potness" and so forth are not modes; therefore, it is impossible for there to be an appearance of the relation of a pot qualified by potness within that cognition. Furthermore, a cognition of a pot qualified by potness cannot occur if potness is not its mode, because there is a rule that the cognition of any category other than a universal (jāti) or an impartite adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi) must necessarily have some property as its mode. Thus concludes the determination of the supersensible nature of indeterminate cognition.
Greatness is the cause in six ways; the sense organ is considered the instrument. ||58||

Regarding "largeness" (*mahattva*): largeness is the cause in the perception of a substance by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). It is the cause in the perception of qualities, actions, and universals inherent in a substance by way of the relation of inherence in its own substratum (*svāśraya-samavāya*), and it is the cause in the perception of quality-ness, action-ness, and so forth, which are inherent in those [qualities and actions] inherent in a substance, by way of the relation of inherence in what is inherent in its own substratum (*svāśraya-samaveta-samavāya*). Thus concludes the establishment of largeness as the cause of perception.

Regarding the term "sense organ" (*indriya*): here too, the phrase "of six kinds" is to be supplied. Sense-organhood (*indriyatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), because it would involve a logical overlap (*sāṅkarya*) with earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such properties; rather, sense-organhood is the state of being the substratum of the mind-contact that is a cause of cognition, while being a non-substratum of manifested special qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) other than sound. The term "while being [a non-substratum]" (*satyantam*) excludes the self (*ātman*) and so forth. The phrase "other than sound" (*śabdetara*) is included because manifested special qualities exist in the ear. The term "manifested" (*udbhūta*) is included because special qualities such as color (*rūpa*) exist in the eye and other organs as well.

Manifestness (*udbhūtatva*) is not a universal (*jāti*), because it would result in a logical overlap (*saṅkara*) with qualities such as whiteness (*śuklatva*). Nor should it be argued that there are multiple instances of manifestness each pervaded by whiteness and so forth; for in that case, it would be impossible for [the quality of] being a manifested color (*udbhūtarūpatva*) to function as a cause for visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*) and the like. Rather, non-manifestness (*anudbhūtatva*) consists of multiple instances each pervaded by whiteness and so forth, and manifestness is the collection of the absences of those [instances of non-manifestness]. This [manifestness] also exists in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other qualities. Thus, since conjunction and the like—which are manifested qualities other than sound—also exist in the eye and other sense organs, the word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) is used [in the definition]. The qualifying term (*viśeṣya-dala*) is included to exclude time (*kāla*) and other such entities.

In the view of the ancients, since the contact between the sense organ and its own parts is also a generator of perception, the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) is included to exclude those parts of the sense organ. In the view of the moderns, it is included to exclude time and other such entities which, by being the substratum of the visual contact that serves as a constituent of the *sannikarṣa* (contact) in the perception of the absence of color in time and so forth, act as causes. The phrase "cause of knowledge" (*jñānakāraṇa*) is also for the very purpose of excluding those [parts of the sense organ]. Regarding the term "instrument" (*karaṇa*): an instrument is an uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇa-kāraṇa*). Uncommonness consists in possessing an operation (*vyāpāravattva*). 58.
Thus concludes the examination of the sense faculties.
The contact between the object and the sense organ is the operation (vyāpāra), and that too is of six kinds:
the apprehension of substance occurs through conjunction (saṃyoga) and through inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya). ||59||
Likewise, [cognition arises] for those [qualities] inherent in substances through their inherence therein;
and for those inherent even in that [inherence], it arises through the inherence of the word. (60)
The apprehension of the qualities residing in those [substances] occurs through inherence-in-the-inherent (samavetasamavāya);
however, the perception of inherence itself occurs by way of being a qualifier (viśeṣaṇatā). 61.
The apprehension of absences as qualified by that [locus] would occur only in cases where it is applicable to say, "If it were present, it would be perceived. (62)

"The connection between the object and the sense-organ" refers to the operation, namely, *sannikarṣa* (contact). He demonstrates the sixfold nature of contact by way of examples: "In the apprehension of substance," etc. The perception of a substance is produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with the sense-organ. The perception of that which is inherent (*samaveta*) in a substance is produced by inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*). The same applies to the subsequent cases as well.

In reality, however, visual conjunction (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyoga*) is the cause of the visual perception of a substance; visual conjunction-inherence (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samavāya*) is the cause of the visual perception of that which inheres in a substance; and visual conjunction-inherence-inherence (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*) is the cause of the visual perception of that which inheres in what inheres in a substance. Thus, in other cases as well, the causal relationship is established specifically [according to the nature of the object].

But why is it that blueness in a blue earth-atom and earthness in an earth-atom are not perceived by the eye? For in those cases, there exists a connection with manifested color (*udbhūta-rūpa*) and a connection with magnitude (*mahattva*) through a causal chain (*paramparā*). To explain: the single universal (*jāti*) of blueness resides both in the blueness of a jar and in the blueness of an atom; likewise, the connection with magnitude resides in the blueness of the jar.

However, the relation with manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) exists only by taking both [the substance and the quality] together; likewise, even in the case of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), the relation with magnitude (*mahattva*) should be understood as existing by taking the jar and so forth together. In this way, there would be visual perception (*cākṣuṣapratyakṣa*) of existence (*sattā*) in air and its touch and so forth. Therefore, one must state that the cause of the visual perception of what is inherent in a substance is the inherence in what is conjoined with the eye (*cakṣuḥsaṃyuktasamavāya*), qualified by manifested color and qualified by magnitude; and the cause of the visual perception of what is inherent in what is inherent in a substance is the inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined with the eye (*tādṛśacakṣuḥsaṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*). And thus, there is no apprehension of blueness and so forth in the blue color of an atom.

Because in an atom, there is an absence of the visual contact being delimited by magnitude (*mahattva*). Likewise, there is no visual perception of existence (*sattā*) and so forth in air and the like, because in those cases, the visual contact is not delimited by color (*rūpa*). Similarly, where there is a contact with light delimited by the back of a jar, while the visual contact is delimited by its front, there is an absence of the perception of the jar; therefore, the property of being "delimited by contact with light" must be added as a qualification to the visual contact.

Thus, in the tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*) of a substance, the cause is conjunction with the skin (*tvak-saṃyoga*); in the tactile perception of that which is inherent (*samaveta*) in a substance, it is inherence in what is conjoined with the skin (*tvak-saṃyukta-samavāya*); and in the tactile perception of that which is inherent in what is inherent in a substance, it is inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined with the skin (*tvak-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*). Here too, as before, it should be understood that [the object] must be delimited by magnitude (*mahattva*) and delimited by manifested touch (*udbhūta-sparśa*). Similarly, in the perception of odor (*gandha*), the cause is inherence in what is conjoined with the nose (*ghrāṇa-saṃyukta-samavāya*); and in the olfactory perception of that which is inherent in odor, it is inherence in what is inherent in what is conjoined with the nose (*ghrāṇa-saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*).

In the case of gustatory perception (*rāsanapratyakṣa*), the cause is inherence in that which is conjoined with the tongue (*rasanāsaṃyuktasamavāya*); in the case of gustatory perception of what inheres in taste (*rasasamavetarāsanapratyakṣa*), the cause is inherence in that which inheres in what is conjoined with the tongue (*rasanāsaṃyuktasamavetasamavāya*).

In the case of auditory perception of sound (*śabdapratyakṣa*), the cause is inherence delimited by the ear (*śrotrāvacchinnasamavāya*); in the case of auditory perception of what inheres in sound (*śabdasamavetaśrāvaṇapratyakṣa*), the cause is inherence in that which inheres in what is delimited by the ear (*śrotrāvacchinnasamavetasamavāya*).

Here, all such perception should be understood as ordinary (*laukika*). The extraordinary (*alaukika*) perception to be described hereafter can occur even without the conjunction of the sense organs and so forth.

Thus, in the case of mental perception of the self (*ātman*), the cause is conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*); in the case of mental perception of what is inherent in the self (*ātma-samaveta*), the cause is inherence in that which is conjoined with the mind (*saṃyukta-samavāya*); and in the case of mental perception of what is inherent in what is inherent in the self (*ātma-samaveta-samaveta*), the cause is inherence in that which is inherent in what is conjoined with the mind (*saṃyukta-samaveta-samavāya*).

In the perception of absence (*abhāva*) and the perception of inherence (*samavāya*), the cause is the state of being a qualifier of that which is connected to a sense organ (*indriya-sambaddha-viśeṣaṇatā*). However, in the Vaiśeṣika system, inherence is not perceptible. Although the state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatā*) here is of various kinds—for instance, the absence of a jar on the ground is perceived through the state of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā*)—[the rest follows as per the original].

The absence of color and so forth in number and the like [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier of that which is inhering in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamaveta-viśeṣaṇatā*); the absence of color and so forth in the universal "number-ness" (*saṅkhyātva*) and the like [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier of that which inheres in what inheres in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavetasamaveta-viśeṣaṇatā*); the absence of sound [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier delimited solely by the auditory organ (*kevalaśrotra-avacchinna-viśeṣaṇatā*); the absence of "kh-ness" (*khatva*) and so forth in the letter *ka* and the like [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier of a qualifier inhering in what is delimited by the auditory organ (*śrotra-avacchinna-samaveta-viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣaṇatā*); likewise, the absence of "ga-ness" (*gatva*) and so forth in the absence of "ka-ness" (*katva*) and the like [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier delimited by the auditory organ (*śrotra-avacchinna-viśeṣaṇatā*); and so it is in the case of the absence of a jar and the like.

The absence of cloth [is perceived] by way of being a qualifier of a qualifier conjoined with the eye. This should be inferred in other cases as well; nevertheless, it is counted as only one in terms of its nature as "qualifier-ness" (viśeṣaṇatā), otherwise the traditional doctrine of the ancients that there are six types of contact would be contradicted. Thus ends the determination of ordinary (laukika) contact.

In this case, the non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is the cause for the perception of absence. To explain: when the cognition of a jar or the like has arisen with respect to a surface such as the ground, the absence of that jar and so forth is not cognized. Therefore, the non-perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the cause for the apprehension of absence. In this regard, perceptibility (*yogyatā*) is also required.

And that [non-existence] consists in having as its counter-positive (pratiyogin) that which is implied by the implication of the existence of the counter-positive; and the meaning of this is that the cause for the perception of non-existence is that whose counter-positive is of the nature of a perception implied by the contingency of the existence of the counter-positive, such as a jar. To illustrate: where there is contact with light and so forth, one can apply the following reductio (*āpatti*): "If a jar were here, it would be perceived."

In that regard, the perception of the absence of a jar and so forth occurs; however, it cannot be brought about in darkness. Therefore, there is no visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*) of the absence of a jar and so forth in darkness, but tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*) certainly does occur, because tactile perception can be brought about even without the conjunction of light and other such factors.

That which is unfit for perception, such as gravity and the like, its absence is not fit for perception, because it is impossible to bring about the perceptual apprehension of gravity and so forth in that case. However, the absence of manifest color in air, the absence of fragrance in stone, the absence of bitterness in molasses, the absence of non-heat in fire, the absence of sound in the auditory organ, the absence of pleasure and so forth in the self—these and others are perceived by their respective sense organs, because it is possible to bring about the perceptual apprehension of those respective absences.

In the perception of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is required; in the perception of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), the fitness of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is required. Therefore, even the difference between a pillar and a *piśāca* (demon) is apprehended by the eye. 59 || 60 || 61 || 62 ||
But the extraordinary operation (alaukika-vyāpāra) is proclaimed to be of three kinds:
that characterized by generality (sāmānyalakṣaṇa), that characterized by cognition (jñānalakṣaṇa), and likewise that born of yoga (yogaja). ||63||
The proximity of the substrata, however, is held to be the cognition of their commonality;
that depends upon the causal complex consisting of the sense organ and the apprehension of its properties. (64)

Thus, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is of two kinds, distinguished as worldly (*laukika*) and non-worldly (*alaukika*). Among these, six types of contact (*sannikarṣa*) have been described regarding worldly perception. Now, the non-worldly contact is being stated: "The non-worldly," and so forth. "Contact" means an operation (*vyāpāra*). Regarding the term "characterized by the universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): the meaning is that its characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is the universal (*sāmānya*). In this context, if the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the essential nature (*svarūpa*), then the meaning obtained is that the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) has the universal as its essential nature.

And that [universal] should be understood as being the qualifier (*prakāra*) of a cognition whose qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is connected with a sense-organ; for instance, when smoke or the like is in contact with a sense-organ, and a cognition "this is smoke" arises having that [smoke] as its qualificand, then "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) is the qualifier in that cognition. Thereupon, by means of the sense-contact consisting of smokeness, there arises a cognition in the form "all these are smoke," which has all instances of smoke as its object.

In this context, if it were stated merely that "that which is related to the sense organ has become the qualifier," then after the error of perceiving "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) in a mass of dust, there would be no cognition having all instances of smoke as its object; for in that case, there is no sensory relation with "smokeness. According to my view, however, the mass of dust is related to the sense organ, and the cognition "this is smoke" has that [dust] as its qualificandum; therein, "smokeness," which has become the qualifier, serves as the means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Furthermore, the sensory relation to be understood here is the ordinary (*laukika*) one.

And this [is the case] in the context of the external sense-faculties; however, in the context of the mental faculty, the universal that serves as the qualifier of the cognition is the means of proximity (pratyāsatti). ||63||

However, the state of being common (*sāmānya*) is "generality" (*sāmānya*); and that is sometimes eternal, such as "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*), and sometimes non-eternal, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*). When one jar is known to be on the ground by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), or in its constituent parts (*kapāla*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*), there subsequently arises knowledge of all those grounds or parts that possess that same jar; in this case, it should be understood as follows: however, by whatever relation the generality is known, by that same relation there is the proximity (*pratyāsatti*) of the loci.

However, in a case where the recollection of the possessor of that jar occurs after the destruction of that jar, there would be no manifestation of all those possessing such jars through the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇā), because at that time the universal no longer exists.

Furthermore, why is it that such a cognition—which has as its qualifier the universal that serves as the mode (*prakāra*) of the cognition "this is a jar" produced on a previous day—is not generated the following day even in the absence of sense-object contact? Since the universal serving as the mode of that cognition exists [at that time], why is such a cognition not produced? Therefore, he says "proximity" (*āsatti*), meaning that the cognition having the universal as its object is the "proximate cause" (*pratyāsatti*), and not the universal itself. "Proximity" (*āsatti*) means "the proximate cause" (*pratyāsatti*).

And likewise, in the expression "having a universal as its characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) has the meaning of "object" (*viṣaya*). Therefore, the sense obtained is that proximity (*pratyāsatti*) is a cognition whose object is a universal. Now, one might object: even in the absence of contact between the eye and the object, where there exists a cognition of a universal, there would follow visual perception of all jars and so forth; therefore, he says "that" (*tad*).

The meaning of this is as follows: when a cognition characterized by a universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is to be produced by an external sense organ, then a certain substrate (dharmin) requires the causal complex (sāmagrī) for the cognition of that universal produced by that sense organ. And that causal complex consists of the contact between the eye and the object, the contact with light, and so forth. Therefore, in darkness and similar conditions, such a cognition is not produced by the eye or other senses. ||64||
Thus concludes the examination of the proximity of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*).
The operation characterized by cognition belongs to that very [object] which is its object.

Now, if the cognitive proximity (jñānalakṣaṇā) is of the nature of cognition, and the universal-characterized proximity (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) is also of the nature of cognition, then there would be no distinction between the two; therefore, he says "the object" (viṣayī). For the proximity characterized by the universal produces a cognition of its substratum, whereas the proximity characterized by cognition is the proximity of that very [object] which is the content of the cognition.

The meaning here is as follows: in perception, manifestation without sensory contact is impossible; and likewise, without the "universal-characteristic" (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) [type of perception], how could there be the manifestation of all instances of smoke by way of the universal "smokeness," or of all instances of fire by way of the universal "fireness"? It is for this purpose that the universal-characteristic is accepted. Nor should it be argued: "What loss is there if there is no manifestation of all fires and all smokes?"

Since the connection of fire with smoke has already been apprehended in the case of perceptible smoke, and since other smoke is not present [to consciousness], the doubt as to whether "smoke is pervaded by fire or not" would be untenable. In my view, however, once all instances of smoke are presented through *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* (the generic character), it is possible to have a doubt regarding the pervasion of fire in smoke belonging to another time or place. Nor should it be argued that if *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* is accepted, omniscience would result when the knowledge of all objects of cognition arises through the property of "knowability" (*prameyatva*).
Even when the knowledge of all knowable objects has arisen through their status as "knowable" (*prameyatva*), omniscience is not established because specific details of all things remain unknown.

Likewise, if the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) is not accepted, how could there be the manifestation of fragrance in the cognition "this is fragrant sandalwood"? Although the manifestation of fragrance is possible even through the "characteristic of the universal" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), the manifestation of the property of "fragrance-ness" (*saurabhatva*) occurs through the characteristic of cognition. Similarly, where a mass of dust is known as smoke by virtue of its being smoke, the manifestation of that mass of dust in the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) occurs through the characteristic of cognition.
Thus concludes the examination of the proximity characterized by knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇapratyāsatti*).
That which is born of yoga is said to be of two kinds, distinguished by the states of being "constantly engaged" (yukta) and "practicing" (yuñjāna). ||65||
"For one who is constantly disciplined (yukta), there is manifestation at all times; the other [type of knowledge] is accompanied by reflection (cintā).

It is born of yoga (yogaja)" means that it is a specific dharma produced by the practice of yoga, as propounded in the Śruti, Purāṇas, and so forth. The sense is that because there are two types of yogis—namely, the "constantly disciplined" (yukta) and the "practicing" (yuñjāna)—there is also a twofold nature of this dharma. ||65||

Regarding the phrase "of the one who is disciplined": for one who is disciplined, cognition whose object is the entirety of categories—such as space, atoms, and so forth—ought to arise at all times by means of the mind aided by the dharma born of yoga; for the second [type of practitioner], a specific form of reflection is also a contributing factor.
Thus concludes the examination of the proximity born of yoga.
Thus ends the chapter on perception in the *Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī*, composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.
Now begins the section on inference (anumāna): the operation (vyāpāra) is the reflective judgment (parāmarśa), while the instrument (karaṇa) is the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti). (66)

He explains inference (*anumiti*). Regarding the phrase "the operation, however": in the case of inference—that is, in inferential cognition—the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*).

To explain: by whatever person the pervasion of fire by smoke has been apprehended in a kitchen or similar location, that same person later perceives a streak of smoke with an unbroken base on a mountain or elsewhere; immediately thereafter, he experiences a recollection of the pervasion in the form "smoke is pervaded by fire"; subsequently, there arises the cognition "this [mountain] possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire"—this very cognition is called *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection); and following that, the inferential knowledge "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*) is produced.
Thus concludes the examination of the causes of inferential cognition.
Furthermore, the inferential mark (liṅga) being known at the time of inference is certainly not the instrument;
for otherwise, there would be no inference from a future or other such [unperceived] mark. (67)
The cognition that the pervaded (the probans) resides in the subject is called "consideration" (parāmarśa).

In this regard, the ancients maintain that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) known as being pervaded (*vyāpyatvena jñāyamāna*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inference. He refutes that by saying "known" (*jñāyamānam*). He provides the reasoning for why the inferential mark is not the instrument of inference by stating "future, etc. (*anāgatādi*):

if the inferential mark were the instrument in inference, then there would be no inference from a future mark or from one that has perished, because the inferential mark—which is the instrument of inference—would be non-existent at that time. Thus ends the refutation of the view that the inferential mark known [as being pervaded] is the cause of inference.

Regarding the phrase "of the pervaded" (*vyāpyasya*): the cognition that apprehends the qualified relation between the pervaded (the reason) and the subject (*pakṣa*) is the generator of inference. This [cognition] consists either in the knowledge "the pervaded is in the subject" (*pakṣe vyāpyaḥ*) or the knowledge "the subject possesses the pervaded" (*pakṣo vyāpyavān*). From the former cognition—"the pervaded is in the subject"—the inference takes the form "the probandum (*sādhya*) is in the subject"; from the latter cognition—"the subject possesses the pervaded"—the inference takes the form "the subject possesses the probandum.
Others hold that from both types of *parāmarśa*, the resulting inference is exclusively of the form "the subject possesses the probandum."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that even without the cognition 'the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire,' where there is first the perception 'the mountain has smoke' and then the recollection 'smoke is pervaded by fire,' an inference is observed to arise from these two cognitions alone? Therefore, a cognition apprehending the qualification of that which is qualified by the pervasion (*vyāpti-viśiṣṭa-vaiśiṣṭya-avagāhi-jñāna*) is not the cause in all cases. Rather, since it is necessary for the status of being a cause to be as the cognition of the property-in-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) having the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) as its qualifier, and because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate a qualified cognition in such instances, [such a cognition is not required]. [Reply: No.

Even when the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) is unknown, an inference arises from the cognition "this possesses the pervader of fire" (*vahnivyāpyavān*); furthermore, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), the cause [of inference] is the cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*) having pervasion as its qualifier (*vyāptiprakāraka*).

Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence of an inference arising from the cognition "the mountain has smoke," because there exists a cognition of the property of the subject whose qualifier is the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*), which serves as the delimiting factor of pervasion.

Nor should it be argued that the cause is a cognition of the property of the subject whose qualifier is a currently being grasped delimiting factor of pervasion; for in that case, an inference would arise in Maitra from his cognition of the property of the subject, even though Caitra is the one who has grasped the pervasion.

If it is asserted that the cognition of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatājñāna) for a particular person—having as its qualifier the delimitor of pervasion (vyāpyatāvacchedaka) as perceived by that person—is the cause of that person's inference, then there would be an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations. In my view, however, a cognition having pervasion as its qualifier produces an inference through the relation of inherence (samavāya); thus, there is no infinite regress of cause-and-effect relations.

If, however, it is asserted that the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the cognition of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) are independent causes [of inference], then there would be two distinct causal relations; consequently, an inference would arise even from the cognition "smoke is pervaded by fire and the mountain possesses light. And thus, even in cases where there are two separate cognitions, a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) must be postulated, since complexity resulting from the nature of the effect (*phalamukhagaurava*) is not a fault. Thus concludes the determination of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection).
Pervasion (vyāpti) is declared to be the absence of connection with anything other than that which possesses the probandum. ||68||

The "pervaded" (vyāpya) is that which is the locus of pervasion (vyāptyāśraya). To the question "What is pervasion (vyāpti) in this context?", he says: "Pervasion... In cases such as "That [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke," fire is the probandum (sādhya); a kitchen and the like are the loci possessing the probandum (sādhyavat); other than those are things such as lakes; and the fact that smoke exists in those [lakes] is the application of the definition. Since fire exists in the lump [of clay] and so forth, there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).

In this context, by whatever relation the probandum (*sādhya*) exists, by that same relation must the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavat*) be understood. Otherwise, if one were to consider a mountain as distinct from fire by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), then since smoke exists in a kitchen—which is other than that [mountain]—there would be the undesirable consequence of an over-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Furthermore, "other than the locus of the probandum" (*sādhyavadanya*) should be understood as possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the state of being the locus of the probandum. By this, there is no fault even if smoke exists on a mountain, which is distinct from some particular locus of fire such as a kitchen.

By whatever relation the status of being a reason (*hetutā*) is established, by that very same relation the absence of occurrence in what is other than that which possesses the probandum (*sādhyavadanyāvṛttitva*) must be understood as the definition. By this, there is no fault even if smoke exists in a part of smoke—which is other than that which possesses the probandum—by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, "absence of occurrence in what is other than that which possesses the probandum" means an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of occurring in what is other than that which possesses the probandum; therefore, in the case of "smoke-possessing [mountain] because of fire," there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*), even though there is an absence of occurrence in things like lakes, which are other than that which possesses the probandum.

In this context, although in an inference such as "Substance [is] distinct from quality and action because it possesses existence" (*dravyaṃ guṇakarmānyatvaviśiṣṭasattvāt*), there is no non-occurrence in qualities and so forth—which are other than that which possesses the probandum—because qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) and pure existence (*śuddhasattā*) are one and the same, nevertheless, non-occurrence must be stated in terms of the delimiting property of the reason (*hetutāvacchedakarūpeṇa*). The resulting meaning is that the delimiting property of the reason is not a delimiting property of the occurrence (*vṛttitānavacchedaka*). ||68|| Thus ends the section on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the exposition of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Alternatively, pervasion (vyāpti) is said to be the co-occurrence (aikādhikaraṇya) of the reason with a probandum that is not the counter-positive of an absence residing in the locus of the reason. (69)

[Objection: But surely, when a property such as "knowability" (*jñeyatva*)—which is purely positive (*kevalānvayin*)—is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) because another instance of that which possesses the probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore, in cases such as "existence (*sattā*) is present in generality (*jāti*)," there is no occurrence (*vṛtti*) in something other than that which possesses the probandum (namely, in universals like *sāmānya*) by means of the relation that delimits the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*), which is inherence (*samavāya*). To this, he says: "Or else (*atha vā*). That which has its residence (*niṣṭha-vṛtti*) in the locus of the reason (*hetumat*) is so [described]; "absence" (*viraha*) means non-existence (*abhāva*). Thus, pervasion is said to be the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the reason with a probandum that is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogin*) of that absence which resides in the locus of the reason.

In this regard, although in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," there is non-pervasion (avyāpti), since the counter-positiveness of absences residing in the locus of the reason—such as the mountain—belongs to that very fire and so forth. Nor should it be said that pervasion belongs only to fire and smoke that are co-locative; for even in the case of specific instances of fire and smoke, the absence of both exists, based on the cognition that "even when one is present, the pair is not. Furthermore, there is non-pervasion in cases such as "it possesses quality because it is a substance. Nevertheless, it must be stated that pervasion is the co-locativity with that which is delimited by the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka), provided that such a delimitor is not itself a delimitor of the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitānavacchedaka).

[Objection: But in cases such as "Earth-ness because it possesses a genus pervaded by color-ness" (*rūpatvavyāpyajātimattvāt*), the delimiters of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) are the genera pervaded by color-ness. Since those [genera], which are essentially whiteness and so forth, serve as the delimiters of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of absences residing in blue jars and the like, there is an instance of under-extension (*avyāpti*). [Reply: This is not so. In that case, what serves as the delimiter of the probandumhood is precisely the property of being a genus pervaded by color-ness (*rūpatvavyāpyajātitva*) through a mediated relation (*paramparayā*). For there is no absence delimited by such a property anywhere in earth; otherwise, there would arise the cognition: "That which possesses a genus pervaded by color-ness does not exist [in earth]."
