They also maintain that because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) varies according to the distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and other factors, in such cases the defining condition of the definition is simply that the delimitant of the delimitation of the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*) is not the non-delimitant of the delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatānavacchedaka*).

The locus of the reason (*hetu*) must be understood as the locus qualified by the delimitant of the reason-ness (*hetutāvacchedakaviśiṣṭādhikaraṇa*). By this, in an inference such as "Substance (is) because of existence qualified by being other than quality and action," there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding substantiality (*dravyatva*), even though it is the counter-correlate of an absence residing in qualities and so forth—which are loci of bare existence (*śuddhasattā*).

The locus of the reason (*hetu*) should be understood by means of the relation that delimits the state of being a reason (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*). By this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding fire, even though fire is the counter-positive of an absence residing in the parts of the locus of smoke (e.g., a mountain) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, the absence should be understood as being non-co-locative with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). By this, in cases such as "this tree possesses monkey-contact because it is a tree," there is no lack of pervasion regarding monkey-contact, even though monkey-contact is the counter-positive of an absence of monkey-contact residing in this tree, delimited by the root.

Furthermore, if "having a different locus from the counter-positive" (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇatva) means "subsisting in what is not the locus of the counter-positive," then the same lack of pervasion (avyāpti) remains; for the absence that subsists in qualities (guṇa) and so forth—which are not the loci of the counter-positive, namely the conjunction with a monkey (kapisaṃyoga)—exists indeed in the tree, delimited by its root.

If, however, [the definition] were "not occurring in the locus of the counter-positive," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in cases such as "this [substance] possesses conjunction because it exists" (*saṃyogī sattvāt*), since the absence of conjunction existing in a quality (*guṇa*)—which is a locus of existence—is present in a substance (*dravya*), which is the locus of the counter-positive. This is not so, because what is intended is [an absence] qualified by its occurrence in a locus of the reason that is not a locus of the counter-positive. The refined formulation is: "an absence occurring in a locus of the reason that does not become the locus of its own counter-positive."

Furthermore, "not being the locus of the counter-positive" must be understood as "not being the locus of that which is delimited by the delimitor of counter-positiveness. By this, in cases such as "possessing qualified existence (viśiṣṭasattā) because of being a genus (jāti)," there is no fault even though qualities (guṇa), which are loci of the genus, are loci of the existence that is the counter-positive of the absence of qualified existence.

Here, "not being the locus of the counter-positive" must be understood in terms of the relation that delimits the state of being the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha); therefore, in cases such as "possessing cognition because of existence," there is no fault even though a jar, which is a locus of existence, is a locus of cognition through the relation of objectivity (viṣayatā).
And thus, in cases such as "this [mountain] possesses fire because of smoke," there is no defect even if the absence of fire exists in the locus of smoke by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

Now, is it intended that [the locus] be non-locus of any counter-positive whatsoever delimited by the delimitor of counter-positiveness, or non-locus of that generality [of counter-positives], or non-locus of whatever is delimited by some delimitor of counter-positiveness?

In the first case, regarding the inference "this [tree] is in contact with a monkey because it is this kind of tree," there is likewise a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*); for even a monkey-contact that does not reside in the tree is delimited by the delimitor of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the absence of monkey-contact, and the tree is the non-locus (*anadhikaraṇa*) of that [contact].

In the second case, however, there is the non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*) of an absence that is non-co-located with its counterpositive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), because every absence whatsoever is co-located with its counterpositive—which consists of its own absence qualified by existence in the preceding moment.

Furthermore, it should not be argued that in cases such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," although a locus like a mountain is indeed a non-locus of the counter-positive—which consists of the absence of itself qualified by existence in the preceding moment—such as the absence of a pot, nevertheless, it is still a non-locus of that counter-positive with respect to the relation delimiting the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha). Thus, how can there be an unestablished [instance of] an absence whose counter-positive is non-locus-resident? This is what must be addressed.

The absence of fire that exists where there is an absence of a jar is, by virtue of being of the nature of the absence of a jar, such that fire is also its counter-positive (pratiyogin), and its locus is the mountain and so forth; thus, in this manner, because an absence whose counter-positive is non-locus-resident (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa) is unestablished [in this case].

Furthermore, even if it is asserted that the absence of fire (*vahnayabhāva*) and so forth is distinct from the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāva*) and so forth, there would still be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "that which possesses the absence of smoke possesses the absence of fire. In that instance, the delimiting relation of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*) is the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*); and by means of that relation, every absence whatsoever has its counter-positive—which consists of its own absence qualified by existence in the preceding moment—as its locus within the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*).

However, in the third [definition], there is non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in such cases as "the self possesses the absence of conjunction with a monkey, because it is a self" (*ātmatvāt*). In that instance, the absence of the absence of conjunction with a monkey—which resides in the self—is "conjunction with a monkey. Since this is a quality (*guṇa*), the property of being the general absence of qualities (*guṇasāmānyābhāvatva*) is also a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of its counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*). Consequently, the locus of the reason—the self—would not be the locus of that which is delimited by that [property]. This is not so. For what is intended is the non-delimitation of such a counter-positiveness as is characterized by the non-locusness of the locus of the reason with respect to the delimitors of that counter-positiveness.

Now, an objection is raised: in the inference "Time possesses a jar, because it has the dimension of time," there is the problem of the non-establishment of an absence that is non-co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇābhāvāprasiddhi*). This is because the locus of the reason, Great Time (*mahākāla*), being the substratum of the entire universe, every absence whatsoever has its counter-positive located within it by virtue of the temporal relation (*kālikaviśeṣaṇatā*), which serves as the delimiting relation for the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*). To this, some respond: the absence of a jar qualified by the difference from Great Time (*mahākālabhedaviśiṣṭaghaṭābhāva*) is indeed non-co-located with its counter-positive in that context. For although Great Time is the substratum of jars, it is not the substratum of jars qualified by the difference from Great Time; this is because the difference from Great Time does not exist in Great Time itself.

In reality, however, it should be understood that a property (*taddharma*) delimited by a relation (*tena sambandhena*) is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of a given reason (*taddhetu*), provided that there is an absence of both "being delimited by that relation" and "being delimited by that property" within the generality of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāsāmānya*) of absences residing in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*), which itself is a non-locus of the counter-positive (*pratiyogyanadhikaraṇa*) with respect to the delimitor of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandha*).

And thus, in such cases as "Time possesses a pot, because it has temporal dimension," the very same absence of a pot by way of conjunction—which exists in Great Time (mahākāla), the locus of the reason, even though that Great Time is not the locus of the pot which is the counter-positive of the pot-absence—is the relevant absence. Since there exists, in the counter-positiveness of that absence, the absence of both "being delimited by the temporal relation" and "being delimited by potness," there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).

[Objection: But is it not the case that in an inference such as "the subject possesses a cognizable fire because of smoke," the property of being delimited by "cognizable fire-ness" (*prameya-vahni-tva*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), since a cumbersome property (*guru-dharma*) cannot serve as a delimiter? [Reply: No. For, through the cognition "there is no [thing] possessing a conch-like neck and so forth," the counter-positive-ness (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by "possessing a conch-like neck and so forth" (*kambugrīvādimattva*) is apprehended; thus, it is accepted that even a cumbersome property can function as a delimiter. This is the summary. (66) Thus ends the section on the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) from the Siddhānta text.
Where there is no established conclusion devoid of the desire to prove it, that is the thesis;
from the knowledge of its subsistence therein, inference arises. (70)

Regarding the phrase "subsistence in the subject" (*pakṣavṛttitvam*), what is meant by "subject-ness" (*pakṣatva*)? To this he says: "by the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣayā*). Subject-ness is the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove; for even without the desire to prove, there is inference of rain from the thundering of clouds. For this very reason, doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasandeha*) is also not subject-ness, because that inference occurs even without such doubt. Even when proof exists, if the desire to prove is present, inference certainly takes place; therefore, being qualified by the absence of the desire to prove is a qualification applied to the proof.

And thus, where there is no proof (*siddhi*), there is the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) provided there is a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), whether that desire exists or not. Where there is a desire to prove, there is the status of being a subject whether proof exists or not. Where proof exists and there is no desire to prove, there is no status of being a subject, because the "proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" is present.

Now, it might be argued: where there is proof (*siddhi*) immediately after the consideration (*parāmarśa*), and from that arises the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), then at the time of the desire to prove, the consideration has perished, so there is no inference (*anumiti*). Where proof, consideration, and the desire to prove occur in succession, there at the time of the desire to prove, since the proof has perished, the inference occurs precisely due to the absence of the obstructing factor. But where the desire to prove, the proof, and the consideration occur [in reverse order], there at the time of the consideration, the desire to prove itself does not exist; likewise in other cases as well, [the desire to prove] does not exist at the time of the proof or at the time of the consideration.

If it is argued that there can be no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) because simultaneous existence of the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of fit and all-pervading substances (*yogyavibhu*) is prohibited, and therefore how can "being qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" be a qualification of the established conclusion (*siddhi*), we say: no. For in a case where there is either a perception or a recollection that "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire" and consequently there arises a desire to prove [the presence of fire], that qualification is necessary to ensure the status of the subject (*pakṣatā*).

This, however, must be understood: the *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject) for an inference based on a particular mark (*liṅga*) is the absence of a proof (*siddhi*) qualified by the absence of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) of that same kind which, when present along with a proof, results in an inference having that mark as its basis. Therefore, even when there is a proof and a *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection), no inference occurs if there is a desire such as "let some knowledge arise"; yet, when there is a perception such as "the mountain possesses smoke pervaded by fire and is fiery," an inference does indeed occur if there is a desire such as "let knowledge other than perception arise."

Thus, even when there is the cognition of smoke, if there is a desire such as "I shall infer fire by means of light," no inference occurs. It must be stated that, at a time when there is no desire to prove (siṣādhayiṣā), a specific kind of established knowledge (siddhi) whose presence prevents inference must be identified as the inhibitor of each respective inference. Consequently, there is no contradiction in the occurrence of inference even when there exists the knowledge: "The mountain is luminous" or "The mountain is made of stone and possesses fire."

However, since it is observed that an inference occurs even when the probandum (sādhya) is established in a relation of co-inherence with the delimitant of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka), it is the establishment of the probandum as delimited by the delimitant of the subjecthood that acts as the inhibitor for an inference delimited by the delimitant of the subjecthood; whereas for an inference in a relation of co-inherence with the delimitant of the subjecthood, mere establishment [of the probandum] is the opponent.

This, however, must be understood: where a person does not know [something] and, immediately after the doubt, there arises the cognition "this one possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by being a person," in that case, provided there is no desire for inference (*anumitsā*), perception of the person occurs, and not inference.

Therefore, the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*) that possesses the same object as the subject, when qualified by the absence of a desire to infer (*anumitsā*), is an independent inhibitor, just like the desire to know a beautiful woman (*kāminījijñāsā*). Likewise, since the perception of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth does not arise immediately after the consideration of the logical mark (*parāmarśa*) in the absence of a desire for perception, the causal complex for inference, when qualified by the absence of a desire for perception, is an inhibitor of perception regarding a different object. Thus ends the determination of the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*).

The fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are fivefold: the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), the counter-balanced (*pratipakṣita*), and the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). (Verse 71)

In connection with the discussion of the *hetu* (logical reason), he analyzes the *hetvābhāsas* (fallacious reasons) starting with "anaikāntika" (inconclusive), and so forth. Its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), however, is: that property by virtue of being the object of which a cognition possesses the quality of being an obstacle to inference. For instance, those [reasons] such as the inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*) are defects because a cognition having them as its object is an obstacle to inference. Furthermore, "having something as its object" means "having a particular qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) as its object. By this, there is no deficiency even though a misconception regarding sublation (*bādhā*) is an obstacle to inference; for in that case, since the qualified entity—"the mountain possesses the absence of fire"—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), it does not constitute a defect of the reason.

Nor should it be argued that at the time of the *parāmarśa* "this possesses stoniness, which is pervaded by the absence of fire," the smoke—which is pervaded by fire—would not be a fallacious indicator (*ābhāsa*), because the qualified entity "the subject possessing that which is pervaded by the absence of fire" is unestablished (*aprasiddha*) there. This objection is untenable, for such a consequence is accepted; otherwise, sublation (*bādha*) would result in being an occasional defect (*anityadoṣa*).

Therefore, at the time of the *parāmarśa* (inferential reflection) "this [mountain] possesses stoniness, which is pervaded by the absence of fire," there is no fallaciousness (*ābhāsatva*) regarding the smoke that is pervaded by fire; rather, there is merely an obstruction to inference due to error, but the reason (*hetu*) itself is not defective. And thus, according to the Neo-logicians (*navya*), a defect (*doṣa*) consists in the reason's subsisting in a locus where the probandum is absent, and its possession of that [defect] in the reason occurs through any relation whatsoever.

Others, however, maintain that the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) consists in possessing that property by virtue of which a cognition has the capacity to oppose an inference. In the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), it is precisely the contradictory pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth that possesses such a capacity. Furthermore, the possession of this property by the reason occurs through a relation consisting of cognition itself. It should not be argued that, in cases such as "the mountain is fiery because of smoke," even a valid reason would incur the status of being *bādhita* (sublated), since a mistaken cognition of sublation regarding the subject (*pakṣa*)—by virtue of having the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) as its object—would oppose the inference, and thus the reason would possess that property through the relation of cognition. [This objection is rejected because]...

In that case, they say that because the relation of knowledge is not postulated there, whereas it is postulated here through the conventional usage "this is counter-balanced" (*satpratipakṣita*), and because the conventional usage "this is sublated" (*bādhita*) does not occur there. Furthermore, being an opponent to inference means being an opponent to either the inference or its instrument; by this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicārin*).

Furthermore, the knowledge of a defect (doṣajñāna) that has a specific cause as its object acts as an obstacle to the inference whose cause is that very same factor. Consequently, when there is a knowledge of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding one cause, an inference can still arise through another cause; and since the knowledge of deviation does not apprehend the absence of that [specific cause], it follows that there is no harm even if such knowledge lacks the capacity to directly oppose the inference. This is the summary.

The definition of a fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) in a given case is the state of being "one or another" among all the defects that may exist in that particular probandum (sādhya), subject (pakṣa), and reason (hetu). The enumeration of five types, however, is intended to refer to the possible instances where these defects occur.
Thus, the state of being "inconclusive" (anaikāntika) consists in being one or another of the common (sādhāraṇa) and other such fallacies.

The common (*sādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive reason] is that which occurs in what is other than the locus of the probandum; by it, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is obstructed. The uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive reason] is a reason that does not have a common locus with the probandum; by it, the apprehension of the reason's co-occurrence in the same locus as the probandum (*sādhyasāmānādhikaraṇya*) is obstructed. (For example, in "Sound is eternal, because it has the nature of sound" (*śabdo nityaḥ śabdatvāt*), there is inconclusiveness due to being uncommon; whereas in "Sound is non-eternal, because it has the nature of sound," there is the error of [thinking it is] uncommon.)

Others, however, maintain that the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason] is that which does not occur in the similar instances (sapakṣa). A similar instance is one where the probandum (sādhya) is ascertained. Thus, in cases such as "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound," they argue that when the probandum is ascertained in the subject (pakṣa), there is no "uncommonness," because the reason is then ascertained therein. Furthermore, the "non-conclusive" (anupasaṃhārī) [reason] is that whose probandum is the counter-correlative of an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) and so forth; by this, the cognition of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) is obstructed.

The contradictory (*viruddha*), however, is that which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence that pervades the probandum (*sādhya*). This [contradictory reason] acts as an obstacle by virtue of being the causal complex for the apprehension of the absence of the probandum. In the case of a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*), the opposing reason (*pratihetu*) is the prover of the absence of the probandum; here, however, the difference is that it is the [original] reason itself. Furthermore, there is a distinction because [the contradictory reason] presents a specific incapacity, in that a reason which is actually a prover of the absence of the probandum is put forward as a prover of the probandum. A counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*) is a subject (*pakṣa*) possessing the pervader of the absence of the probandum.

Others hold that it is the object of an occurrence of the cognition of its being pervaded by its absence—which has not had its lack of validity apprehended—at a time when there is an occurrence of the cognition of its being pervaded by the probandum—which has not had its lack of validity apprehended. And in this case, the result is the mutual obstruction of inferences due to the cognitions of their respective states of being pervaded by each other's absence.

On this point, some [maintain]: just as even when there is a cognition of the presence of a property pervaded by the absence of a jar, a cognition of the presence of the jar arises upon contact of the eye with the jar; and just as, even when there is a cognition of the presence of "conch-ness"—which is pervaded by the absence of yellowness—in a conch, the cognition "the conch is yellow" occurs due to a defect such as jaundice; likewise, even upon perceiving properties pervaded by both alternatives, a doubt in the form of a direct perception regarding both alternatives arises, and similarly, in the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), an inference in the form of a doubt certainly occurs.

And where there is the perception of a property pervading one alternative (koṭi), there is no doubt because the manifestation of the second alternative is obstructed by its superior strength. They say that the status of being "stronger" or "equal in strength" is postulated on the basis of the resulting cognition (phala). That is not correct. For when there is a cognition of a locus as possessing a property pervaded by the absence of that [object], there is no arising of a specific manifested appearance (upanītabhāna) of that object, nor of verbal cognition (śābdabodha), and so forth; therefore, its status as an obstructor applies to all cognitions—provided they are not produced by ordinary sense-contact and are not produced by a specific defect—due to parsimony (lāghava). It does not, however, apply separately as an obstructor to specific manifested appearances or to verbal cognition, due to prolixity (gaurava).

And thus, since there exists an impediment (*pratibandhaka*), how can there be an inference? For, unlike the case of perception where ordinary sense-contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*) occurs, an inference in the form of a doubt (*saṃśaya*) is not epistemically valid in the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), such that one would need to qualify [the definition] by adding "distinct from inference. Where there is a cognition of the presence of the pervader (*vyāpyavat-tājñāna*) for both sides, a doubt arises there because of the cognition of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-jñāna*) regarding both; it does not arise otherwise, because only a contradictory cognition whose invalidity has not been grasped acts as an impediment.
As for "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*), it consists in being any one of the varieties such as unestablishedness of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

Non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) is the absence of the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). For example, when it is sought to be proved that "the golden mountain possesses fire," the result [of this fallacy] is the obstruction of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) regarding a golden mountain, while the cognition "the mountain is not golden" is present. This is because a certainty regarding the absence of a property in a particular locus is an obstacle to any cognition of that property in that locus, provided such cognition is not produced by ordinary sensory contact and is not caused by a specific defect.

However, it is not tenable to claim that the cause of inference is the cognition of the connection between the probandum and the subject (pakṣa) as being common to doubt, and that sublation (bādha) and the counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa) constitute fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) precisely because they contradict that [cognition]. For, otherwise, there would be no occurrence of an inference where the probandum is unestablished (aprasiddhasādhya), and furthermore, an inference arises even in the absence of doubt regarding the probandum and so forth.

Thus, even the cognition of the truth (prāmāṇya) regarding the knowledge of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is not an obstacle [to inference], because there is a lack of evidence for it and because it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Otherwise, in cases such as a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*), the cognition of the presence of that which is pervaded by its absence would also result in being an obstacle simply by virtue of having the truth of that [absence] as its object. Rather, it is the sublation-cognition (*bādhajñāna*) when it is not overridden by a cognition of its own falsity (*bhramatva*) that constitutes the obstacle; in that case, the cognition of truth is useful in some instances for dispelling the suspicion of falsity.

Nor should it be argued that when there is sublation (*bādha*), if the reason (*hetu*) exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*); whereas if the reason is absent in the subject, the fault is simply the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*). This is because the cognition of sublation is distinct from the cognition of inconstancy and other such defects.

Furthermore, in cases where a sublation-cognition (*bādhabuddhi*) arises immediately after the consideration (*parāmarśa*), since the cognition of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth is ineffective there, it must be stated that sublation itself acts as an obstacle to inference. Likewise, in a case such as a jar at its moment of origination, where there is a cognition of the presence of earthness—which is pervaded by smell—sublation alone must be stated to act as the obstacle. Nor should it be argued: "How can there be sublation when smell exists in the jar, which is the subject (*pakṣa*)? For it is established by experience that inference occurs with respect to the specific place and time delimited by the delimitors of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Those fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) which are distinct from those pervaded by sublation (*bādha*), their own pervasions (*vyāpya*) are also included within that very same category; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an excess of fallacious reasons. However, the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) that is pervaded by sublation is indeed distinct [from the sublated], because the Sage, acting according to his independent will, taught it separately. The point of this section is that what is pervaded by a counter-balanced reason is not an obstructer [of the inference]. ||73||
Thus concludes the general examination of fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
The inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason is of three kinds: the first is common (sādhāraṇa), the other is uncommon (asādhāraṇa), and likewise there is the non-conclusive (anupasaṃhārī). ||72||

That which exists in both the similar class (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is the common (sādhāraṇa) [inconclusive reason]; whereas that which is excluded from both is considered the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) [inconclusive reason]. (73)

"That which has a similar instance (sapakṣa)" means that which occurs in both the similar instance (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa); this is the meaning of "common" (sādhāraṇa). A "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is one where the probandum (sādhya) is ascertained; a "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa) is that which is different from what possesses the probandum. The occurrence in the similar instance is mentioned to exclude the "contradictory" (viruddha) reason. In reality, however, only occurrence in the dissimilar instance need be stated, because although the contradictory reason is also common, it is treated separately due to its distinct nature as a source of fallacy. This concludes the definition of the common (sādhāraṇa) reason.

"But that which [is excluded] from both" means that which is excluded from both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). A *sapakṣa* is that which is ascertained as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhya*); a *vipakṣa* is that which is ascertained as being devoid of the property to be proven. In cases such as "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*), when there is doubt regarding the impermanence of sound, then only things like a jar possess the status of *sapakṣa* and *vipakṣa*, and since the nature of sound (*śabdatva*) is not excluded from them, it is then an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason. However, when there is certainty regarding the impermanence of sound, then it is not uncommon.
This, however, is the view of the ancients; the new view has been stated previously. (72–73) Thus ends the examination of the uncommon [probans].

In the same way, the "non-conclusive" (*anupasamhārī*) [reason] has as its subject (*pakṣa*) that which possesses only positive concomitance (*kevalānvayin*). Regarding the term "possessing only positive concomitance": in cases such as "Everything is nameable, because it is knowable," since everything is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no other locus for grasping co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); therefore, no inference occurs. However, this is not correct, because there is no deficiency even if co-presence is grasped in only one part of the subject. Or, let us grant that co-presence is not grasped; even so, this is merely a case of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) consisting in non-cognition, and not a formal fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Nevertheless, it has been stated that its defining characteristic is having a probandum (*sādhya*) that is purely positively concomitant.
Thus concludes the examination of the non-distributed [inconclusive reason].
That which does not exist at all in that which possesses the probandum is declared to be the contradictory (viruddha) [reason]. ||74||

The first would be the unestablishedness of the locus (āśrayāsiddhi), then the unestablishedness of the essential nature (svarūpāsiddhi), and another would be the unestablishedness of the pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi); thus, unestablishedness is threefold. (75)
Where the subject (pakṣa) would be a mountain made of jewels, as in "The lake possesses smoke because it is a substance," there is another type of non-establishment (asiddhi). //76//

Another [type of] unestablishedness of pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi) occurs in cases such as "blue smoke" and the like. By the word "only" (eva), the absence of the reason is indicated as being delimited by the possession of the probandum (sādhyavattva). Thus, its meaning is: being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum. (74)
Thus concludes the examination of contradictions.
He analyzes the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth: "The unestablished locus," etc. (75).
"Pakṣāsiddhiḥ" means "āśrayāsiddhiḥ" (non-establishment of the locus).
"Aparā" means "svarūpāsiddhiḥ" (non-establishment of the essential nature). ||76||

Regarding the phrase "blue smoke, etc.": the property of being blue smoke (*nīladhūmatva*) and so forth cannot serve as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the reasonhood because of its complexity (*gurutva*). This is because only that which is not constituted by another property co-extensive with itself and which delimits the pervasion (*vyāpyatā*) can function as such a delimiting factor. The qualification "co-extensive with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) is included in order to include the state of being the prior absence of smoke (*dhūmaprāgabhāvatva*). Thus ends the determination of the unestablished (*asiddhi*).
When two contradictory reasons are apprehended, there is the state of counter-balanced opposition (satpratipakṣatā). ||77||

Regarding the phrase "of two contradictory [reasons]": even when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the possession of a pervader of both the conjunction with a monkey and its absence, there is no state of being a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣatva*). Therefore, it is stated "of two contradictory [reasons]. Thus, the meaning is: that which is the object of a reflective awareness of the possession of a pervader of the probandum at a time when there is a reflective awareness of the possession of a pervader of the absence of the probandum—which is contradictory to the probandum of one's own [thesis]. ||77||
Thus concludes the examination of the counter-balanced reason (satpratipakṣa).
Where the subject (pakṣa) is devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya), that is declared to be sublation (bādha);
as when fragrance and so forth are being proved in a jar at the time of its production. (78)

"Devoid of the probandum" (*sādhyaśūnya*) means the subject (*pakṣa*), that is to say, that which is qualified by the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). By this, there is no fault even if odor exists in a jar. The same should be understood in the case of "the tree delimited by its root is conjoined with a monkey."...||
Thus concludes the examination of sublation.

Thus ends the section on inference in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Now begins the section on comparison (*upamiti*). Verse 79: For a villager seeing a gavaya and so forth for the first time, the cognition of similarity with a cow and so forth that arises is considered the instrument (*karaṇa*).
The function of memory is said to be the extension (atideśa) of the meaning of the sentence;
however, the result of comparison (upamāna) is the cognition of the word-potency (śakti) of terms such as "gavaya. ||80||

"Devoid of the probandum" (sādhyaśūnya) means the subject (pakṣa)—that is, that which is qualified by the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka). By this, there is no fault even if odor exists in a jar. The same should be understood in the case of "the tree delimited by its root is conjoined with a monkey. ||78||
Thus concludes the investigation of sublation.
Thus ends the section on inference (*anumāna*) in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.

Now, he explains analogy (*upamiti*). Regarding the phrase "of a villager": when a certain forest-dweller tells a villager, "The word 'gavaya' denotes that which is similar to a cow," and subsequently the villager sees a gavaya in some forest or other, the perception of its similarity to a cow that arises there is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of analogical cognition. Immediately following that, the recollection of the meaning of the instructional statement (*atideśavākya*), namely, "The word 'gavaya' denotes that which is similar to a cow," which occurs, is the operation (*vyāpāra*).

Immediately following that, the knowledge that arises—"the gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'"—is *upamiti* (analogical cognition). It is not the case, however, that "this [specific] gavaya is denotable by the word 'gavaya'" constitutes *upamiti*, because that would entail the impossibility of grasping the word's denotative power (*śakti*) with respect to other gavayas. ||76||
Thus ends the section on Analogy in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.

In the section on words (śabdakhaṇḍa): the cognition of the word is the instrument (karaṇa), the cognition of the word-meaning is the intermediate operation (dvāra), and verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) is the fruit; in this process, the cognition of the word's expressive power (śakti) is the auxiliary cause (sahakārin). ||81||

He demonstrates the manner of verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) with the words "padajñānaṃ tu" (but the cognition of the word). However, the word being cognized is not the instrument (karaṇa), because verbal comprehension occurs even in the absence of a physical word, as in the case of silent poetry (mauniśloka) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "cognition of the word-meaning" (*padārthadhī*): the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the recollection of the word-meaning produced by the word. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) even when the meaning of a word is presented through perception or other means to one who already possesses the knowledge of that word. In this case as well, it should be understood that "being produced by the word" occurs through *vṛtti*. Otherwise, if the recollection of "ether" (*ākāśa*) were to arise from a word such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), there would be the undesirable consequence of ether also being verbally cognized. *Vṛtti* is a relation consisting of either denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). It is precisely here that the knowledge of denotation (*śaktijñāna*) is required.

In the absence of the apprehension of *śakti* (denotative power), even if there is knowledge of the word, the recollection of its meaning through that relation would be impossible; for the recollection of the meaning by the knowledge of the word occurs by way of the cognition of one member of a related pair (*ekasambandhijñāna*). And *śakti* is the relation between a word and its referent (*padārtha*), which consists in the will of God (*īśvarecchā*) in the form: "This meaning is to be understood from this word. There is indeed *śakti* in a name given recently, because the will of God exists [in the form]: "On the eleventh day, the father shall give a name. However, the traditional doctrine (*sampradāya*) holds that there is no *śakti* in a convention established by a modern person.

The moderns (Navyas), however, say: "The will of God (īśvarecchā) is not the *śakti*; rather, it is desire (*icchā*) itself. Therefore, *śakti* exists even in that which is designated by contemporary convention.
The apprehension of *śakti*, moreover, arises from grammar and other sources. For instance:
"The apprehension of *śakti* [is derived] from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the speech of reliable persons, and linguistic usage."
The elders state that the apprehension of the expressive power (śakti) of words is derived from the remainder of a sentence, from explanation, and from the proximity of established terms.

The apprehension of the power of roots, bases, suffixes, and so forth, arises from grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). In some cases, however, this [conventional view] is abandoned when there is a subverting reason (*bādhaka*). For example, grammarians assert that the expressive power of a finite verb (*ākhyāta*) resides in the agent (*kartṛ*). In sentences such as "Caitra cooks" (*caitraḥ pacati*), there is a relation of identity between Caitra and the agent. But that [view] is abandoned due to prolixity (*gaurava*); rather, the power resides in the action (*kṛti*), because of parsimony (*lāghava*). And the action appears as the qualifier (*prakārībhūya*) in Caitra and the like.

Nor should it be argued that because the agent is not denoted, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would follow after words such as *caitra*; for what is required there is the non-denotation of the agent's number. And that which is fit for the denotation of number is that which is presented by a word ending in the nominative case (*prathamānta*), provided it is not already occupied by [the role of] being an object (*karmatva*) and so forth. The phrase "being an object and so forth" means not being the intended object of the speaker's intention to have it as a qualifier of something else. Therefore, in sentences such as *caitra iva maitro gacchati* ("Maitra goes like Caitra"), the number does not apply to Caitra. The inclusion of the term "ending in the nominative case" is for the purpose of excluding those cases where there is no intention to have the object and so forth function as a qualifier.

Alternatively, the meaning of the first part [of the definition] is "not being a qualifier of anything other than the root-meaning. By this, Caitra and others are excluded in sentences such as "Maitra goes like Caitra. To exclude "stoka" (a little) and so on in cases like "he cooks a little," the second part [of the definition] is included; its exclusion [of such words] follows from the fact that they are presented by a word ending in the second case-suffix (*dvitīyā*). Thus, there is no denotative power (*śakti*) even for the operation (*vyāpāra*), due to the principle of complexity (*gaurava*). In sentences such as "the chariot goes," however, there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) either for the operation or for the substratum (*āśrayatva*). In "he knows," it is for the substratum; but in "it perishes," there is conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) for the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*).

It has already been stated how the apprehension of meaning (*śaktigraha*) occurs through analogy (*upamāna*). Similarly, the apprehension of meaning also arises from a lexicon (*kośa*). However, when there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), the [literal] sense is sometimes abandoned. For example, although the lexicon teaches that words such as *nīla* (blue) have their denotative power (*śakti*) both in the quality of blueness and in the object qualified by blueness, nevertheless, on account of parsimony (*lāghava*), the power resides only in the quality of blueness, while with respect to the object qualified by blueness, there is only figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The same applies to the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*). For instance, from a statement such as "the cuckoo is denoted by the word *pika*," one apprehends the denotative power of the word *pika* and others in the cuckoo.

The same applies to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For example, when an elder (the instigator) says, "Bring the jar," and having heard that, another elder (the prompted one) brings the jar, a child standing nearby observes this and concludes that the action consisting of bringing the jar was prompted by the utterance of the words "Bring the jar. Subsequently, through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpodvāpa*) regarding sentences such as "Bring the jar" and "Bring the cow," he determines that the word-potential (*śakti*) of words like "jar" resides in the jar and so forth as conjoined with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvita*).

And thus, according to some, there is no verbal cognition (śābdabodha) from sentences such as "there is a blue jar on the ground," because the capacity of words like "jar" is determined to lie in the cognition of a jar as connected to an action (kārya); and since the optative suffixes (liṅ) and so forth have the capacity to produce the cognition of an action, in their absence there is no verbal cognition.

That is not so; for even if the capacity [of words] is initially determined as residing in objects such as jars as conjoined with an action, it is more appropriate to subsequently abandon that [view] on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). For this very reason, in cases such as "Caitra! A son is born to you" or "Your daughter is pregnant," one infers pleasure and pain from the brightness of the face or the frown of the face, respectively. Having determined through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that these are caused by verbal cognition, and having identified the specific word as the cause of that [cognition], one determines its denotative power. Thus, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the capacity does not reside in that which is conjoined with an action.

Nor should one supply another word such as "does not see him" (*na ca tatra taṃ paśyati*) and so forth, because there is no evidence for doing so; and furthermore, because such [supplying] is absent in cases like "a son has been born to you" or "he is dead.

Thus, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), having abandoned the assumption of a power (*śakti*) for the word "pot" in the sense of a pot as related [to an action], one determines the power of the word "pot" to reside in the pot alone.

In this way, the apprehension of meaning also occurs through the remainder of a statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). For example, regarding the sentence "The sacrificial pap (*caru*) consists of barley (*yava*)," the word *yava* is used by the Āryas to denote a specific kind of long-bearded grain, whereas for the Mlecchas, it denotes the *kaṅgu* millet. This is because of the supplementary statements: "When other plants wither, these remain rejoicing," and "In spring, the shedding of leaves occurs for all crops;
yet the barley remains rejoicing, adorned with its ears."

Thus, by the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), the expressive power (*śakti*) is determined to reside in the long-awned variety of rice (*dīrghaśūka*). However, the usage of the word for *kaṅgu* (a type of grain) arises from a misconception regarding its expressive power, because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate multiple expressive powers. In the case of words such as "lion" (*hari*), however, one must postulate multiple expressive powers due to the absence of any decisive factor (*vinigamaka*).

Similarly, the apprehension of expressive power occurs through paraphrase (*vivaraṇa*). Paraphrase is the explanation of the meaning of a word by means of another word having the same meaning; for example, from the paraphrase of "the pot exists" (*ghaṭo'sti*) by "the jar exists" (*kalaśo'sti*), the expressive power of the word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) is apprehended to reside in the jar.

Thus, because the expression "pacati" (he cooks) is explained by "pākaṃ karoti" (he performs cooking), it is inferred that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has effort (*yatna*) as its meaning. Similarly, the apprehension of a word's power (*śakti*) occurs through the proximity of a well-known word; for example, in such cases as "On this mango tree, the *pika* sings sweetly," the power of the word *pika* is apprehended as referring to the cuckoo. This concludes the determination of the means of apprehending the power of words.

In this regard, the apprehension of the word’s power (śakti) occurs only with respect to the genus (jāti), and not with respect to the individual (vyakti), because of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) and because of infinity (ānantya). Some maintain that since the manifestation of the genus is impossible without the individual, the individual is also manifested.

That is not so; for it is impossible for the cognition of the universal to occur without the manifestation of the individual (vyakti). Nor is there a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the individual, because the individual is understood even without the recollection of an apparent inconsistency (anupapatti). Furthermore, there is no infinite regress regarding the power (śakti), since we accept a single power residing in all individuals. Nor is there a lack of uniformity (ananugama), because the universal such as "cowness" (gotva) itself serves as the unifying factor. Moreover, if the apprehension of the power is in the form "the cow is the object of the power," then the power resides in the individual.

If, however, the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) were that "cowness (*gotva*) is the denotable object," then there would be no recollection of the referent characterized by the mode (qualifier) of cowness, nor would there be verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); for the recollection of the referent and verbal cognition are caused by the knowledge of the word's power through the relation of having the same mode. Furthermore, if the power resides in cowness, then "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) must be stated as the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). Cowness-ness, moreover, is the state of being inherent in all cows while not being inherent in anything other than cows.

And thus, because the individual cows would have to enter into the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), your position alone incurs the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the expressive power (*śakti*), which is postulated because the cognition of those respective individuals as qualified by their respective universals and forms would otherwise be inexplicable, ultimately rests upon the individual itself as qualified by its universal and form. Thus ends the doctrine that the expressive power resides in the universal (*jātiśaktivāda*).

A word (*pada*) is that which is expressive; it is of four kinds: in some cases etymological (*yaugika*), in some cases conventional (*rūḍha*), in some cases both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*), and in some cases both etymological and conventional by way of a single integrated sense (*yaugikarūḍha*).
To illustrate: where only the meaning of the constituent parts (*avayavārtha*) is understood, that is etymological, such as the word *pācaka* ("cook") and the like.

Where something is understood solely through the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*), independent of the powers of the constituent parts, that is conventional, such as the words *gomaṇḍala* ("cow-pen") and the like.

However, where there is a conventional power (*samudāya-śakti*) in addition to the scope of the power of the parts (*avayava-śakti*), that is a word formed by both etymological derivation and convention (*yogarūḍha*). An example is the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born"). For instance, the word *paṅkaja*, through the power of its parts, conveys the meaning "that which has the nature of being produced from mud," while through the power of the whole, it conveys a lotus in its form as a lotus. Nor should it be argued that the word would be used for a water-lily (*kumuda*) by the power of the parts alone; for the ancients maintain that the cognition of convention acts as an obstacle to the cognition of a purely etymological meaning.

In reality, however, the connection of the meaning of the constituent parts—the agent of the production from mud—occurs with the lotus presented by the power of the whole (samudāyaśakti), due to proximity.

However, where the sublation of the conventional meaning is recognized, there the understanding of the white water-lily (*kumuda*) and so forth occurs through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But where there is no knowledge of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) for an understanding in the form of "white water-lily-ness," and where the lotus-ness is sublated, they say that the explanation is achieved through the power of the word's components alone. Where, however, as in the case of a "land-lotus" (*sthalapadma*), the meanings of the components are sublated, there the understanding occurs in the form of "lotus-ness" through the power of the whole word. If, on the other hand, the land-lotus is indeed of a different species altogether, then it is only by secondary indication.

However, where there is a cognition of both the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) and the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyartha*) independently, that is *yaugikarūḍha* (etymologically-conventional). An example is the word *udbhid*. For in that case, both a tree, shrub, or the like—the agent of breaking forth—is understood, as well as a particular sacrifice. Thus ends the examination of the word (*pada*).
Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a relation with the denotable meaning (*śakyasambandha*), [arising] from the failure of the intended meaning (*tātparyānupapatti*).

Regarding the statement "indication is a relation with the denotable meaning": in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), where either the impossibility of the connection of the hamlet with the denotable meaning of the word "Gaṅgā"—namely, the form of a flowing current—or the failure of the intended meaning is perceived, there is the cognition of the bank (*tīra*) through indication. And that [indication] consists in a relation with the denotable meaning. For instance: because the relation between the denotable meaning in the form of a current and the bank has been previously apprehended, there is the recollection of the bank; from that, verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) arises.

However, if the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) were the sole seed of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then there would be no metaphorical indication in such cases as "Bring in the sticks" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), because there is no impossibility of connecting the act of entering with the sticks themselves. Therefore, in that instance, metaphorical indication applies to the holders of the sticks, due to the impossibility of the intended purpose—namely, eating—being fulfilled by the entrance of the sticks alone. Similarly, in "The curd must be protected from crows" (*kākebhyo dadhirakṣyatām*), the word "crow" (*kāka*) indicates "anything that spoils the curd," because the intended purport (*tātparya*) is the protection of the curd from all sources of harm.

Thus, in expressions such as "the umbrella-bearers are going," the word *chatrin* (umbrella-bearer) possesses a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the state of traveling in a single caravan. This very [type of signification] is called *ajahatsvārthā-lakṣaṇā* (signification that does not abandon its own primary meaning), because there is a cognition of both the umbrella-bearer and those other than him by way of their being travelers in a single caravan. Alternatively, if the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) were the sole basis for secondary signification, then there would be no fixed rule that the word *gaṅgā* signifies the bank in some cases, while the word *ghoṣa* (village/settlement) signifies fish and so forth in others.

This, however, must be understood: if the relation with the denotable meaning (*śakyārtha*) is apprehended in the form of "bankness" (*tīratva*), then there is a cognition of the bank in the form of "bankness. But if it is apprehended in the form of "the bank of the Gaṅgā," then there is recollection in that very same form. For this very reason, there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) regarding the delimiting factor of the indicated object (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*); for the cognition of that as a qualifier (*tatprakārabodha*) is possible there even without secondary signification.

However, one should reflect that by this same logic, there would likewise be no primary power (*śakti*) regarding the delimiting factor of the denotable meaning (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), since it can be easily stated that the capacity of that word lies in producing the recollection of the denotable meaning qualified by that [delimiting factor].

However, where there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) consisting of a mediated relationship with the primary meaning, that is called "signification of the signified" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*). For example, from a word such as *dvirepha*, the connection to the two *repha* sounds (the syllable *ra*) is known in the word *bhramara*; and the connection of the word *bhramara* to the bee is known. In that case, it is *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*.

However, a word with a metaphorical (lakṣaṇika) meaning is not itself the cause of comprehension; rather, for the verbal cognition of a metaphorical meaning, another word is the cause. This is because it is determined that words possess the capacity to bring about a verbal cognition of their own denoted meaning as related to the meanings of other words, through either the relation of primary denotation (śakti) or metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā).

Since there is no denotative power (*śakti*) in a sentence, even indication (*lakṣaṇā*), which consists of a relation with the denoted, does not exist [in the sentence as a whole]. When it is said, "A hamlet on the deep river," there is indication of the word *nadī* (river) as meaning the river-bank. The meaning of the word *gabhīra* (deep) is then construed with the river through identity (*abhedānvaya*), because the acceptance of partial construal (*ekadeśānvaya*) is admitted in some cases. If partial construal is not accepted there, then there is indication of the word *nadī* as meaning the bank of a deep river; in that case, the word *gabhīra* serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*).

The same applies to *bahuvrīhi* compounds as well. For in cases such as the word *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows"), when partial co-referentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*) is accepted, there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *go* (cow) in the sense of "the possessor of cows," and the word *citra* (brindled) enters into a relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with the cow. However, if partial co-referentiality is not accepted, then there is a secondary signification of the word *go* in the sense of "the owner of brindled cows," while the word *citra* serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Similarly, in the expression *ārūḍhavānaro vṛkṣaḥ* ("a tree climbed by a monkey"), there is a secondary signification of the word *vānara* (monkey) in the sense of "the act of climbing performed by a monkey," while the word *ārūḍha* (climbed) serves to indicate the intended meaning. The same principle applies elsewhere as well.

In a *tatpuruṣa* compound, however, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member. For instance, in a word such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), the meaning of the word "man" does not directly connect with the meaning of the word "king," because it is an unestablished rule that two nominal meanings—other than those involving particles—can be understood as connected through difference (*bheda*). Otherwise, in the case of "the king is a man" (*rājā puruṣaḥ*), such a connection would also occur. In expressions like "a pot is not a cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), the negative particle (*nañ*) connects directly with "pot" and "cloth"; thus, the phrase "other than particles" is used. In "a blue pot" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), since the meanings of the two nouns connect through the relation of identity (*abheda*), the phrase "through difference" is used.

Nor should it be argued that in expressions such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), one must assume the recollection of an elided case-ending (*luptavibhakti*), because comprehension arises from it even for one who does not recall such an ending. Therefore, in the word *rāja* and similar terms, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with respect to the king’s relation; and this [relation] is then construed as non-different (*abhedānvaya*) with the "man" (*puruṣa*). In a copulative compound (*dvandva*), however, as in *dhavakhadirau chindhi* ("cut the dhava and the khadira trees"), both the *dhava* and the *khadira* are understood through the meaning of the dual case-ending as the qualifiers of duality; in that case, there is no indication. Nor should it be said that there is indication with respect to "conjunction" (*sāhitya*), since we observe copulative compounds even between things devoid of conjunction.

Nor should it be argued that "conjunction" (sāhitya) consists in the state of being connected to a single action; for we observe such expressions as "Look at the Dhava and Khadira trees" or "Cut the Dhava and Khadira," even when the actions differ, and because conjunction is not actually experienced there. For this very reason, in the case of the injunction "The King and the Priest, desiring union, should sacrifice," the *dvandva* compound is adopted precisely because there is no need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, conjunction and the like are not the meaning [of the compound]. Rather, the *dvandva* occurs where there is actual difference; and one should not ask how this applies in cases such as "there is no non-difference between the blue and the jar."

In that context, there is indication (lakṣaṇā) of the word "blue" in its quality of blueness, and of the word "pot" in its quality of potness; and the phrase "non-difference" means non-difference of substratum.

If, however, it is argued that in a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), the collection itself is also experienced [as denoted], then in cases such as *ahinakula* ("the snake and the mongoose"), there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the final member for the collection of the snake and the mongoose, while the initial member serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparya-grāhaka*). Nor should it be asked: "How can the collection be construed in the expression *bherīmṛdaṅgaṃ vādaya* ('beat the kettle-drum and the mṛdaṅga drum')? For that which consists of a specific cognition of relation (*apekṣābuddhi*) cannot be 'beaten'. This objection is invalid, because the collection is construed through an indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*). The same applies to cases such as *pañcamūlī* ("the five roots").

Others, however, maintain that in examples such as *ahinakulam* ("snake-and-mongoose"), both the snake (*ahi*) and the mongoose (*nakula*) are understood; there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with oneness (*ekatva*) for each member individually. Furthermore, they assert that the technical designation of a collective compound (*samāhāra-sañjñā*) applies only where the rule *prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* prescribes oneness and neuter gender; elsewhere, they say that the singular number is ungrammatical.

In cases such as *pitarau* ("parents") and *śvaśurau* ("parents-in-law"), there is figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *pitṛ* for the father and mother (the couple who beget), and in the word *śvaśura* for the wife’s parents (the couple who beget her). This is likewise in other instances. However, in cases such as *ghaṭāḥ* ("pots"), there is no figurative indication, because it is possible for various pots to be presented to the mind through the form of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

In the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*) and the like, the referent of the word "blue" is the qualifier (*prakāra*) of the referent of the word "lotus" by way of the relation of identity (*abheda-sambandha*). Furthermore, there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in that instance. For this very reason, in the injunction "one should cause the *niṣāda-sthapati* to sacrifice," it is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound.

Because it would result in the fault of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it is instead a *karmadhāraya* compound, as there is no need for metaphorical indication here. Nor should it be argued that because a *niṣāda*—who is a specific mixed caste—is not entitled to Vedic study, officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) is impossible; for the application of knowledge (*vidyā*) by the *niṣāda* is inferred from that very [textual authority]. Since the primary meaning can be construed with economy (*lāghava*), the assumption [of a secondary meaning] based on its apparent inconsistency is not a fault, as such a burden is "fruit-oriented" (*phalamukha*).

In cases such as *upakumbham* (near the jar) and *ardhapippalī* (half a pepper), there is metaphorical indication in the subsequent word regarding that which is related to it, and the comprehension of the syntactic relation occurs with the meaning of the prior word as predominant.
And thus, in a compound, there is no semantic power (śakti) whatsoever, since the required function is accomplished through the powers of the individual words alone.
Thus ends the section on defining characteristics.
Proximity, semantic competency, expectancy, and knowledge of the speaker's intention are held [to be the causes of verbal comprehension]. (82)

The proximity (*sannidhāna*) of a word is called *āsatti*. Regarding the phrase "proximity, etc.": the cognition of proximity, the cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and the cognition of intention (*tātparya*) are the causes for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). Thus ends the statement on the causes of verbal comprehension.

In this regard, he states the meaning of the term *āsatti* (proximity): "Proximity (*sannidhāna*), however... Proximity is the non-intervention [of other words] between the word that is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and the word that is the sub-correlate (*anuyogin*) in a syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Some hold that the knowledge of such proximity is the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), because verbal cognition occurs even in some cases where there is intervention, due to an illusion of non-intervention. In reality, however, since the knowledge of non-intervention is not required, the cause of verbal cognition is the presentation (*upasthiti*) of those two word-meanings—whose mutual connection is required—with non-intervention.

Therefore, there is no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) in cases such as "The mountain has fire because Devadatta has eaten," and proximity (*āsatti*) includes the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*). In instances such as "A blue pot, a cloth is a substance," verbal comprehension occurs due to a misconception regarding proximity. There is no deficiency even if there is no misconception of proximity when a misconception of verbal comprehension arises from a misconception of proximity. Now, an objection: in a case where it is said, "Devadatta [is] the one with the umbrella, the one with the earring, [and] the one with the garment," since the recollection of the preceding word is destroyed by the recollection of each subsequent word, it is impossible to have the recollection of those respective words without an interval. To this, we say: no.

This is because the final recollection having all those words as its object arises without interruption from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of each individual word; for it is possible for a single recollection to arise from multiple impressions, just as a single perception arises from multiple sense-contacts. This is because the cognition of the final phoneme, accompanied by the impressions of all those preceding words, acts as the awakener (*udbodhaka*). Otherwise, how could a single word be recollected from multiple phonemes?

However, some maintain that through the recollection of those various word-meanings simultaneously—according to the maxim of the pigeons on a threshing floor (*khalekapotanyāya*)—there arises a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) consisting of the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) of those meanings as action and object. As it is said: "Just as these old men, young men, children, and pigeons fall upon the threshing floor all at once, so too do all the word-meanings become mutually related simultaneously."
Others, however, maintain:
"Whatever is desired, whatever is capable, and whatever is present—
by each of these [factors] being combined, the word's own meaning is understood by the words themselves."

And likewise, they say that after the comprehension of the meaning of the constituent parts (*khaṇḍavākya*), there occurs the comprehension of the meaning of the whole sentence (*mahāvākya*) through the recollection of the word-meanings in the same manner. By this, the *padasphoṭa*—the theory that the word is manifested by the individual phonemes—is also refuted; for its manifestation is accounted for simply by the perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of each preceding phoneme.

This, however, must be understood: where "the door" is stated, the cognition [of the sentence] arises from the word "close" alone, and not from the cognition of an object such as "closing," because the recollection (*upasthiti*) of each respective word-meaning produced by the words is the cause of that respective verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, since verbs and their objects are expected in their specific forms, how could there be a cognition without those corresponding verbal elements?

Likewise, in cases such as *puṣpebhyaḥ* ("for the flowers"), the dative case would be inexplicable without the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of a verb such as *spṛhayati* ("desires"); thus, the ellipsis of a word is necessary.
This concludes the determination of proximity (*āsatti*).
In that context, the fitness (yogyatā) regarding a thing is proclaimed to be its possession of that [property]. ||83||

He defines *yogyatā* (compatibility) as "the meaning of a word" (*padārtha*). The meaning is that compatibility is the relation between the meaning of one word and the meaning of another word. And because of the absence of knowledge of that [relation], there is no verbal cognition in cases such as "he sprinkles with fire. If it is objected: "Knowledge of this compatibility is not possible in all cases prior to the verbal cognition, because the meaning of the sentence is something previously unknown (*apūrva*)," we say: No. For when there is recollection of the respective word-meanings, knowledge of compatibility—whether in the form of doubt in some cases or in the form of certainty in others—is possible.

The moderns, however, maintain that the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatājñāna*) is not a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). In cases such as "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), no verbal comprehension occurs because it is obstructed by the ascertainment of incompatibility (*ayogyatāniścaya*), namely the absence of fire as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the act of sprinkling. Since the ascertainment of the absence of that [compatibility] acts as an obstacle to any cognition of it—provided it is not produced by ordinary sense-contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*) or by a specific defect—it is established that it also acts as an obstacle to verbal comprehension. Furthermore, they argue that the delay in verbal comprehension is not proven to be caused by a delay in the cognition of compatibility. (82–83)
Thus concludes the determination of fitness.

The definition of *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) is stated as "that which, in the absence of a certain word, would lack the capacity to produce comprehension," and so forth. The meaning is that when one word (*yatpada*) lacks the capacity to bring about the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) in the absence of another word (*yena padena*), then there is *ākāṅkṣā* between that word and the other. For instance, a word denoting a factor of action (*kāraka-pada*) does not generate the cognition of syntactic connection in the absence of a verb (*kriyā-pada*); therefore, it has *ākāṅkṣā* for the verb.

In reality, however, the proximity (*sannidhi*) of words denoting actions and their factors (*kāraka*) fulfills its purpose through mere contiguity (*āsatti*). Nevertheless, for the cognition of "pot-ness as the object" (*ghaṭakarmatā*), the knowledge of the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*)—in the form of the accusative case-suffix following the word "pot"—is the cause. Consequently, there is no verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) in cases such as "pot, object-ness, bringing, effort," and so forth. However, in cases such as "The king's son comes; let the man be removed," since there exists a grasp of the speaker’s intention (*tātparya*) regarding the word "king" in connection with "son," the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is understood with that [son] alone. But if the grasp of intention were with respect to "man," then the syntactic relation would indeed be understood with him.
Thus concludes the determination of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
The desire of the speaker, however, is proclaimed as the intended meaning (tātparya). ||84||

He explains *tātparya* (intention): "the speaker's intention," and so forth. If the knowledge of *tātparya* were not a cause [of verbal cognition], then in cases such as "bring the *saundhava*," there would be no understanding of either a horse in some instances or salt in others. Nor should it be argued that contextual factors (*prakaraṇa*) and the like, which grasp *tātparya*, must themselves be the causes of verbal cognition; for these factors lack a commonality (*ananugama*). If they are made common by virtue of being generators of the knowledge of *tātparya*, then it is simpler (*lāghava*) to hold that the knowledge of *tātparya* itself is the cause.

Thus, even in the case of the Vedas, God is postulated for the sake of knowing the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Nor should it be argued that in that case, the knowledge of the teacher’s intention is the cause; for at the beginning of creation, there is no teacher. Nor should it be asked whether there is no dissolution (*pralaya*) at all, or where the beginning of creation occurs; for the dissolution is established in the scriptures (*āgama*). And so, even in the case of the words of Śuka, it is the knowledge of the divine intention that is required. However, in the case of the contradictory words of Śuka, it must be stated that the knowledge of the intention of the instructor alone is the cause.

Others, however, say: "In cases such as words with multiple meanings, the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) is the cause [of verbal cognition] only in some instances. Thus, in the speech of Śuka, there is verbal comprehension even without the knowledge of intention. In the Veda, however, the determination of meaning occurs through reasonings refined by beginningless Mīmāṃsā."
Thus concludes the determination of the intended meaning.
Thus ends the section on Verbal Cognition in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. 4.

Now follows the examination of recollection (*smaraṇa*). Previously, it was stated that cognition (*buddhi*) is twofold, distinguished by experience (*anubhava*) and recollection. Among these, the types of experience have been shown; however, recollection was not shown because it is easily understood. For in that case, prior experience is the cause.

Regarding this, some say: "Causality does not reside in the state of being an experience (*anubhava*), but rather in the state of being a cognition (*jñāna*) alone. Otherwise, there would be no recollection following a recollection; for, according to that view, the prior latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would have been destroyed by the recollection of the same type. In my view, however, by that very recollection, another recollection is produced through the mediation of a further latent impression. This is not correct.

In cases where, following a collective cognition (*samūhālambana*), there arises a sequential recollection of jars, cloths, and so forth, but no recollection of all the objects simultaneously occurs, it must be maintained that—since the result (*phala*) does not destroy the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in those instances—the destruction of the impression is caused by time, disease, or the final result in all such cases. Thus, there is no inconsistency regarding sequential recollection. Nor should it be argued that the production of stronger impressions through repeated recollection would be untenable.

For the very meaning of "firmness" (dāḍhrya) consists in the presence of an immediate awakening factor. Nor should it be argued that, due to a lack of a deciding factor (vinigamanāviraha), causality would also exist by way of the general property of being a cognition (jñānatva); because when there is no knowledge of deviation (vyabhicāra) with respect to a specific property, the general property is otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddha). Otherwise, how could a staff not be a cause by way of its being a substance (dravyatva) through the mediation of its being a wheel? Nor should it be argued that there is a doubt regarding deviation because of the suspicion that intermediate recollections might destroy the latent impression (saṃskāra).

Because, rather than postulating the destruction of an infinite number of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is more parsimonious to postulate that the final recollection itself is what destroys the impression; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule] and no doubt [of its validity]. This concludes the determination of the causes of recollection. This concludes the process of recollection.
The mind is said to be the instrument for the direct perception of pleasure and so forth;
its atomicity is asserted here because cognitions do not occur simultaneously. (85)

Now, in order to define the mind (*manas*) as it follows in the sequence, he says: "In direct perception" (*sākṣātkāre*). By this, the proof for the existence of the mind is shown. To explain: the inference—"The direct perception of pleasure has an instrument (*sakaraṇaka*), because it is a produced direct perception, like the visual direct perception"—establishes that the mind is an instrument. Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, there must be other instruments for the direct perceptions of pain and so forth; for, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), it is established that a single entity serves as the instrument for all such direct perceptions.
