In this manner, the existence of the mind (*manas*) is to be understood through its being the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of pleasure and so forth. Regarding that, he states the proof for the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the mind: "Because of non-simultaneity" (*ayaugapadyāt*). It is established by experience that there is no simultaneity—that is, no production at one and the same time—of cognitions such as those of sight, taste, and so on. In this regard, even when the objects of various sense organs are present, it is due to the connection with [the mind] that a cognition arises through one sense organ, and due to the lack of connection with it that no cognition arises through the others; therefore, if the mind were all-pervading (*vibhu*), such non-proximity would be impossible, and thus the mind is not all-pervading.

Nor should it be argued that at that time the delay in that cognition is due solely to a delay in the cognizer caused by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*); for if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence of not postulating the existence of the eyes and other sense organs at all. Nor should it be asked: "In cases such as eating a long piece of bread or when one possesses multiple attentions, how can there be simultaneous cognitions produced by multiple sense organs?"

Because of the extreme lightness of the mind (*manas*), cognitions arise sequentially due to its rapid movement and its connection with various sense organs. This is because the cognition of simultaneity—such as in the case of piercing a hundred lotus petals—is an illusion. Nor should it be argued that both [simultaneity and succession] are possible because the mind possesses contraction and expansion; for that would involve the cumbersome assumption of multiple parts and their destruction, whereas, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), the mind is postulated to be partless and atomic in form. This is the summary. Thus ends the examination of the mind.
Thus ends the exposition of the category of substance (*dravya*) in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*.
Now follows the determination of qualities (*guṇa*). Now, qualities are to be known as residing in substances, being devoid of qualities themselves and devoid of action.

Having defined substance, he defines qualities with the words beginning with "atha" (now). If it is asked what the proof is for the universal "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), [the answer is]: that causality which resides in something distinct from substance and action, yet possessing a commonality (*sāmānyavat*), must be delimited by some property (*kiñciddharmāvacchinnā*), because causality cannot be non-delimited. Neither "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth, nor "existence" (*sattā*), can serve as the delimiter there, because they subsist in a narrower or wider domain than the relevant locus. Therefore, it is established that there must be something common to all twenty-four [qualities], and that very thing is quality-ness.
Thus ends the proof for the genus *guṇatva* (the quality-ness).

Regarding the phrase "residing in a substance" (*dravyāśrita*): although residing in a substance is not a defining characteristic because it overextends to action (*karman*) and so forth, its meaning here is "possessing a genus that is distinct from existence (*sattā*) and is the delimitor of the pervasion of substance-ness (*dravyatva*). For *guṇatva* is indeed the delimitor of the pervasion of substance-ness, and qualities possess that [genus]. Action-ness or substance-ness is not the delimitor of the pervasion of substance-ness, because substance and action are absent in [entities] such as space (*ākāśa*). Furthermore, substance-ness-ness or generality-ness (*sāmānyatva*) and so forth are not genera; thus, they are excluded.

Regarding the phrase "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇā*): although the state of being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) also applies to action (*karman*) and so forth, it should nevertheless be understood here as being "devoid of qualities while possessing generality (*sāmānyavat*), and while being distinct from action. Since generality and the like do not possess generality, action does not possess the state of being distinct from action, and substance does not possess the state of being devoid of qualities, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to those cases. The term "inactive" (*niṣkriya*) is a description of the essential nature (*svarūpa-kathana*), but it is not a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), because it would over-extend to space (*ākāśa*) and other such entities. Thus concludes the statement of the general definition of quality.
Color, taste, touch, smell, priority, and posteriority. ||86||
Fluidity, gravity, viscidity, and momentum—these are the qualities of corporeal substances.
(Regarding "momentum": by this term, elasticity is also to be understood by implication.

Regarding "qualities of corporeal substances": the meaning is that they do not reside in incorporeal substances. Their definition, for now, is simply their mutual distinctness; the same applies hereafter.
Thus ends the description of the qualities of material objects.
Dharma and adharma, mental cultivation (bhāvanā), sound, and also the intellect and so forth. ||87||

All these, beginning with number and ending with disjunction, are proclaimed by the learned as the qualities of the formless substances; they are considered to be the qualities common to both [the eternal and the non-eternal]. (88)

"Qualities of the formless" (amūrtaguṇāḥ) means that they do not exist in things possessing form. This is the description of the qualities of the formless. "Of both" (ubhayeṣām) means the qualities of both the formed and the formless.
This is the description of the qualities of the formed and the formless. ||86||87||88||
Conjunction, disjunction, number such as duality and so forth, and likewise separateness such as dual separateness—these qualities reside in multiple substrata. (89)

Therefore, all the remaining qualities are considered to be single-locus (ekaikavṛtti), whereas [others] are multi-locus (anekāśrita). It should be understood that conjunction, disjunction, duality, and so forth, have two loci; while triadness, tetradness, and so on, have three, four, and more loci respectively. This concludes the description of qualities with multiple loci. The word "therefore" (ataḥ) refers to color, taste, smell, touch, unity, dimension, absolute separateness, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, gravity, viscidity, mental impression (saṃskāra), unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and sound. This concludes the description of qualities with a single locus.
The group of six beginning with intellect and ending with touch, as well as viscidity and natural fluidity. ||90||
These Vaiśeṣika qualities—beginning with cognition (buddhi) and ending with touch (sparśa)—are those whose names have not been previously mentioned.

"Cognition and so forth" means cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. "Ending with touch" means color, taste, smell, and touch. "Fluidity" (drava) means the state of being liquid (dravatva). They are called "Vaiśeṣika" because they are indeed "particular" (viśeṣa); the suffix *ṭhak* is used here in its own sense, meaning "particular qualities. This concludes the enumeration of the particular qualities.
Number and the rest, up to fluidity, as well as non-natural fluidity, [are the nine qualities of earth]. (91)
Heaviness and velocity—these are proclaimed as the general qualities;
as well as number and the rest, ending with remoteness, fluidity, and viscidity. (92)
"Number and so forth" means number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority. ||62||
Thus ends the definition of the general qualities.

Now, these [qualities] beginning with touch and ending with sound are perceptible by two sense organs; whereas gravity, the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and mental impressions (bhāvanā) are perceptible by each of the external sense organs individually. (93)

"Perceptible by two sense-faculties": because it is capable of being grasped by both the eye and the skin; this is the definition of a quality perceptible by two sense-faculties. "External": because color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] are graspable by the eye and the other [external organs]. ||93||

Thus ends the description of the qualities perceptible by each individual sense-organ. As for those specific qualities that belong to the all-pervading substances, these are proclaimed to be produced without [corresponding] qualities in their causes. (94)

"Vibhūnaṃ" (of the all-pervading) means: intellect (*buddhi*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and sound (*śabda*). Those qualities which are produced in an effect by means of the qualities of its cause are preceded by the qualities of the cause, such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, which will be explained later; however, intellect and the others are not like that, because there is no [material] cause for the self (*ātman*) and so on. Thus ends the statement regarding qualities produced without the qualities of a cause.
But those produced by non-heat (apākaja) consist of touch, as well as fluidity of that same kind, viscidity, velocity, gravity, singleness, and dimension. (95)
"Constituent-attribute-born" refers to these [qualities], such as elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*).

Regarding the phrase "not produced by heating" (*apākaja*): since qualities such as color (*rūpa*) produced by heating do not have constituent attributes as their antecedents, they are described as "not produced by heating. Such [qualities] are those not produced by heating. This should also be understood to apply to singularity (*ekatva*). This is clear.
Thus ends the description of qualities produced from a collection of constituent causes.
Conjunction, disjunction, and velocity—these, moreover, are born of action. ||96||

And [the definition] includes "conjunction" (saṃyoga). Although being produced by action (karmajanyatva) is not a common property (sādharmya), because it would over-extend (ativyāpti) to jars and the like, and under-extend (avyāpti) to conjunctions produced by conjunction, nevertheless, it should be understood as the state of possessing a genus (jāti) that is pervaded by the quality-ness (guṇatva) residing in what is produced by action.

In touch, the final dimension (parimāṇa), singularity (ekapṛthaktva), viscidity (sneha), and sound, there may be the status of non-inherent causality (asamavāyitva) with respect to a specific Vaiśeṣika quality. ||97||
In this same manner, it should be inferred in other cases as well. 95 || 96 ||
Thus concludes the description of the qualities arising from karma.

Regarding the phrase "ending with touch" (*sparśānta*): here, "touch" should be understood as non-hot (i.e., cold or neutral). In the term "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*), because the suffix *-tva* applies to each member individually, both unity and separateness are to be understood. By the word "separateness," one-separateness (*eka-pṛthaktva*) is meant. "It would be the non-inherent cause" (*asamavāyitvam*): the color, taste, smell, and touch of a jar and so forth arise from the color, taste, smell, and touch of the potsherds and so forth. Likewise, the dimensions (*parimāṇa*) of the potsherds and so forth serve as the non-inherent causes for the dimensions of the jar and so forth. This also applies to sound in relation to a second sound. The same should be understood for elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) and one-separateness as well.
Thus concludes the description of the non-inherent causes that are qualities.

The self (ātman) may be the efficient cause (nimitta) of heat-contact and gravity; "efficient cause" means that it is the cause of desire and so forth for the intellect and other faculties—this is the sense. Thus ends the description of the qualities of the efficient cause.
And likewise in velocity, in fluidity, and in the two types of conjunction and so forth. (98)
Causality would be of only two kinds; or else, it would be localized. Likewise, the specific quality (vaiśeṣika-guṇa) is all-pervading, as are conjunction and the other [qualities]. ||99||

"Only in two ways": namely, as non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) and as efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). To illustrate: hot touch is the non-inherent cause of [another] hot touch, but it is the efficient cause of [qualities] produced by heating (*pākaja*). Velocity is the non-inherent cause of velocity and motion, but it is the efficient cause of impact. Fluidity is the non-inherent cause of fluidity and motion, but it is the efficient cause of cohesion (*saṅgraha*). The conjunction of the drum and the stick is the efficient cause of sound, while the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause. The disjunction of the two halves of a bamboo is the efficient cause of sound, while the disjunction of the bamboo half and space is the non-inherent cause.
Thus concludes the description of the qualities of the two kinds of causes.
Visible form (rūpa) is that which is perceivable by the eye and is the means of apprehending substances and so forth.
It is localized—that is, it has non-pervasive occurrence (avyāpyavṛtti). This concludes the description of qualities with non-pervasive occurrence.

Regarding the term "eye" (*cakṣus*): although the word "color" (*rūpa*) is employed [to denote it], nevertheless, the specific universal (*jāti*) inherent in blue, yellow, and so forth is indeed established by experience. Even when the word "color" is not used, there certainly exists a cognition that delineates specific colors, such as "this is a blue color" or "this is a yellow color.
In this way, "blueness" (*nīlatva*) and so on are also established by perception. Thus concludes the proof for the universal "color-ness" (*rūpatva*).

Nor should it be argued that because blue, red, and other such individual instances are each unique, "blueness" and the like cannot be a universal (*jāti*) since they reside in only a single individual; for this is not so, because blueness and the rest possess multiplicity due to being subject to production and destruction, as evidenced by cognitions such as "the blue is no longer there" or "red has arisen. Otherwise, upon the destruction of a single blue thing, the entire world would become non-blue. Nor should it be argued that this cognition has as its object only the production and destruction of the inherence of blueness and the inherence of redness respectively, for in the actual cognition, inherence is not perceived.

Nor should it be argued that identity [between the blue object perceived now and the one perceived previously] is established by the force of perception and by parsimony (lāghava), as in the thought "this is that very same blue. This is because perception has for its object only that which belongs to the same class (tajjātīya), just as in the case of the thought "this is that same *gurjarī* [flute]. Furthermore, parsimony is sublated by perception;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the identity of jars and other objects, and it would follow that the cognitions of production and destruction have inherence (samavāya) as their objective support. By this, taste and the rest are also explained. Thus ends the refutation of the identity of forms such as blue.
It may be a cooperative cause for the eye, such as white and other various colors. (100)

"Perceptible by the eye" means a specific quality that is perceptible by the eye. The same applies to "of substance and so forth" in what follows. "Apprehending" means the cause of apprehension. He explains this very point with the words "of the eye. Manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the cause for the visual perception of substances, qualities, actions, and universals. Thus ends the section on the definition of color.
"White and so forth are of many kinds. That color (rūpa) becomes manifold through distinctions such as blue, yellow, red, green, brown, variegated, and so on. Thus ends the classification of color.

Now, how can a variegated color (*karbura*) be a distinct [independent] color? It is as follows: a composite whole (*avayavin*) composed of parts such as blue and yellow cannot be devoid of color, for that would entail the consequence of its being imperceptible. Nor does a color such as blue arise as something that pervades [the whole].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving blue even when yellow is present as a delimiting factor. Nor does a non-pervasive color such as blue arise [in the whole], because there is a contradiction between qualities belonging to a pervasive class being non-pervasive. Therefore, from colors of various classes, a heterogeneous variegated (*citra*) color is produced in the composite whole (*avayavin*). For this very reason, the experience that "there is one variegated color" is possible, since postulating multiple distinct colors would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, by postulating that blue and other colors act as inhibitors (*pratibandhaka*) toward the production of yellow and other colors, the production of yellow and so forth in the composite whole is prevented.
By this, touch (*sparśa*) is also explained.

Taste and the other qualities are also not non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). However, there is no fault even if taste is absent in a composite whole (avayavin) produced by parts possessing tastes of various distinct classes; for in that case, it is only the taste of the parts that is perceived by the gustatory organ, since the sense organs such as the tongue lack the capacity to perceive a substance, and thus there is no contradiction even if the composite whole is tasteless. The Neo-Naiyāyikas (navya), however, maintain that in such cases there are indeed multiple colors existing as non-pervasive [in different parts], because it would be cumbersome (gaurava) to assume that blue and other colors possess the power to obstruct yellow and other colors. For this very reason, it is said:
"He who is red in color at the head, but white at the face and tail... [and so forth].

The scriptural passage, "That white [bull] with black hooves and horns is called a blue bull," and so forth, is also thus justified. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between two universals (jāti) that subsist respectively as pervading and non-pervading properties, for there is a lack of evidence [for such a contradiction]. Nor can it be argued that color is one [universal] on the grounds of parsimony (lāghava), because that would contradict experience. Otherwise, by the same principle of parsimony, even jars and other objects would be one.
By this, they say, touch and the rest are also explained. 100. Thus ends the examination of variegated color (citrarūpa).

"In the atoms of water and so forth, that [color] is eternal; the other is caused. Regarding "water and so forth": color in the atoms of water and in the atoms of fire is eternal, whereas the color of the atoms of earth is not eternal, because in that case another color arises through baking (*pāka*). For indeed, after the baking of a jar, no part of it is perceived as unbaked. Indeed, the potsherd of a red jar does not have blue parts. In this manner, baking is established for the atom as well. "The other"—that is, color distinct from the colors of the atoms of water and fire—is "caused"—meaning it is produced.
This concludes the section on color (*rūpa*).
Taste, however, is that which is perceivable by the tip of the tongue; it is of many kinds, beginning with sweet. ||101||
The auxiliary cause for the sense of taste, as well as its permanence and other qualities, is as previously described.
Odor is that which is apprehended by the olfactory organ and serves as the specific aid to the olfactory organ itself. (102)
That [tangible quality] is proclaimed to be of two kinds: fragrant and non-fragrant.
Tangibility is perceivable by the sense organ of touch (tvag-indriya), and it serves as an auxiliary to the skin. 103.
It is considered to be of three kinds based on the distinctions of non-hot-cold, cold, and hot-cold.
Hardness and so forth exist only in earth; its eternality and other qualities are as previously described.

He defines taste (*rasa*). Regarding the phrase "taste, however": the meaning is that taste is the cause in gustatory cognition. Regarding the phrase "as before": the meaning is that taste in the water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu*) is eternal, while all other taste is non-eternal. Thus ends the section on taste.

He defines odor: "that which is apprehended by the olfactory organ" and "that which is beneficial. The meaning is that it is an auxiliary factor in the cognition produced by the olfactory organ. Furthermore, every odor is indeed impermanent. Thus ends the section on odor.

He defines touch (*sparśa*). Regarding the term "touch": it means that touch is the cause in tactile perception (*spārśana-pratyakṣa*). Regarding "neither hot nor cold": in earth and air, touch is neither hot nor cold; in water, it is cold; in fire, it is hot. The meanings of "hard" and "soft" touches belong to earth alone. Hardness and so forth, however, are not specific universals (*jāti*) residing in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that would entail their being perceivable by the eye. "As before" means that the touches of the atoms of water, fire, and air are eternal (*nitya*), while those other than these are non-eternal (*anitya*). ||101-104|| Thus ends the section on touch.

Of these—namely, color, taste, smell, and touch—"not elsewhere" means that in earth alone, the transformation of color, taste, smell, and touch is observed through contact with fire. Indeed, even when water is heated a hundred times, its color and other qualities do not undergo such change. That fragrance and heat in water are merely adventitious (aupādhika) is determined through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), just as the cold touch and so forth are found in air and earth.

In that regard—even among the various types of earth—the Vaiśeṣikas maintain that the baking (chemical transformation) of color and other qualities occurs only in the atom (*paramāṇu*). Their intention is as follows: baking is not possible while the constituent parts (*avayava*) are held together by the whole (*avayavin*). However, through contact with fire, once the wholes have perished, baking occurs in the independent atoms. Then, through the conjunction of these baked atoms, there is a re-origination starting from dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth, up to the level of the great whole again. This occurs because the excessive velocity of the fire causes the destruction of the previous configuration and the immediate production of a new configuration.

Here, for the sake of clarifying the student's understanding, is the analysis of moments (*kṣaṇaprakriyā*) concerning how many moments it takes, starting from the destruction of a dyad (*dravyaṇuka*), for it to arise again and possess color and other qualities.

In that regard, if one does not accept a disjunction produced by a disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*), there are nine moments; however, if one accepts it, a disjunction would produce another disjunction while depending on something else. If it were independent [of anything], it would be an action (*karman*), for the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra states: "Action is the cause of conjunction and disjunction that is independent [of other causes]."

Its meaning is the independence from any entity produced subsequent to itself. Otherwise, there would be a lack of pervasion (avyāpti), because even in the case of an action (*karman*), the production of a subsequent conjunction depends upon the destruction of the preceding conjunction. In that regard, if the disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*) were to occur depending on a time characterized by the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance, then it would take ten moments (*daśakṣaṇā*). Alternatively, if the disjunction produced by disjunction were to occur depending on a time characterized by the destruction of the substance, then it would take eleven moments. To explain: [The sequence of the ten-moment process follows: 1. Conjunction of the two atoms (*paramāṇu-saṃyoga*). 2. Action (*karman*) in one atom. 3. Disjunction (*vibhāga*) from the previous location. 4. Destruction of the prior conjunction (*pūrva-saṃyoga-nāśa*). 5. Production of the subsequent conjunction (*uttara-saṃyoga*). 6. Production of the substance (*dravyotpatti*). 7. Action in the other atom. 8. Disjunction from the previous location. 9. Destruction of the prior conjunction. 10. Production of the subsequent conjunction. 11. Production of the disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgaja-vibhāga*). [The sequence of the eleven-moment process follows: 1. Conjunction of the two atoms. 2. Action in one atom. 3. Disjunction. 4. Destruction of the prior conjunction. 5. Production of the substance. 6. Action in the other atom. 7. Disjunction. 8. Destruction of the prior conjunction. 9. Production of the subsequent conjunction. 10. Production of the disjunction produced by disjunction. 11. Separation from the original location. Thus, it is established.

Now, from the conjunction with fire during the ninth moment, there is motion in the atom; from that, disjunction from another atom; from that, the destruction of the originating conjunction; from that, the destruction of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) [1]; from that, the destruction of the black color and so forth in the atom [2]; from that, the production of red color and so forth [3]; from that, the action conducive to the commencement of a substance [4]; from that, disjunction [5]; from that, the destruction of the prior conjunction [6]; from that, the originating conjunction [7]; from that, the production of the dyad [8]; from that, the production of color and so forth. Thus are the nine moments.

If it is objected: "Could there not be, at the very moment of the destruction of the black color (śyāma) and so forth, or at the moment of the production of the red color (rakta), an action in the atom that is conducive to the commencement of a substance?"—we say no. This is because when an atom is conjoined with fire, there is no other action in that atom except for the destruction of the [previous] action and the production of the [new] quality; for no second action arises in that which already possesses an action, and an action conducive to the commencement of a substance cannot occur in a substance that is devoid of qualities. Even so, if it is argued: "In that case, the production of the red color and so forth would occur simultaneously with the cessation of the black color and so forth in the atom"—we say no. This is because the destruction of the previous color and other qualities is also a cause for the subsequent state.

Now, the ten moments: this occurs when, depending upon a time characterized by the destruction of the originating conjunction, a disjunction produces another disjunction. To explain: from the conjunction with fire, there is motion in the atom that originates the dyad; from that, disjunction; from that, the destruction of the originating conjunction; then, simultaneously, the destruction of the dyad and the disjunction produced by the [previous] disjunction (1); then, simultaneously, the destruction of the black color and the destruction of the prior conjunction (2); then, simultaneously, the production of the red color and the posterior conjunction (3); then, the destruction of the motion in the atom produced by the impulsion of fire (4).

Then, from the conjunction of the soul with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭavat-ātma-saṃyoga*), there arises an action conducive to the production of a substance (1); then, disjunction (2); then, the destruction of the prior conjunction (3); then, the originating conjunction (4); then, the production of the dyad (*dravya-aṇuka*) (5); then, the production of redness (6)—thus, there are ten moments.

Then, in the eleventh moment: from conjunction with fire, there is action in the atom; thence, disjunction; thence, the destruction of the conjunction that initiates the substance; thence, the destruction of the dyad (1). Then, depending upon the time characterized by the destruction of the dyad, there is the disjunction produced by disjunction and the destruction of blackness (2). Thence, the destruction of the prior conjunction and the production of redness (3). Thence, conjunction with the subsequent location (4). Thence, the destruction of the action in the atom produced by the impulsion of fire (5). Thence, from conjunction with a soul possessing unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), there is an action conducive to the initiation of a substance (6).

Then there is disjunction (7), then the destruction of the prior conjunction (8), then the posterior conjunction that initiates the substance (9), then the production of the dyad (10), and then the production of redness and so forth (11). Thus, there are eleven moments. Unlike the case of a middle-sized sound, the destruction and production of color do not arise from a single conjunction with fire, because a single fire is not stable for such a duration. Furthermore, if the very cause of destruction were also the cause of production, then once color and other qualities had been destroyed, the atom would remain devoid of color for as long as that fire did not perish. Conversely, if the cause of production were the cause of destruction, then when the fire perished upon the production of redness, the subsequent intensification of that redness (raktataratā) would not occur.

Now, considering the action in another atom, the production of qualities occurs even in the fifth moment and thereafter. To explain: in one atom there is an action; from that, a disjunction; then two things occur simultaneously—the destruction of the originating conjunction and an action in another atom; then the destruction of the dyad (dvy-aṇuka) and the disjunction produced by the action in the other atom—this is the first moment (1). Then, the destruction of the black color and so forth, along with the disjunctions and the destruction of the prior conjunction—this is the second moment (2). Then the production of the red color and the conjunction that initiates the substance—this is the third moment (3).
The third moment is time; then, fourth, the production of the dyad; then, fifth, the production of redness. Thus, there are five moments.

The production of the quality [of color] occurs at the sixth moment, due to the consideration of action in another atom simultaneous with the destruction of the substance. To explain: first, action in the atom; then, the destruction of the originating conjunction; then, the destruction of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) (1); then, the destruction of the blackness (śyāma) (2); then, the production of redness—this involves action in another atom (3); then, the disjunction produced by the action in that other atom (4); then, the destruction of the previous conjunction (5); then, the conjunction with the other atom (6); then, the production of the dyad (7); and finally, the production of redness (8). Thus, there are eight moments. (102) This concludes the exposition of the Pīlupākavāda (the theory of baking in the atom).
According to the system of the Naiyāyikas, however, it is accepted even in the case of dyads and the like.
Regarding the phrase "of the Naiyāyikas": in the view of the Naiyāyikas, transformation by heat (pāka) occurs even in substances such as dyads and so forth.

Their intention is this: since composite objects possess interstices, cooking is not contradicted even when the parts are obstructed by the subtle particles of fire that have entered within; furthermore, there is the burden of postulating an infinite number of such parts and their destruction. In this way, even recognition such as "this is that same jar" becomes consistent. However, where there is no recognition, the destruction of the composite object is also accepted. Thus concludes the exposition of the theory of cooking in the pot (piṭharapākavāda). Now, number is stated to be the cause for the usage of the term "group" (gaṇa). ||106||
He speaks in order to define number: "calculation" (gaṇanā). The meaning is that number is the unique cause for the linguistic usage of calculation. ||106||

In eternal things, unity is held to be eternal; in non-eternal things, it is non-eternal. Regarding the phrase "in eternal things": in eternal things—such as atoms and the like—unity is eternal. In non-eternal things—such as jars and the like—unity is non-eternal; this is the meaning.
Numbers beginning with duality and ending with the highest number (parārdha) are considered to be produced by relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi). ||107||
Regarding "duality and so forth": duality and the rest are numbers that exist as distributed entities (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) and are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). ||103||
"But these [numbers] are proclaimed to be pervasively resident in multiple substrata.

Regarding the word "multiple": although the inherence of duality and so forth exists in each individual object such as a jar, nevertheless, because there is no cognition of "one is two" and because there is the presence of the cognition "one is not two," some relation characterized by *paryāpti* (pervasive residence) is accepted for duality and the rest, which resides in multiple substrata.
Furthermore, their destruction is described as resulting from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). (108)

First is the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); then the production of duality; then the cognition of the qualifier, which consists of a non-conceptual [perception] of the nature of duality-ness (*dvitvatva*); then the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of that which is qualified by duality-ness and the destruction of the enumerative cognition; and finally, the destruction of duality.

Although cognitions generally persist for only two moments—since the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) of a capable omnipresent substance (vibhu) are destroyed by the quality that arises immediately after them—nevertheless, it is postulated that the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) persists for three moments. Otherwise, at the time of the indeterminate perception (nirvikalpaka), following the destruction of the enumerative cognition, duality itself would be destroyed rather than the perception of duality; for at that time, the object [of the perception] would be absent, since it is accepted that the eye and other senses produce knowledge only of what is currently present. Therefore, the perception of duality and so forth is postulated to be the destroyer of the enumerative cognition.

Nor should it be asked how the destruction of duality occurs through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). This is because there is no perception of duality at a later time; thus, one postulates that the enumerative cognition is its producer, and its destruction leads to the destruction of duality. For this very reason, it is postulated that duality and so forth produced by a person's own enumerative cognition is perceived by that same person. Nor should it be argued that the enumerative cognition should be the cause for the perception of duality; rather, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is more appropriate for it to be the cause of duality itself.

In the case of supersensible objects such as dyads and the like, the cause of duality and so forth is the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) of yogis; in the case of atoms and the like at the time of creation, it is the enumerative cognition of the Lord (*īśvara*); or, in the case of atoms existing within other cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), it is the enumerative cognition of yogis residing therein. ||108||

The cognition of "many-ness" and "one-ness" is held to be the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). To the question "What is relative cognition?", he says: "The cognition of many-ness and one-ness. This means it has the form "this is one, this is one," and so forth. However, this must be understood: where there is a cognition of indefinite unity, the number "plurality" (*bahutva*), distinct from three and so on, arises there—as in the case of an army, a forest, and the like; such is the view of the author of the *Kandalī*.

The teachers, however, maintain that plurality (*bahutva*) is simply the state of being three or more. Consequently, the universal "plurality-ness" (*bahutvatva-jāti*), which pervades the states of being three and so forth, does not exist as something distinct [from the number three itself]. Even when a triad or similar number has arisen in such cases as an army or a forest, the non-apprehension of that triad and so forth is due to a defect [of perception]. In this way, the cognition "this army is very large" becomes logically possible. It should be noted, however, that if plurality were a separate category of number, this would not be possible, as there would be no gradation (*tāratamya*) within it. Thus ends the determination of number (*saṅkhyā-nirūpaṇa*). "Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause of the conventional usage of measurement. (109)

"Minute, long, large, and short"—thus its divisions have been stated. He defines dimension (*parimāṇa*) as follows: "Dimension. The meaning is that dimension is the unique cause for the conventional usage of measurement. It is of four kinds: minute, large, long, and short. In an impermanent [substance], it is impermanent; in an eternal [substance], it is declared to be eternal. (110)
It arises from number, from dimension, and also from aggregation; it is non-eternal. However, in the case of dyads and so forth, that which is produced by number has been illustrated. (111)

It has that [same] dimension. In the word "eternal" (*nityam*), the term "dimension" (*parimāṇam*) is supplied by ellipsis. In the word "is produced" (*jāyate*), the term "dimension" likewise follows. "Non-eternal" (*anityam*) is connected with the preceding [term]. Thus, the meaning is that non-eternal dimension is produced by number, produced by dimension, and produced by aggregation (*pracaya*).

Therein, he provides an example of that which is produced by number: "in the case of the dyad and so forth. With respect to the dimension of a dyad or a triad (trasareṇu), neither the dimension of an atom nor the dimension of a dyad is the cause; for there is a rule that a dimension produces a dimension of its own kind that is superior to it. However, the atomic dimension of a dyad is not superior to the atomicity of an atom.

However, the magnitude of a *trasareṇu* is not of the same class [as its constituent parts]; therefore, the meaning is that the number two in an atom is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) of the magnitude of a *dvyaṇuka*, and the number three in a *dvyaṇuka* is the non-inherent cause of the magnitude of a *trasareṇu*. ||109||110||111||

Regarding size (*parimāṇa*) in jars and the like, it is said to be produced from size. He provides an illustration of size being produced from size with the words, "Regarding size in jars and the like. The size of a jar and so forth is produced by the size of its constituent parts, such as the potsherds.
It is also produced by that conjunction which is called "looseness" (*pracaya*). ||112||
He defines accumulation (pracaya) in order to provide an illustration of that which is produced by accumulation. Regarding "accumulation":
it is [the cause of] dimension (parimāṇa) in things such as cotton-wool; its destruction, however, results from the destruction of its substratum.

He states that dimension perishes precisely through the destruction of its substrate: "destruction" [refers] to that of dimension itself. One might ask: how can the destruction of the whole (the composite object) be the cause of the destruction of its dimension? It should not be argued that even when the whole exists, if there is a separation or an addition of three, four, or more atoms, a different dimension is established by perception despite the recognition of the same whole. For it must necessarily be admitted that upon the separation of atoms, the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is destroyed; and upon the destruction of that dyad, the triad (tryaṇuka) is destroyed.

Thus, since the destruction of a large composite whole (mahāvayavin) is necessarily required in this sequence, and because once a cause of destruction exists, its destruction cannot be denied merely by non-acceptance; furthermore, when there is an accumulation of parts in the body and so forth, the destruction of the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) is necessary, and thus the destruction of the composite whole is inevitable. Nor should it be argued that even in the absence of the destruction of a cloth or similar object, there would be no increase in dimension due to the conjunction with other threads.

In that case as well, because the destruction of the cloth is necessary due to the destruction of the non-inherent cause—the conjunction of the threads—by the impact of the shuttle and other tools; furthermore, if another thread were a constituent part (*avayava*) of that cloth, that cloth would not have existed previously, because of the absence of its cause in the form of that other thread. And if the other thread were not a constituent part, there would be no increase in dimension (*parimāṇa*) by means of it, just as in the case of a separate conjoined substance. Therefore, it must necessarily be admitted that when another thread is conjoined there, first the previous cloth is destroyed, and subsequently another cloth is produced.

The recognition of the whole (*avayavin*), however, occurs by way of its belonging to the same genus (*sājātya*), like that of a lamp-flame and so forth. Nor should it be argued that the very same prior threads, through the cooperation of other threads, begin to produce another cloth while the previous cloth still exists; for there is a contradiction in two corporeal entities occupying the same location, as two cloths cannot coexist there, and because the perception of multiple substances in that place at one time is contradicted by experience.

Therefore, since the destruction of the obstructing prior substance must necessarily be admitted before the production of another substance, [the whole is distinct]. Thus ends the determination of dimension (*parimāṇa*).
He defines conjunction (*saṃyoga*). [The verse says: "Of two things not previously in contact... (112). He analyzes it: "It is proclaimed... (112).
This—namely, conjunction—is like number; distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) should be the cause of the cognition of separation. (113)
Its purpose is not considered to be fulfilled by mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), for the cognition "this is not separate from that" is indeed of a different character. 114.

He defines separateness (*pṛthaktva*). "Like number" means that separateness is the specific cause of the cognition of "distinct. Its eternality and other properties are like those of number. To explain: in eternal things, singularity is eternal; in non-eternal things, it is non-eternal. Non-eternal singularity, however, arises in the second moment following the [first] moment of its substratum and perishes upon the destruction of that substratum. The same applies to singular separateness. Furthermore, just as with duality and so forth, there is also dual separateness and so on—this is the meaning.

The attainment of two things that were previously unattained is what is called conjunction; this is said to be of three kinds, the first being produced by the action of one of the two. (115)
Likewise, another [conjunction] may be produced by the movement of both [objects], arising from conjunction;
the first is proclaimed as the conjunction between a hawk and a mountain, and so forth. (116)
The conjunction that occurs between two rams is cited as the second type;
from the conjunction of a potsherd and a tree arises the conjunction of the tree and the jar. (117)
Conjunction (*saṃnipāta*) is contact (*saṃyoga*). The second [type] is that produced by the action of both [substances].
The third is also proclaimed to be of two kinds: that produced by action alone.
Of these, the first is impact (*abhighāta*) and propulsion (*nodana*), which is the cause of sound. (118)

"Third" means that the conjunction produced by conjunction (*saṃyogaja-saṃyoga*) would be the third; this is connected with what precedes. The first is *abhighāta* (impact); the second is called *nodana* (pushing). Thus ends the definition of conjunction.
The second [type of conjunction] would be the non-cause of sound; disjunction (*vibhāga*) also becomes threefold.
The first arises from a single action, while the other arises from two actions. ||119||
The third [type of disjunction] would be that produced by disjunction; this third type also becomes twofold:
that arising from the disjunction of the sole cause, and that arising from the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause.
(120) He defines disjunction as the specific cause for the cognition of "separated. [He states: "Disjunction..."
Regarding "a single action": its illustration, such as the disjunction between a hawk and a mountain, is to be understood as before.

The third [type of disjunction]—disjunction produced by disjunction—is also twofold: that produced by the disjunction of the cause alone, and that produced by the disjunction of the cause and its own cause. Regarding the first: where there is motion in one potsherd, then follows the disjunction of the two potsherds; then the destruction of the conjunction that originated the jar; then the destruction of the jar; then, by that very same disjunction of the potsherds, a disjunction of the moving potsherd from space is produced. Then follows the destruction of the conjunction with space, then the conjunction with a subsequent location, and finally the destruction of the motion.

Nor should it be argued that why that very action does not produce a disjunction from another location; for there is a contradiction between an action's producing a disjunction that opposes a constituent conjunction and its producing a disjunction that opposes a non-constituent conjunction. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the bursting open of a blooming lotus bud.

Therefore, if this [action] were to produce a disjunction that is the opposite of a non-productive conjunction, it would not produce a disjunction that is the opposite of a productive conjunction. Nor should it be asked: "Since the substance is destroyed by the very disjunction of its causes, why is a disjunction from another location not produced prior [to that destruction]? For as long as the substance exists, a disjunction from another location is impossible for a constituent part that possesses a disjunction which is the opposite of a productive conjunction.

First, consider the second case: where there is a division between the hand and the tree due to the action of the hand, there arises the cognition of a division in the body as well; however, in that case, the action of the hand is not the cause of the division between the body and the tree, because they reside in different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). Furthermore, there is simply no action in the body [at that moment].

Because the action of a whole is necessarily restricted by the actions of its parts, therefore, through the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause, the disjunction of the effect and the non-effect is produced. For this very reason, disjunction is a distinct quality (*guṇāntara*). Otherwise, there would be no cognition of "being separate" with respect to a body. Therefore, disjunction is not established as being otherwise [i.e., as a mere absence] through the destruction of conjunction. Thus ends the determination of disjunction (*vibhāga-nirūpaṇa*).
Remoteness (paratva) and proximity (aparatva) are proclaimed to be of two kinds:
spatial and temporal; however, spatial [remoteness and proximity] exist only in corporeal things. 121.

Remoteness (paratva) arises from the cognition of a greater number of conjunctions with corporeal objects, while nearness (aparatva) results from the cognition of their lesser number; so it has been stated. (122)
The non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa) for those two [cognitions] is the conjunction with space (dik-saṃyoga) residing in their substratum;
this arises from the cognition of the greater or lesser extent of the sun's movement.
Priority and posteriority, however, arise from the cognition of their relative proximity and distance.
In this case, however, the conjunction between time and the body would be the non-inherent cause. ||124||
The destruction of these [qualities] has been described as occurring through the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Now he defines distance and proximity (*paratva* and *aparatva*), which are the causes for the conventional usage of "prior" and "posterior. These are "distance" (*paratva*) and "proximity" (*aparatva*). Regarding "spatial" (*daiśika*): spatial distance arises from the cognition that [an object] is separated by a greater number of conjunctions with corporeal substances. Likewise, proximity arises from the cognition that it is separated by fewer such conjunctions. In this context, the ablative case is required to express the sense of a limit (*avadhi*), as in: "Prayāga is distant from Pāṭaliputra with respect to Kāśī," and "Prayāga is near from Pāṭaliputra with respect to Kurukṣetra. (121)

Of these two—namely, spatial priority (*daiśika-paratva*) and posteriority (*daiśika-aparatva*). "Non-inherent" means the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). "In their substratum" means in the substratum of spatial priority and posteriority. Regarding the word "divākara" (the sun): here, temporal priority and posteriority (*kālika-paratva-aparatva*) are to be understood. He whose solar motion is greater relative to another's solar motion is the elder; he whose is less is the younger. Temporal priority and posteriority exist only in produced substances (*janyadravya*). "Here" refers to temporal priority and posteriority. "Of them" refers to temporal and spatial priority and posteriority. ||123||124||
Thus concludes the determination of priority and posteriority.
The proliferation of conceptualization regarding cognition has already been examined for the most part. (125)
Now, another remaining method is being demonstrated.
He defines *buddhi* (intellect/cognition) as it follows in the sequence: "Of intellect...
Cognition is held to be of two kinds: invalid (*apramā*) and valid (*pramā*). (126)
When there is an absence of that [object], whatever cognition of it may arise is determined to be invalid (apramā).
Its elaboration is proclaimed to be error (viparyāsa) as well as doubt (saṃśaya). ||127||

Therein, he defines invalid cognition (*apramā*). "Lacking that" means that a cognition which has a particular feature (*tad-prakāraka*) as its object when that feature is absent (*tad-abhāvavati*) is an error (*bhrama*); this is the meaning. Its elaboration is the "elaboration of invalid cognition. ||125||126||127||

The first is the notion of a self in bodies, and the cognition of yellowness in conch shells and the like; that which takes the form of a certainty is [the first], whereas doubt is now demonstrated. (128)
The cognition "Is this a man or a post? and so forth is doubt;
a cognition that does not have the absence of that [object] as its qualifier is certainty, while one that has that [absence] as its qualifier is doubt. (129)

"Ādyaḥ" means "the opposite. It refers to that cognition which has the form of a certainty (*niścaya*) regarding the body and so forth, having "selfhood" as its qualifier; that certainty is an error (*bhrama*). "Kiṃsvit" is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). This concludes the definition of error and valid cognition (*pramā*).

He states the definition of certainty (*niścaya*): "In the absence of that... [verse 128/126]. Certainty is a cognition that does not have the absence of that [object] as its qualifier (*aprakāraka*), but rather has that [object] itself as its qualifier (*tatprakāraka*). Thus ends the exposition of certainty.
Doubt is that cognition which consists of both non-existence and existence regarding a single object.
He defines doubt: "That is doubt. The meaning is: doubt is a cognition whose modes (prakāra) are contradictory existence and non-existence with respect to a single substratum (dharmin).
The cognition of a common property (sādhāraṇadharma) and so forth is the cause of doubt. ||130||

Regarding the term "common" (*sādhāraṇa*): the knowledge of a property that is common to both [alternatives] is a cause of doubt. For example, having perceived height—which is common to both a post (*sthāṇu*) and a person—one doubts, "Is this a post or not? Similarly, the knowledge of an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is a cause; for example, because the property of being audible (*śabdatva*) is apprehended as being excluded from both the eternal and the non-eternal, one doubts regarding sound, "Is sound eternal or not? However, contradiction (*vipratipatti*), consisting of words such as "Sound is eternal or not," is not itself a cause of doubt.

This is because words, the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and so forth, have the inherent nature of producing only certainty (*niścaya*). However, in that case, the word produces a cognition of both alternatives; the doubt itself, however, is purely mental. Likewise, from doubt regarding the validity of a cognition arises doubt regarding the object. Similarly, it should be understood that from doubt regarding the pervaded (*vyāpya*) arises doubt regarding the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and so on. Nevertheless, in the case of doubt, the cause is either the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*) or the sensory contact with the locus (*dharmīndriya-sannikarṣa*). || 130 || Thus ends the definition of doubt.
A defect (doṣa) is the producer of invalid cognition (apramā), whereas a quality (guṇa) is the producer of valid cognition (pramā).
Defects are considered to be of various kinds, such as bile (pitta), distance, and so forth. (131)

Regarding the term "defect" (*doṣa*): a defect is the cause of invalid cognition (*apramā*), while a quality (*guṇa*) is the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*). Even in that regard, defects such as bile (*pitta*) and the like are not uniform; their causality is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, the fact that a quality produces valid cognition is established through inference (*anumāna*). For example: valid cognition is produced by a cause distinct from the general causes of cognition, because it is a produced cognition, just like an invalid cognition. Nor should it be argued that the mere absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) is the cause [of valid cognition].

Even in the case of the cognition "the conch is yellow," there would be the undesirable consequence that no valid cognition (*pramā*) of the conch's whiteness arises, because the defect of bile (*pitta*) is present; furthermore, since there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*), it is more reasonable to accept the quality (*guṇa*) as the cause rather than the absence of an infinite number of defects. Nor can it be argued that even when a quality is present, the cognition of whiteness does not arise in the conch due to the obstruction caused by bile, and therefore the absences of defects such as bile must necessarily be accepted as causes; for if that were so, what would be the point of postulating the quality as a cause?

Nevertheless, since the status of a quality (*guṇa*) as a cause is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is equally easy to state that the absence of a quality (*guṇābhāva*) is the cause with respect to error (*bhrama*). In response to the inquiry as to what those defects (*doṣa*) are, he says: "Bile," etc. The meaning is that defects which produce error are indeed non-uniform (*ananugata*): in some cases of an error regarding yellow and so forth, bile is the defect; in some cases of an error regarding the small size of the moon and so forth, distance is the defect; and in some cases of an error regarding a bamboo-snake, the application of frog-fat collyrium is the defect. ||131||
In perception, however, there is contact with the qualified object together with its qualifier; but in inference, on the other hand, it would be a quality. ||132||
In the case of inference, however, the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) regarding the subject as qualified by the probandum would be the instrumental cause;
whereas in the case of analogy, the cognition of similarity with respect to the object capable of being compared would be the instrumental cause. ||133||

In verbal cognition, either compatibility (yogyatā), intentionality (tātparya), or truth (pramā) would be the quality (guṇa); however, in this context, "truth" (pramā) is defined as a cognition distinct from error (bhrama). (134)

Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the excellences (*guṇas*) are, he demonstrates them in order, beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*). Regarding perception: the excellence in perception is the contact between the qualifier and the qualified object. In inference (*anumiti*), the excellence is the cognition of the presence of the pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyavaiśiṣṭyajñāna*) in that which possesses the probandum. The same should be understood for the subsequent cases as well.
Thus ends the section on the theory of validity (*prāmāṇyavāda*), specifically the theory of its production (*utpattivāda*).

Alternatively, that cognition which has as its qualificandum that which possesses the aforementioned mode is valid knowledge (*pramā*); indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), however, would be neither valid knowledge nor error. (135)
For that [definition] which is devoid of the nature of being a qualifier (*prakāratā*) and so forth does not comprehend the relation;
it defines valid cognition (*pramā*) as "that which is distinct from error. Now, one might object:

in a case where the cognition "these two are silver" arises with respect to a mother-of-pearl shell and silver, there would be no valid cognition even regarding the aspect of silver, because that cognition lacks the quality of being distinct from error. To this he says: "Alternatively" (*athavā*). The meaning is: valid cognition is a cognition which, while having that [object] as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyaka*), has that [property] as its qualifier (*tatprakāraka*). Now, if this were so, even memory (*smṛti*) would possess the status of valid cognition. If it is asked what follows from that, one might say: "If that were the case, the instrument (*karaṇa*) of such [memory] would also have to be a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). But this is not so.

This is because only that which produces a cognition of an object as it truly is (yathārthānubhava) is intended to be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, this must be understood: by whatever relation a thing possesses a certain property, the definition of valid knowledge must specify that the cognition has that very thing as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) with respect to that relation, and that it has that property as its qualifier (*prakāra*) with respect to that same relation. By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of a cognition of a jar in a potsherd by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth. If this were the case, indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) would not be valid knowledge, because it lacks the quality of having a qualifier; therefore, he says: "not [indeterminate] knowledge. Now, one might object: "In that case, the cognition of the conjunction of a monkey with a tree would be both an error (*bhrama*) and valid knowledge (*pramā*). This is not so.

Because the cognition of conjunction in that which possesses the absence of conjunction whose counter-positive is non-co-located [with it] is erroneous. Nor should it be argued that the cognition of conjunction in a tree, as delimited by the absence of conjunction with a monkey, would not be erroneous, since in that case the absence of conjunction is co-located with its counter-positive; for in that instance, the cognition of conjunction as delimited by the absence of conjunction is indeed erroneous. There is no harm in the definition being non-uniform even if the definiendum (the object to be defined) is non-uniform. Thus ends the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*).
Validity is not apprehended intrinsically, because otherwise doubt would be impossible. (136)

Regarding "validity" (*prāmāṇya*): the Mīmāṃsakas indeed maintain that validity is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*). In this regard, according to the view of the Guru (Prabhākara), because cognition is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), the validity of that cognition is grasped by that very [cognition]. According to the view of the Bhaṭṭas, cognition is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); rather, the "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) produced by cognition is perceptible, and by means of that, the cognition is inferred. According to the view of Murārimiśra, cognition is grasped by a subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*). In the view of all these [schools], however, the validity of that cognition is grasped by a cognition that has that [original] cognition as its object.

For knowledge is determined by its object; therefore, the object is known through the cognition of the cognition itself. He refutes that view, stating: "It is not apprehended by itself. [He explains: "In the case of doubt," etc. If the validity of a cognition were apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then there would be no doubt regarding the validity of a cognition occurring in a state of non-habituation.

For in that case, if the cognition is known, then according to your own view, its validity must also be known; so how can there be doubt? But if the cognition is not known, then, due to the absence of knowledge of the subject (*dharmijñāna*), how can there be doubt? Therefore, validity is to be inferred with respect to the cognition. For instance: "This cognition is valid, because it generates a successful activity; whatever is not so [valid] is not so, like an invalid cognition. This cognition, which has 'earth-ness' as its qualifier, is valid, because it is a cognition having 'water-ness' as its qualifier in a substrate possessing moisture."

Nor should it be asked how the knowledge of the cause arises; for the state of having "earth-ness" as its qualifier (*pṛthivītvaprakārakatva*) is graspable by itself (*svataḥ*), and since there is the apprehension of odor therein, the state of having that which possesses odor as its qualificandum (*gandhavadviśeṣyakatva*) is also easily grasped. Only the state of having that [odor] as its qualifier delimited by the state of having that [earth] as its qualificandum is not grasped, due to the necessity of accounting for doubt. Thus ends the section on the apprehension of validity (*jñaptivāda*) within the *Prāmāṇyavāda*.

Now, since all cognitions are in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), the qualification "having that [object] as its qualificandum" (*tadvad-viśeṣyakatva*) is redundant in the definition of valid knowledge (*pramā*). Nor should it be argued that, on your view, the activity of one seeking silver toward mother-of-pearl (*raṅga*) would not be produced by error, because for you there is no such thing as error; for in that case, the cause is simply the non-apprehension of the difference between the silver independently presented [to the mind] and the object before one, which is dependent upon a defect (*doṣa*). In the case of real silver, however, since a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*) exists, that alone is the cause; or let it be that even there, it is the non-apprehension of the difference from silver that is the cause.

That alone is the cause. Nor is the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) possible, because of the absence of the contact between the sense-organ and silver, which is the cause for the perception of silver; for otherwise, the cognition of silver in relation to a mother-of-pearl shell would be inexplicable. If it is argued that this is not so, because in the case of real silver, a specific cognition has been established as the cause of purposeful activity, and therefore it must be postulated elsewhere as well—then it should not be said that such a cognition is the cause only for successful activity, while non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) is the cause for unsuccessful activity.

Because its status as a cause is postulated merely for the sake of simplicity in producing [the cognition]. And thus, even if one assumes the "cognition-characterized" (jñānalakṣaṇa) proximity in order to account for the cognition of silver qualified by [the property of] being silver in the case of a piece of cloth, there is no fault; for a complexity that results from the nature of the effect is not a defect. Furthermore, in a case where the cognition "these two are silver and cloth" or "silver and cloth" has arisen with respect to a piece of cloth and silver, there is no sublation of the cause either.

Furthermore, in a case where there is the cognition "these are silver and mother-of-pearl" regarding both mother-of-pearl and silver, there would have to be simultaneous engagement with and withdrawal from both; for, according to your view, due to the fear of *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension), there is—precisely because of a defect—the non-apprehension of the difference between silver and mother-of-pearl in the case of mother-of-pearl, and the non-apprehension of the difference between mother-of-pearl and silver in the case of silver. Moreover, if the non-apprehension of difference were the cause of inference, then in a body of water, an inference [of fire] would be unavoidable due to the non-apprehension of the difference between it and smoke, which is pervaded by fire.

And if qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) were the cause [of inference], then, in accordance with the requirement for inference, the cognition of smoke as being pervaded by fire would necessarily arise even in the case of a red-hot iron ball (*ayogolaka*). Thus, this is a rope with a noose at both ends. And so, in the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), perception itself is the proof, based on the experience: "I know the silverness of the mother-of-pearl. This is the summary. (136) Thus ends the discussion on the theory of misapprehension.

The non-perception of deviation and likewise the perception of concomitance are [the means] for the grasping of pervasion in a reason; in some cases, reductio ad absurdum (tarka) serves to remove doubt. (137)

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) was stated previously, but the means for its apprehension was not shown; therefore, he shows it with the words "of deviation" (*vyabhicārasya*). The meaning is that the non-apprehension of deviation and the apprehension of concomitance (*sahacāra*) are the causes for the apprehension of pervasion. Since the apprehension of deviation acts as an obstacle to the apprehension of pervasion, its absence is a cause. Likewise, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the apprehension of concomitance is also established as a cause. However, repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is not the cause, because even upon a single observation, pervasion is sometimes apprehended provided there is no manifestation of deviation.
In some cases, repeated observation is useful by way of dispelling the suspicion of deviation. Thus concludes the determination of the means for grasping pervasion (vyāpti).

However, where suspicion does not depart even through repeated observation, a subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is required. For instance, if the suspicion arises that smoke might exist even in the absence of fire, then that suspicion is removed by the recognition of the causal relationship between fire and smoke: "If this [mountain] were not possessed of fire, it would not be possessed of smoke, because an effect cannot arise without its cause."

If one were to suspect that [an effect] might sometimes occur even without a cause—that is, that it would be entirely causeless—then that suspicion must be removed by means of *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum). For if an effect could exist without a cause, then for you there would be no necessity for the regular employment of fire for the sake of smoke, or of food for the sake of satiety. Where a suspicion does not arise of its own accord, there is no need for *tarka* at all. This is what was stated: "Tarka [is required] in some cases. (137)
Thus concludes the exposition on reasoning.
That which is a pervader of the probandum (sādhya) but likewise a non-pervader of the reason (hetu) is an extraneous condition (upādhi); its definition is now demonstrated. (138)

Now, [the author] defines the *upādhi* for the purpose of obstructing the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) belonging to another [party]. "Of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*) means: that which, while being the pervader of what is intended as the probandum, is not the pervader of what is intended as the probans.

Now, [one might object]: in the case of "He is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Mitrā," *śākapākajatva* (being produced by cooking vegetables) would not be a valid *upādhi*, since it lacks pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*). This is because dark complexion exists even in jars and other such things. Similarly, in the argument "Air is perceptible because it is the substratum of perceptible touch," *udbhūtarūpavattva* (possessing manifested color) would not be an *upādhi*, since perceptibility exists even in the self (*ātman*) and so forth, yet color is absent there. Likewise, in the argument "Destruction is perishable because it is produced," *bhāvatva* (existence as a positive entity) would not be an *upādhi*.

If it is argued that [the reason] is not over-pervasive because existence is present even in the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of perishability, and because in that case there is an absence of being an entity (*bhāvatva*), we say no; for the intended meaning is that [the counter-example] must be a pervader of the probandum as delimited by the property of existence (*saddharma*), while being a non-pervader of the prover as delimited by that same property (*taddharma*).

The state of being produced from the cooking of vegetables (*śākapākajatva*) is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the dark color (*śyāmatva*) as delimited by being the son of Mitrā, and it is a non-pervader (*avyāpaka*) of the probans (*sādhana*) as delimited by that same [sonship]. Similarly, in the case of "the external substance is perceptible because it is a substance," the possession of manifest color (*udbhūtarūpavattva*) is a pervader of perceptibility as delimited by being an external substance, and it is a non-pervader of the probans as delimited by being an external substance. Likewise, in the argument "destruction is perishable because it is produced" (*dhvaṃso vināśī janyatvāt*), one should understand that "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) is a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by being produced.

In a valid reason (*saddhetu*), however, there is no such property that could be a pervader of the probandum as delimited by a certain [condition] while being a non-pervader of the probans as delimited by that same [condition]. In a deviant reason (*vyabhicārin*), on the other hand, it is possible for a condition (*upādhi*) to be a pervader of the probandum as delimited by "being either of two things"—namely, the locus of the probandum which is the locus of the condition, and the locus which determines the deviation from the probandum while being devoid of the condition—and a non-pervader of the probans. ||138||
All conditions (upādhi) would be co-locus with the probandum (sādhyasamānādhikaraṇa), for they possess deviation from their own probandum within a single locus of the reason (hetu). (139)

For this very reason, he shows that the *lakṣya* (the object to be defined) is also of the nature of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), in accordance with this [definition]. He says: "all" (*sarva*). "By its own probandum" (*svasādhya*): "its own" (*sva*) refers to the limiting condition; "probandum" (*sādhya*) refers to the thing to be proven. The meaning is: "that which deviates from both its own [limiting condition] and its probandum. ||139||

The purpose of an *upādhi* (limiting condition) is the inference of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). He states the reason for the *upādhi*'s capacity to invalidate [an argument] with the words "of deviation. The meaning is that the purpose of an *upādhi* is the inference of deviation from the probandum (*sādhya*) based on its own deviation. For instance, where an *upādhi* is a pervader of the pure probandum, there [deviation is inferred] by means of the pure deviation of the *upādhi*.

Inference based on deviation from the probandum (*sādhyavyabhicārānumāna*): for example, in the case of "smoke-possessing [mountain] because of fire," one might argue that "fire deviates from smoke because it deviates from moist fuel. This is because wherever there is a deviation from the pervader (*vyāpaka*), a deviation from the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is necessary. However, where a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is a pervader of the probandum as delimited by some particular property (*dharma*), then in a locus possessing that property, one may infer a deviation from the probandum through the deviation of the limiting condition.

For example, in the argument "He is dark-complexioned because he is the son of Mitrā," the property of being Mitrā’s son is not an *upādhi* (limiting condition), because it is non-deviant from being dark-complexioned in the case of Mitrā’s son who was born from cooked vegetables (*śākapākaja*). However, a "different-from-the-pakṣa" (*pakṣetara*) that is inferred by sublation (*bādhānunnīta*) is indeed an *upādhi*, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish its pervasion of the probandum (*sādhya*), and because it would involve self-contradiction. On the other hand, a "different-from-the-pakṣa" that is inferred by sublation is certainly an *upādhi*.

For example, in the argument "Fire is not hot because it is produced," since the heat of fire is apprehended by perception, "being other than fire" (*vahnitaratva*) is a pseudo-restrictive condition (*upādhi*). However, when the pervasion of a pseudo-restrictive condition with the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) and so forth is doubted, that is a doubtful pseudo-restrictive condition (*sandigdhopādhi*). Nevertheless, even if it is a doubtful pseudo-restrictive condition, the "other-than-the-pakṣa" (*pakṣetara*) should not be pointed out, in accordance with the tradition of the debaters.

Some, however, maintain that the production of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) is the result of a limiting condition (*upādhi*). For instance, in the case of "the iron ball possesses smoke because it possesses fire," a counter-argument is possible: "the iron ball lacks smoke because it lacks moist fuel. Thus, in this way, a limiting condition may sometimes be pervasive even of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*). As in the argument, "ice is earth because it possesses solid contact," where the condition is "possessing a touch that is neither hot nor cold. Nor should it be said that in such cases the only defect is the lack of essential connection (*svarūpāsiddhi*), for in all instances a limiting condition involves a confusion with other types of defects.

And here they say that a limiting condition (*upādhi*) is that which pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) but does not reside in the subject (*pakṣa*). Thus concludes the definition of the limiting condition.
The authority of verbal testimony and comparison is not admitted as being separate [from that of perception and inference]. (140)
"Because its meaning is already understood through inference"—this is the view of the Vaiśeṣikas.

Regarding "of verbal testimony and comparison": in the view of the Vaiśeṣikas, perception and inference are the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, verbal testimony and comparison possess validity only by way of inference. For instance, sentences such as "Bring the cow with a stick" or Vedic sentences are preceded by a knowledge of the connection between the word-meanings recalled through their intended meaning (*tātparya*), because they are clusters of words possessing expectancy and so forth, like the cluster of words "Bring the jar."

Alternatively, these word-meanings possess mutual relations because they are presented by words possessing semantic competency (*yogyatā*) and so forth, like such word-meanings [already known]. In the case of the example as well, the probandum is established by means of another example. Thus, immediately after the perception of the individual gavaya, the word "gavaya" has "gavaya-ness" (*gavayatva*) as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because it is employed by elders there when no other basis for application exists.

And when no other basis for application exists, that which is employed by elders for a given object has that very thing as its basis for application, just as the word "cow" has "cowness" (*gotva*) as its basis for application.

Alternatively, by the inference "the word *gavaya* must have a basis for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), because it is a correct word," the fact that "being a *gavaya* (*gavayatva*)" is the basis for its application appears through the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
That is not correct, because [such] verbal and other cognitions occur even without the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). (141)

He refutes that view, stating: "That is not correct. For it is established by experience that verbal cognition occurs even without the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Indeed, there is no evidence for the existence of a knowledge of pervasion immediately following the hearing of words in every instance. Furthermore, one should consider this: if a knowledge of pervasion is postulated in every case of verbal cognition, then why not simply accept that verbal cognition itself occurs in every case of inference by postulating the knowledge of words? (140–141)
Thus concludes the examination of the separate validity of verbal testimony and analogy.
Inference is of three kinds based on the distinction of the purely positive (kevalānvayin);
however, it is of two kinds according to whether its pervasion (vyāpti) is positive (anvaya) or negative (vyatireka). ||142||

"Of three kinds": inference is indeed threefold, distinguished as purely positive (*kevalānvayin*), purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*), and positive-negative (*anvayavyatirekin*). Among these, the purely positive is that which lacks a negative instance (*asadvipakṣa*).
