For example, in such cases as "that which is knowable is expressible," and so forth; for there, because everything is indeed knowable, there is no absence of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). [Objection: But since all properties are excluded [from some things], how can the establishment of a purely positive inference be possible? [Reply: No, for if the property of being excluded were common to all things, then that very property would itself be purely positive.

Furthermore, *kevalānvayin* (purely positive) is that which is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of its own occurrence (*vṛtti*). This is well-established in cases such as the absence of ether (*gaganābhāva*). A *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative) is one for which there is no similar instance (*asatsapakṣa*). For example, "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor," and so forth. In that case, since the distinction from the thirteen [categories] beginning with water was previously unestablished, there is an absence of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) possessing a determined probandum (*sādhyavat*). An *anvayavyatirekin* (positive-negative) is one for which there exist both similar instances (*satsapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). For example, "It possesses fire because it possesses smoke," and so forth. In that case, because there exists a similar instance such as a kitchen (*mahānasa*) and a dissimilar instance such as a lake (*jalahrada*), [it is an anvayavyatirekin]. ||142||
Thus concludes the exposition of the threefold nature of inference.

The positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) has already been stated; now the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and so forth are being discussed. That which constitutes the pervasion of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) by the absence of the probans (*hetvabhāva*) is what is meant here. In that case of negative inference (*vyatirekin*), the cognition of negative concomitance is the cause; for that purpose, he defines negative concomitance as "the state of being the pervader of the absence of the probandum. This means: the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence that itself pervades the absence of the probandum. Here, this should be understood:

When, by means of a certain relation and in a certain form, the pervasion of one thing with respect to another delimited [thing] is apprehended, then from the cognition of the absence—delimited by that same relation and delimited by that same property—of that [pervading thing], there follows the establishment of the absence of that [pervaded thing], which is delimited by that same property and has a counter-positivehood delimited by that same relation. Thus, where the pervasion of "otherness" (itaratva) by the absence of smell is apprehended through a relation such as *viśeṣaṇatā* (qualifier-hood), there the absolute absence of otherness is established by means of the absence of the absence of smell.

However, where the pervasion of one thing by another is apprehended through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*), there the absence of that other is established through the relation of identity; this very [absence] is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Likewise, where the pervasion of fire by smoke is apprehended through the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), there the absence of smoke—qualified by the relation of conjunction—is established in a lake through the absence of fire, whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the relation of conjunction.
And in this case, the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) is the cause for the apprehension of negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*).

Some, however, maintain that it is only the positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*) that is apprehended through negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*), and not even the cognition of negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāptijñāna*) which serves as a cause. Where the apprehension of pervasion arises from negative concomitance, that is called "negative" (*vyatirekī*). They further assert that the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) occurs first in a jar or similar object, and is subsequently established as delimited by the nature of earth (*pṛthivītvāvacchedena*). ||143||
Thus concludes the examination of negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti).

Presumption (arthāpatti), however, is not accepted here as a separate means of valid cognition, because its purpose is already fulfilled by the cognition of negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyāpti). ||144||

Regarding "presumption" (*arthāpatti*): some maintain that presumption is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when it is known from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) that Devadatta lives for a hundred years, and it is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*) that he is not present in his house, then his presence outside is postulated because his hundred-year lifespan would otherwise be inexplicable. However, even that is not accepted [as a separate means], since its purpose is already served by inference (*anumāna*).

For instance, where it has been apprehended that "being alive" (jīvitva) is pervaded by either "being outside" (bahiḥsattva) or "being inside the house" (gṛhasattva), when the establishment of one of these two occurs, since "being inside the house" is sublated, "being outside" appears in the inference. Similarly, in cases such as "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," from the understanding that "fatness" (pīnatva) is pervaded by "eating" (bhojana), eating is established. And when daytime eating is sublated, nighttime eating is established.

Since the perception of non-existence (*abhāva-pratyakṣa*) is an empirical fact, non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is also not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, if non-apprehension were a cause while remaining unknown, it would follow that it is a form of perception because it does not employ cognition as its instrument; however, if it is a cause only when known, then there would be a requirement for another instance of non-apprehension to apprehend that [first] non-apprehension, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Likewise, even gesture (*ceṣṭā*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Because it functions as a reminder of the word that captures the convention, it shares the same nature as writing and the like, and is therefore subsumed under verbal testimony alone. However, where there is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, there is simply inference (*anumiti*).
Thus ends the refutation of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and the others.
Pleasure, which is desired by all people, arises from merit (*dharma*).
Suffering born of unrighteousness would be disagreeable to those possessed of consciousness.

He defines pleasure: "Pleasure, however, belongs only to the worlds. "Desirable" means the object of longing. "By virtue of dharma" means that there is a causal relationship between dharma (as the cause) and pleasure (as the effect). Thus ends the definition of pleasure.

He defines suffering (*duḥkha*). "Adharma" means that there is a causal relationship between being unrighteous (*adharmatva*) and being suffering (*duḥkhatva*). "Disagreeable" (*pratikūla*) means that by the very cognition of its nature as suffering, it becomes an object of natural aversion for everyone. ||145||
Thus concludes the exposition on suffering.
The desire for the state of being free from suffering and for happiness arises solely from the knowledge of those [states];
however, that desire would occur with respect to their means only if there were a cognition of those means as being conducive to what is desired. (146)

He defines desire (*icchā*). Regarding the phrase "freedom from suffering" (*nirduḥkhatve*): desire is indeed directed toward both a result (*phala*) and a means (*upāya*). The result, moreover, is either pleasure (*sukha*) or the absence of pain (*duḥkhābhāva*). Among these, the knowledge of the result is the cause of the desire for the result. For this very reason, it constitutes a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), according to its definition: "that which, being known, is desired as residing in oneself, is a human goal. The essential meaning is: being the object of a desire that is not dependent on another desire. The knowledge of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is the cause of the desire for the means. However, the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is a desire characterized by the mode of "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*).
The cause of that [desire] is the cognition that [the object] is a means to achieve a desired end, which is to be accomplished through volitional effort. (147)
The cognition that something is the cause of intense aversion would be an inhibitor [of activity].

"Desire to act" (*cikīrṣā*) is a desire whose object is that which is to be accomplished by an effort (*kṛti*), as is experienced in the thought, "I shall accomplish cooking by means of an effort. Regarding this desire to act, the knowledge that something is achievable through effort and the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end are the causes. "Its cause" refers to this.
For this very reason, there is no desire to act regarding rain and the like, because of the absence of the knowledge that it is achievable through effort. (147)

Regarding "powerful": the cognition that something is a powerful means to what is undesirable acts as an obstacle in that case; therefore, there is no desire to act toward eating food mixed with honey and poison. Others hold that powerful aversion itself is the obstacle.
Furthermore, according to some, the cognition that [the action] is not a cause for that [undesirable result] is the cause [of the desire to act]. (148)
The cognition that something is a means to what is disliked (*dviṣṭasādhanatābuddhi*) would be the cause of aversion (*dveṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "that being not the cause": the meaning is that the cognition that [an action] does not produce a powerful undesirable result (*balavadaniṣṭājanakatvajñāna*) is the cause in that case. (The underlying dissatisfaction with this view is shown by the fact that, according to some, there is no delay in the arising of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) even for one who possesses the cognition that an action is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) and lacks the cognition that it is a means to what is disliked, provided they lack the cognition that it produces a powerful undesirable result. || 148 ||
Thus ends the determination of desire.

He defines hatred (*dveṣa*). "The state of being a means to what is disliked" means that the cognition of something as a means to what is disliked is the cause of hatred directed toward a painful means. Furthermore, the cognition of it being a means to a powerful desired object acts as an obstacle; therefore, there is no hatred toward cooking and the like, which produce unavoidable suffering. Thus ends the definition of hatred.
Engagement, withdrawal, and likewise the cause of life. ||149||
Thus, the Tantrikas have proclaimed a threefold nature of effort: the desire to act, the performance of the action, and the cognition that it is a means to achieve a desired end. (150)

He defines effort (*yatna*). "And activity" (*pravṛttiśca*): the meaning is that effort is threefold, based on the distinction between the effort of engagement (*pravṛtti*), the effort of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), and the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni*). ||146||

Regarding the passage beginning with "cikīrṣā" (desire to act): the point is that in cases such as eating food mixed with honey and poison, there is no inclination to act because of the absence of desire to act, owing to the fact that [the action] is connected with a powerful undesirable consequence. Furthermore, some maintain that the knowledge of not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence—just like the knowledge that something can be accomplished by one's own effort—is also an independent cause for activity, as established through positive and negative concomitance.

The teachers maintain that the cognition of being an effect (*kāryatājñāna*) is the motivator (*pravartaka*). To explain: in the production of an inclination to act (*pravṛtti*), nothing other than the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) is required. And this desire is produced by the cognition that [the object] is achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*). This is because there is a rule that every desire is produced by a cognition whose object is its own qualifier (*svaprakārakadhī*). For the desire to act is a desire whose qualifier is "being achievable through effort. In that case, "being achievable through effort" is the qualifier; the cognition having that as its qualifier is the cause of the desire to act, and by means of that, it is the cause of the inclination to act.

However, the knowledge that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is not the cause in that case, because it is absent in the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*). Furthermore, it would follow that one would engage in action even toward what cannot be accomplished by effort (*kṛtyasādhya*). If it is argued that the knowledge that something cannot be accomplished by effort is an obstacle, we say no; for the knowledge that something can be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*) is simpler than the absence of that [obstacle]. Nor can both be causes, as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). If it is objected: "In your view as well, there would be the unwanted consequence of engaging in eating food mixed with honey and poison, or in bowing to a *caitya*, since the knowledge that these are 'to-be-done' (*kāryatājñāna*) exists," we say no.

This is because the cognition of "being a thing to be done" (*kāryatājñāna*), which is produced by the recollection of one's own qualification (*svaviśeṣaṇavattāpratisandhāna*), is the motivator [of action]. For in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) such as sacrifice or cooking, desire is one's own qualification. Consequently, from the cognition that something is a means to a desired end that is not followed by a powerful undesirable result, there arises the cognition of it being "to be done," and from that, activity (*pravṛtti*).

Furthermore, one who is satiated does not engage in eating, because at that time desire is no longer a qualification of the person (*puruṣaviśeṣaṇa*). In the case of obligatory rites (*nitya*), however, purity and so forth are qualifications of the person; therefore, activity toward them arises from the knowledge that they are to be accomplished by an effort dependent on the knowledge of purity and the like. Now, it might be argued: for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), let the cause be simply the knowledge of being a task (*kāryatājñāna*) qualified by the knowledge that it is a means to a desired end not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhīṣṭasādhanatājñāna*).

If it is argued that "the state of not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" means either (a) not producing a suffering greater than the suffering that is inseparable from the arising of the desired object, or (b) not producing a suffering that is the object of a powerful aversion—this is not so. For it is impossible to know simultaneously both "being a means to a desired end" (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) and "being achievable through effort" (*kṛtisādhyatva*), because being an effect (*sādhyatva*) and being a cause (*sādhanatva*) are contradictory. For that which is unestablished (*asiddha*) possesses the nature of being an effect, while that which is established (*siddha*) possesses the nature of being a cause. Furthermore, one and the same thing cannot be known at one time as both established and unestablished.
Therefore, both are known through a difference in time.

Not so; for by parsimony (*lāghava*), the cause [of action] is the cognition that something is to be accomplished by effort (*kṛtisādhyatā*) while being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhin*). Nor is there a contradiction between being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) and being a means (*sādhanatva*), because there is no contradiction between being an object to be accomplished and being a means at different times.

[The older Naiyāyikas say: "Sometimes [one acts] because of ignorance regarding the state of being an end (*sādhya*) and the state of being a means (*sādhana*). The Neo-Naiyāyikas (*navya*), however, maintain: "The cognition 'this is achievable by my effort' (*kṛtisādhya*) is not the motivator, because it is impossible to know such a thing regarding a future [action]. Rather, having reflected upon one's own similarity to a person for whom a certain [action] was seen to be achievable by effort, one engages in that [action]. Therefore, for one who desires rice, who knows it to be a means [to that desire], and who possesses the necessary implements, there arises an engagement in cooking after reflecting: 'Cooking is achievable by effort, and I am such a person.'"

That is not so; for [the desire] is absent during the engagement with one's own imagined scripts and the like in youth, as well as during sexual enjoyment and such activities. However, this must be understood: it is the present cognition of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) that prompts action. Therefore, a child does not engage in the future kingship of a crown prince, because at that time there is no cognition of its being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). Likewise, one who is satiated does not engage in eating.

At that time, one does not act because of the lack of knowledge regarding it being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*). Furthermore, one whose mind is corrupted by anger proceeds to consume poison and the like, because at that time there is a cognition that it is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). It should not be asked: "How can there be a cognition of non-concomitance with a powerful undesirable result in the case of an orthodox believer (*āstika*) engaging in forbidden sexual intercourse (*agamyāgamana*) or in acts such as killing an enemy? For the answer is: it is because the cognition of its being a means to hell (*narakasādhanatva*) is obscured by intense passion (*utkaṭarāga*) and the like. However, in the case of rain and similar phenomena, there is no desire to act (*cikīrṣā*) nor actual activity, due to the absence of the cognition that they are achievable through human effort (*kṛtisādhyatājñāna*).

However, [the meaning of the injunction] is merely the desire [to act], based on the cognition that [the act] is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*). And "effort" (*kṛti*) should be understood as being of the nature of an inclination (*pravṛtti*). Consequently, there is no inclination toward the movement of the five vital breaths (*prāṇapañcaka*), which is accomplished by the life-sustaining effort (*jīvanayoni-yantra*).

Thus, in accordance with its character as an instigator (*pravartakatva*), the meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is precisely its being a means to a desired end and so forth. And thus, in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," where no fruit is heard [in the text], heaven (*svarga*) is postulated as the fruit.

[Objection: But how can there be engagement [in action] in cases such as "one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) every day," since no desired result is established? Nor should it be said that the result is the attainment of the world of Brahmā or the absence of sin (pratyavāya), as mentioned in the explanatory passages (arthavāda). For if that were so, it would follow that because it is optional (kāmya), its obligatory nature (nityatva) would be lost; and furthermore, it would follow that one could fail to perform it in the absence of desire. Thus, where a mention of a result occurs, it is merely an arthavāda. [Reply: This is not so. Just as in the case of the *grahaṇa-śrāddha* and other rites, there is no contradiction between the status of being obligatory and the status of being occasional (naimittika), likewise there is no contradiction between the status of being obligatory and the status of being optional. Therefore, even when a result is mentioned, the rite remains both obligatory and optional.

Nor does the absence of desire lead to the non-performance [of the rite], because—as in the case of the recitation of hymns at the three times of day and so forth—it is simply assumed that a desire exists. If it is argued that activity is indeed possible through the knowledge of "task-ness" (*kāryatā*) as taught by the Veda, we say no; for without knowing that something is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), activity cannot occur even with a thousand such cognitions of task-ness. As for the claim that the fruit is the "merit of scholarship" (*paṇḍāpūrva*), that too is incorrect, because the consequence of non-performance due to the absence of desire remains the same. If one must assume a desire, then the fruit mentioned in the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) itself is what should be assumed, according to the logic of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice; otherwise, activity would be inexplicable.

Therefore, others consider that very non-arising to be the transgression. Thus: "Those who constantly perform the twilight worship, firm in their vows, go to the stainless world of Brahmā, their sins shaken off.
And so forth.

"Let him offer the *śrāddha* daily to the ancestors, bringing them satisfaction"—let the fruit [of this injunction] be precisely the attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and so forth, as established by such scriptural statements. Nor should it be argued: "How can the satisfaction of the ancestors be the fruit? For it is situated in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*). For, as in the case of the *śrāddha* at Gayā and elsewhere, it is sometimes postulated that the production of a fruit occurs through the very relationship of being the intended object (*uddeśyatva*). Therefore, it has been said: "The general rule (*utsarga*) is that the fruit shown by the scripture belongs to the performer of the rite."

If the ancestors have attained liberation, however, the fruit for oneself is heaven and so forth, because it is generally postulated that the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites has heaven as its fruit. Furthermore, engagement for the sake of *paṇḍāpūrva* (the unseen merit of learning) is not possible; for that is not happiness, since it lacks the status of a fruit due to its lack of being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in itself, nor is it a means to such a goal.

If it is asked how there can be engagement [in obligatory rites] when no transgression arises, the answer is as follows: namely, when the obligatory rite (*nitya*) is performed, the absence of transgression persists; in its absence, that [absence] is absent. Thus, since the presence of the absence of transgression entails the presence of the antecedent non-existence of suffering (*duḥkha-prāgabhāva*), and its absence entails its absence, it is equally easy to state that the cause common to both acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*) applies even to the antecedent non-existence of suffering. In this very same way, expiation (*prāyaścitta*) also functions as a cause for the antecedent non-existence of suffering.

Objection: In the case of "one should not eat *kalañja*," how can there be a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) with the meaning of the injunction? This is because it is impossible to convey either the absence of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*) or the absence of being achievable through effort (*kṛtisādhyatva*). Response: No. In that context, due to sublation (*bādha*), being a means to a desired end and being achievable through effort are not the meanings of the injunction; rather, the meaning is merely the absence of being connected to a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*). And the absence of that [undesirable connection] is conveyed by the negative particle.

Alternatively, the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is "being achievable through effort while being a means to a desired end that is not followed by a powerful undesirable consequence. The absence of this [meaning], conveyed by the negative particle (*nañ*), is a qualified absence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*); when it resides in that which possesses the qualificandum (*viśeṣyavat*), it ultimately rests upon the absence of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇābhāva*). Now, one might object: how can "not being followed by a powerful undesirable consequence" be the meaning of the injunction in the case of "One who desires to perform malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) should sacrifice with the Śyena"? For the Śyena is a violent act (*hiṃsā*)—being an operation conducive to death—and as such, it is a cause for hell. Nor should it be argued that because it is Vedic (*vaidha*), it is not prohibited; for there are scriptural instructions regarding expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for malevolent magic.

It should not be argued that if *hiṃsā* (harming) were merely any activity conducive to death, then it would follow that a swordsmith or a well-digger are also perpetrators of harm, and furthermore, one who dies from eating food stuck in the throat would incur the sin of having killed oneself. This is because [the definition] includes "having death as its intended object" (*maraṇoddeśyakatva*) as a qualifying attribute. If it is argued that for a Brāhmaṇa whose death was caused by an act directed toward another purpose, there is an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed by scripture, we say no; for in those cases, the meaning of the injunction does not include the absence of connection with a powerful undesirable consequence (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*).

In reality, to exclude the *śyena* sacrifice, the definition must be qualified by the condition "not having the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) as its intermediary. For this very reason, acts such as the worship of Śiva performed for the purpose of dying in Kāśī do not constitute violence (*hiṃsā*). Nor should it be argued that only that which directly produces death is violence, whereas the *śyena* is not such [a direct producer], but rather its produced *apūrva* (unseen force) is;
for if that were so, then when a Brāhmaṇa dies from a series of wound-infections following a sword-strike, the act would fail to be classified as violence.

However, some say that the result of the *śyena* sacrifice is injury (*hiṃsā*), not death; therefore, the meaning of the term "malevolent rite" (*abhicāra*) is the injury consisting of a sword-strike or the like produced by the *śyena*. Since that [injury] generates sin, even though the *śyena* itself does not generate sin because it is prescribed by the Veda, virtuous people do not engage in it after reflecting upon the subsequent sin.

The teachers, however, maintain that the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) is the intention of a trustworthy person (*āpta*). Just as in expressions such as "one should cook," the optative suffix (*liṅ*) alone denotes a desire in the form of a command and so forth, it is simpler to hold that the optative suffix alone denotes desire. Thus, in cases such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*), the meaning is that the sacrifice is desired by a trustworthy person as something to be accomplished by the effort of one who desires heaven. Consequently, having inferred that [the act] is a means to a desired end because it is desired by a trustworthy person, people proceed to act; whereas they do not proceed to act in the case of eating *kalañja* and the like, because that [intention of a trustworthy person] is absent.

As for one who does not accept the human authorship of the Veda, for such a person, the injunction itself serves as the proof of its connection with a person, like the embryo of the maiden of Śruti. Nor is the non-remembrance of an author a subverting argument, because from the time of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others up to the present day, the remembrance of an author is indeed perceived. Otherwise, it would follow that even the Smṛtis would be without authors. If it is argued that there is remembrance of an author only in those cases [of the Smṛtis], then in the Veda as well, there is certainly remembrance of an author in passages such as, "From him the meters were born."
In the same way, it should also be understood that "in each Manvantara, this Veda is ordained in another form.
As it is said: "This Lord Veda was sung by the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) in the past;
from Śiva down to the sages, they are its rememberers, not its creators."

This, however, is merely a praise of the Veda. Nor should it be argued that its lack of authority would follow from the possibility of error and so forth if it were of human origin; for it is free from defects due to being eternally omniscient. For this very reason, because error and so forth are possible in other persons, Kapila and others cannot be the authors of the Veda. Furthermore, since the non-eternality of the phonemes will be stated later, the non-eternality of the Veda as a composition of them follows all the more clearly. || 150 ||
And perception of the means of attainment (upādāna) would be the producer of activity;
whereas cessation [of activity] would arise from aversion, provided there is the cognition that it is a means to what is disliked.
Effort, however, which is the source of life-force (jīvanayoni), would always be beyond the senses (atīndriya).
That is proclaimed to be the cause for the movement of the vital breaths within the body. ||152||
Regarding the phrase "of the substrate" (*upādānasya*): it refers to the substrate (*samavāyikāraṇa*), which is the manifest cause (*adhyakṣa*) of the activity.

Regarding "cessation" (*nivṛtti*): the point is that through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the cognition of something as a means to what is disliked (*dviṣṭasādhanatājñāna*) is the producer of cessation directed toward objects that are means to suffering. ||151||

Regarding "effort" (*yatna*): the effort that is the source of life (*jīvanayoni-yatna*) persists as long as one lives, and it is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). He states the proof for this: "In the body," etc. For the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), such as excessive breathing and so forth, is accomplished through effort. Thus, by inference, all movement of the vital breath is established as being produced by effort; and since perceptible effort is ruled out [in this case], the existence of an imperceptible effort is proven. That very thing is the effort which is the source of life. (152) Thus ends the definition of effort.
Weight is beyond the reach of the senses; however, it exists in two [substances], earth and the rest.
It is non-eternal in what is non-eternal, and is declared to be eternal in what is eternal. (153)
That very [fluidity] would be the non-inherent cause in the action called falling; furthermore, fluidity is of two kinds: natural (sāṃsiddhika) and incidental (naimittika). 154.
The innate [color] exists in water; the second [type] exists in earth and fire.
In the case of water-atoms, it is eternal, while in other cases, it is held to be non-eternal. (155)
Gravity in gold, clarified butter, and the like is occasional (*naimittika*), arising from conjunction with fire. [The author] defines gravity as being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

It is non-eternal (*anitya*) in substances such as dyads (*dravyaṇuka*) and so forth; that is, gravity is non-eternal in the case of the non-eternal. It is eternal (*nitya*) in the eternal—namely, in the atom (*paramāṇu*). The term "gravity" (*gurutva*) carries over [from the previous verse]. ||153||
That [quality]—gravity—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*). "In falling" means in the initial fall. Thus ends the definition of gravity.

He defines fluidity (*dravatva*). "Innate" (*sāṃsiddhika*) means that fluidity is of two kinds: innate and incidental (*naimittika*). Regarding "in the atom": fluidity is eternal in the water-atom; elsewhere—in earth-atoms and so forth, as well as in water-dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth—fluidity is non-eternal. ||122||

In some cases, such as fire, and in some cases, such as earth, there is occasional (naimittika) fluidity. What, then, is the meaning of "occasional"? He shows this by saying "occasional" (*naimittikam*). The word "fire" (*vahnau*) signifies light (*tejas*). Thus, occasional fluidity is that which is produced by conjunction with light. And its meaning is that it exists in light in the form of gold and the like, and in earth in the form of ghee, lac, and so forth.
Fluidity is the cause of flowing; however, it is the cause of cohesion [in solids]. (156)
Viscosity exists in water; it is eternal in the atom and non-eternal in the composite whole.
Due to its excellence within oil, it serves as a favorable condition for fire. (17)
The varieties of *saṃskāra* are momentum (*vega*), elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), and mental impression (*bhāvanā*).
Momentum exists only in corporeal substances; it is produced by action and, in some cases, produced by momentum itself. (158)

"Fluidity is the cause of flowing"—this means it is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). Regarding "in cohesion" (*saṃgrahe*): this refers to a specific kind of conjunction, such as that between barley flour and water. That [fluidity]—namely, fluidity accompanied by viscidity (*sneha*)—should be understood [as the cause]. Therefore, there is no cohesion through mere fluidity, such as that of molten gold and the like. ||156||
Thus concludes the determination of fluidity.

He defines viscidity (*sneha*). "Viscidity is water" means that it exists only in water. This refers to viscidity. Now, an objection is raised: "But viscidity is also perceived in oil, which belongs to the earth; yet this [viscidity] is not aqueous. If it were so, it would follow that it would be antagonistic to fire. To this he replies: "In oil, etc. Due to its excellence—that is, due to the excellence of the viscidity—viscidity perceived even in oil is indeed aqueous; because of its intensity, it is favorable to fire. The point is that water with deficient viscidity destroys fire. (157) Thus ends the definition of viscidity.

He defines *saṃskāra* (impression/disposition). Regarding the term *saṃskāra*: the meaning is that *saṃskāra* is of three kinds, due to the distinction between velocity (*vega*), elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*), and mental impression (*bhāvanā*). Regarding "merely from motion" (*martyamātra*): the meaning is that velocity is of two kinds, due to the distinction between that produced by action (*karmaja*) and that produced by velocity itself (*vegaja*). For in the case of an arrow and so forth, velocity is produced by the action generated by an impulse (*nodana*). By that [velocity], the preceding action is destroyed, and then the subsequent action [occurs]. It is the same for what follows as well. And without velocity, since action would be an obstacle to further action, the destruction of the preceding action and the production of the subsequent action would not occur.
That velocity which is produced in a jar when it is struck by a rapidly moving potsherd is called "velocity-born" (vegaja) velocity. ||158||
The impression of elasticity (sthitisthāpaka-saṃskāra) exists in earth; some maintain it exists in all four [elements].
It is to be understood as beyond the senses, and in certain cases, it is also the cause of motion. (159)

Regarding the term *sthitisthāpaka* (elasticity): it is so called because it is the cause of the restoration to the original state of things such as branches that have been pulled, once they are released. "Some" refers to the fact that some maintain that elasticity exists in the four elements beginning with earth; the sense is that this [view] lacks authoritative proof. "This" refers to elasticity. "In some cases" refers to pulled branches and the like. ||156||

The mental impression (saṃskāra) known as cultivation (bhāvanā), which resides in the living being and is beyond the reach of the senses, has as its cause a certain conviction that is not of the nature of indifference. (160)

Regarding the phrase "called cultivation" (*bhāvanākhya*): since a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) cannot arise from a cognition consisting of equanimity (*upekṣā*), it is stated that [the cause] is "not of the nature of equanimity. Since a mental impression does not arise from doubt, it is stated that it must be a "certainty" (*niścaya*). Therefore, its causality consists in being a certainty other than equanimity. Consequently, there is no recollection in cases such as equanimity. If it is argued that, in this way, let the causality toward a mental impression be simply by way of being a cognition (*jñānatva*), we say no. Because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamanāviraha*), it is established that causality toward a mental impression is indeed by way of being a certainty other than equanimity.

Furthermore, because it is cumbersome to postulate a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the case of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because it has already been established that the cause for a latent impression is a certainty other than equanimity. ||160||
This [latent impression] is said to be the cause of both recollection and recognition.

He shows the proof for this by saying "in recollection. Since that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) generates both recollection and recognition, a latent impression is postulated; for without an operation, the prior experience lacks the capacity to produce recollection and so forth, since causality is impossible in the absence of either its own nature or its operation. Nor should it be argued that if each respective latent impression is the cause of recognition, then recognition—being produced by a latent impression—would necessarily be a form of memory (*smṛti*). This is because the reason provided is not decisive (*aprayojakatva*).

Others, however, maintain that since recognition does not arise from a non-awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*), and given the requirement for an awakened latent impression as a cause, it is more reasonable to postulate that the respective remembrances themselves are the causes of recognition.
Thus ends the examination of latent impressions.
Dharma and adharma would be the unseen force (adṛṣṭa); dharma is the cause of heaven and so forth. ||161||

That activity consisting of bathing in the Gaṅgā, performing sacrifices, and so forth, is what has been described. He defines the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as "dharma and adharma. The meaning is that *dharma* is the means for all pleasures such as heaven, as well as for the body and other instruments that serve as the means for attaining heaven. ||161||

To demonstrate the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in this regard, he says: "from sacrifice" (yāgāt). For it is by virtue of being an activity such as sacrifice that dharma is postulated. Otherwise, because sacrifices and the like perish long ago and are devoid of activity, they could not produce heaven which occurs at a later time. As the Teacher has said: "An action that has long since perished is not capable of yielding a fruit without an extraordinary potency (atiśaya)."

[Objection: But surely the very destruction of the sacrifice (*yāga*) could be the operation (*vyāpāra*). Nor can it be argued that there is no causal efficacy between a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and its destruction in one and the same locus, for there is no evidence that this is the case everywhere. Furthermore, you cannot claim that there would be an infinity of results in your view, whereas in my view there is not, because the final result destroys the *apūrva*. This is not so, because a specific time (*kāla-viśeṣa*) acts as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*). To this he says: "Gaṅgā-snāna... [and so on].

For if bathing in the Gaṅgā were the producer of heaven, rather than postulating an infinite number of conjunctions with water and their subsequent destructions as the operations, one single *apūrva* is postulated due to parsimony (*lāghava*); such is the sense.
This [karma] is considered to be destroyed by contact with the waters of Karmanāśā and other such means. ||162||

[Objection: Let it be granted then that even destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is not an operation (*vyāpāra*). Nor should it be asked how something that is devoid of operation and has long since perished can possess causality; for the property of being a necessary antecedent that is not otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddhaniyatapūrvavartitva*) exists there as well. Indeed, the causality of the contact of the eye and so forth consists in their being immediate antecedents, but this is not the case everywhere—just as the causality of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) consists in its existing at the time of the effect. To this, he says: "By the destruction of the action" (*karmanāśa*).

For if the *apūrva* did not exist, then dharma could not be subject to destruction by means such as contact with the waters of the Karmanāśā river; for it is impossible for that [contact] to effect the destruction or obstruction of a sacrifice (*yāga*) and so forth, since that [sacrifice] has already ceased to exist long before.

By this, the view that the mere pleasure of the deity is the fruit [of religious acts] is refuted. This is because the pleasure of a deity is impossible in all cases such as bathing in the Gaṅgā; and even if the deity were sentient, such pleasure would not be the intended object [of the act]. Furthermore, since pleasure is by nature happiness (*sukha*), it is impossible for it to exist in the "pleasure of Viṣṇu" and similar expressions, because produced happiness and the like do not exist therein. Therefore, by the term "pleasure of Viṣṇu," heaven and other such results—which are desired by others to be produced by the pleasure of Viṣṇu—are actually meant. (162)
Adharma is the cause of rebirth in hell and other such states, born from censurable actions;
it is destroyed by expiatory rites and the like. These two qualities, however, are functions of the individual soul (jīva). ||163||

"Adharma is the cause of hell and so forth. This means that adharma is the means for producing all sufferings, such as the pains of hell, as well as the hellish bodies and other such states. He states the proof [for this]: "By expiation," etc. For if adharma did not exist, then its capacity to be destroyed by expiation and the like would not exist. The point is that it is impossible for those [acts] to effect the destruction or the obstruction of acts such as the killing of a Brahmin, because [the act] has already perished prior to that. "In the living [soul]," etc.; the point is that this is because the Lord lacks both dharma and adharma. ||163||
But these two, produced by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), perish even through cognition.
Sound consists of both *dhvani* and *varṇa*; *dhvani* arises from drums and similar instruments. (164)

The phonemes beginning with *ka* are considered to be produced by the conjunction of the throat and other articulatory organs; every sound resides in space (*nabhas*), but it is perceived only when it has arisen within the range of the auditory organ. (165)
Their arising is proclaimed to follow the analogy of waves upon ripples;
however, according to the view of some, their arising follows the analogy of the Kadamba flower bud. (166)
The notion of impermanence consists in the cognition, "Who has arisen? Who has perished?
whereas the cognition, "This is that very same person," relies upon a commonality of genus (sājātya). (167)

These two are merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*); "residual impression" (*vāsanā*) refers to these. Therefore, the sense is that even when performed by a person of knowledge (*jñānin*), good and evil deeds are not capable of yielding fruit. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even from knowledge," the inclusion of [the exhaustion of] experience (*bhoga*) is intended. Now, one might object: How can the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) be the destroyer of merit and demerit? This would contradict the scriptural statement: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of eons unless it has been experienced. If it is argued that, for those possessing the knowledge of reality, all karma is exhausted through experience by means of a sudden manifestation of multiple bodies (*kāyavyūha*), we say: no.

In this regard, experience (*bhoga*) serves as an indicator of the destruction of [karma] as understood through the Vedas. Otherwise, how could there be the destruction of karmas through such means as expiation (*prāyaścitta*)? As it has been said: "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all karmas to ashes," and so forth; and it is heard in scripture: "And his karmas are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen."

[Objection: "In that case, for one who possesses the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*), there should be no persistence of the body nor experiences such as pleasure and pain, because all karmas are destroyed by that knowledge. [Reply: This is not so, because only those karmas other than *prārabdha* (commenced) are destroyed. For that karma which generates the experience of this particular body is indeed *prārabdha*. It is with reference to this alone that the scriptural statement "what has not been experienced [is not exhausted]" is intended. Thus concludes the exposition of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
He defines sound: "Sound is [of two kinds], articulated sound (dhvani) and [the phoneme] itself.
(163) It exists in space, meaning it is inherent in ether (ākāśa). He says "by the sense of hearing" because a sound located at a distance is not perceived. (165)

[Objection: But how can sound, which has arisen limited by a drum or similar object, be produced in the auditory organ? To this he says: "Like ripples" (*vīcī*). By the first sound, another sound is produced limited to the ten directions outside; by that very sound, yet another is produced which pervades it. In this sequence, that which has arisen in the auditory organ is perceived. [Regarding the term] "like the Kadamba flower" (*kadamba*): the sense is that from the first sound, ten sounds arise in the ten directions, and from those, ten other sounds arise. This is stated according to the opinion of some, because in this alternative there is a heaviness of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*). ||166||

[Objection: But since sound is eternal, how can there be its production? To this he says: "produced" (*utpanna*). The meaning is that sounds are impermanent because they possess the qualities of arising and perishing. [Objection: But the eternity of sounds is established by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) such as "this is that very same letter *ka*"; thus, the notions of production and destruction are merely errors. To this he says: "this is that *ka*. In that case, the object of recognition is similarity to that [previous instance], not the non-difference of the individual entity itself, for that would contradict the aforementioned cognition.
And thus, neither of the two cognitions is an error. (167)
[Objection: But where has it been seen that "sameness of class" (*sajātīyatva*) appears in the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "this is that very same [thing]"? To this he says:
"Because it is observed even in the case of things belonging to the same class, as in 'that same medicine,' etc.;
therefore, all phonemes (*varṇa*) are indeed non-eternal—this is our view. (168)
Thus ends the *Kārikāvalī* composed by Śrī Viśvanātha Pañcānana.
